Bahadur Shah I (Shah Alam I) — Later Mughal period begins; diminishing authority

Farukhsiyar — 1st to fatally extend Ijaradari into royal Khalisa lands; collapse of Emperor's social contract

only Hyderabad (under Nizam24-48) stays outside Maratha control
Peshwa Bajirao20-40 marches to Delhi — plunders capital; briefly holds Md. Shah19-48 as prisoner

Treaty of Bhopal (ToBhopal1738) — Marathas receive legal recognition of control over all lands between Chambal & Narmada + Subah of Malwa
Mughal emperor comes under formal Maratha protection (Maratha Protectorate) — protector becomes protected; emperor accepts Maratha military guardianship against Afghan invasions
Marathas install Alamgir II54-59 as puppet emperor — Mughal ruler chosen by former enemies; emperor now a figurehead

Nadir Shah's invasion — Persian emperor; Mughal weakness + factionalism made victory easy Battle of Karnal — Mughal army routed; Sadat22-39 (Nawab of Awadh) captured; Mir Bakshi dies fighting; Nizam24-48 appointed Mir Bakshi; negotiates Rs 50 lakh settlement to keep Nadir Shah out of Delhi
Sadat22-39 defects — disgruntled at Nizam24-48 being made Mir Bakshi; convinces Nadir Shah to attack Delhi for bigger plunder
Delhi falls — Md. Shah19-48 imprisoned; Nadir Shah rules as emperor of Delhi for 60 days
POLITICAL blow: Md. Shah19-48 publicly humiliated; could not defend his own dignity -> Mansabdars saw emperor unworthy of defence
SOCIAL blow: Nadir Shah's forces massacre ~2 lakh civilians of Delhi -> whatever social legitimacy remained evaporated
MILITARY blow: State that cannot defend its capital invites further challenges -> directly encouraged 1st Afghan Invasion of 1748 by Ahmed Shah Abdali
ECONOMIC blow: ~100 crore rupees extracted; Peacock Throne + Kohinoor diamond taken; Mansabdars forced to contribute personal wealth; empire (already in Jagirdari crisis) loses means to rebuild army
TECHNOLOGICAL blow: resources that could have funded military reform gone -> technology gap with Europeans locked in permanently
Sadat22-39 commits suicide — insulted by Nadir Shah after victory instead of rewarded
Nizam24-48 leaves Delhi permanently — final signal of terminal imperial collapse
1st Afghan Invasion by Ahmed Shah Abdali — directly encouraged by Nadir Shah's 1739 demonstration of Mughal military weakness

former enemies. By 1754 he is installed by them. Decline = simultaneous collapse across all five pillars.
Prelims Alert (2003): Shah Alam II60-06 spent initial years of reign away from Delhi — reason was fear of his own Wazir
(Imad-ul-Mulk), NOT fear of foreign invasion from the North-West frontier.

Bijapur — Adil Shahi Dynasty
Golconda — Qutb Shahi Dynasty
Battle of Talikota — 4-Sultanate alliance (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar) destroys Vijayanagar army; empire continues till 1646 but real power ends here
Vijayanagar Empire formally ends; Bijapur & Golconda conquer & divide Carnatic between themselves
Chhatrapati Shivaji74-80 reigns Shivaji74-80 captures Gingee Fort from Bijapur
Chhatrapati Sambhaji80-89 reigns Aurangzeb58-07 annexes Bijapur — Carnatic comes under Mughal rule
Aurangzeb58-07 annexes Golconda — entire Carnatic under Mughals; Mughals organize southern lands into Hyderabad Subah
Aurangzeb58-07 executes Chhatrapati Sambhaji80-89; next Chhatrapati Rajaram89-00 (1689–1700) makes Gingee his base against Mughals

Mughals finally capture Gingee Fort

phases.label: BENGAL SUCCESSOR STATE — MQK17-27 TO EIC (1700–1765)

events.label: MQK17-27 (Murshid Quli Khan) begins as Diwan of Bengal — starts building revenue base

MQK17-27 elevated to Mansab of Nazim of Bengal Subah — already holding Diwan post; combines finance + executive; Akbar's checks & balances ended; 1st Successor State formed; tribute still sent to Delhi but appointments now paper formality
MQK17-27 dies — by this point 15 intermediary zamindars collecting 50% of Bengal's land revenue

Shuja-ud-din Md Khan rules Bengal — appoints Jagat Seth as Treasurer of Bengal + Daroga of Royal Mint (central bank + personal banker of Nawab in one family) Safdar Jung39-54 — nephew + son-in-law of Sadat22-39; Deputy Governor of Awadh, then Subahdar Alivardi Khan40-56 overthrows & kills sitting Nawab Sarfaraz Khan39-40 with Jagat Seth's backing; pays Emperor Md. Shah19-48 one crore rupees + Sarfaraz's personal wealth for formal approval — emperor reduced to transactional figure

Alivardi Khan40-56 — Nawab of Bengal Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur raids Bengal repeatedly — Alivardi40-56 cannot defeat him Settlement with Raghuji Bhonsle — Bhonsle receives annual Chauth of Bengal & Bihar + direct control of Orissa; Alivardi40-56 stops sending revenue to Delhi + stops seeking imperial approval for appointments → Bengal's virtual break complete
Siraj-ud-Daula56-57 — last independent Nawab of Bengal (grandson of Alivardi40-56 from daughter) Battle of Plassey (BoPlassey1757) — EIC installs Mir Jafar as puppet Nawab

Mir Jafar (1st stint) — EIC-installed Nawab of Bengal Mir Qasim60-63 — Nawab of Bengal (Jafar's son-in-law) Mir Jafar restored (2nd stint) Bengal's Diwani (revenue & civil administration) passes to EIC

phases.label: AWADH SUCCESSOR STATE — SADAT22-39 TO EIC ANNEXATION (1722–1856)

events.label: Sadat Ali Khan (Sadat22-39) appointed Subahdar of Awadh — reward for suppressing local revolts; installs nephew + son-in-law Safdar Jung39-54 as Deputy Governor; own loyalist as Diwan; tribute to Delhi reduced; Awadh Successor State founded
Sadat22-39 convinces Nadir Shah to attack Delhi (angered that Mir Bakshi Mansab went to Nizam24-48 instead of him); commits suicide after being insulted by Nadir Shah post-victory
Safdar Jung39-54 — succeeds as Subahdar of Awadh Safdar Jung39-54 appointed Wazir by Ahmad Shah Bahadur48-54; misuses office to annex Farukhabad into Awadh

Safdar Jung39-54 forced to resign as Wazir (other Mansabdars oppose Farukhabad annexation) — Awadh's virtual break: no more revenue to Delhi, no imperial authority inside Awadh; though legally still part of empire
Shuja-ud-Daula54-75 — Subahdar of Awadh; appointed Wazir by Shah Alam II60-06 3rd Battle of Panipat — Shuja54-75 fights alongside Ahmad Shah Abdali
Battle of Buxar (BoBuxar1764) — Shuja54-75 defeated by EIC
EIC annexes Awadh — last Nawab: Wajid Ali Shah

phases.label: HYDERABAD SUCCESSOR STATE — NIZAM24-48 TO NIZAM-ALI-KHAN (1712–1803)

events.label: Zulfiqar Khan becomes Wazir under Jahandar Shah12-13
Zulfiqar Khan executed (Feb 1713)
Turani + Irani groups remove Sayyid Brothers — formally restore imperial authority; Nizam-ul-Mulk24-48 leads Turani group

Nizam-ul-Mulk24-48 serves as Wazir @ Delhi; simultaneously Subahdar/Governor of Hyderabad — tries to redistribute Jagirs to diffuse Jagirdari crisis; bigger Mansabdars resist Nizam-ul-Mulk24-48 (Chin Qulich Khan / Asaf Jah I) defeats Mubariz Khan (sitting Nazim of Deccan) — Hyderabad Successor State founded; 3rd Successor State
Nizam24-48 defeated by Marathas — forced to pay Chauth + Sardeshmukhi (10% hereditary Maratha claim in Deccan)
Nizam24-48 defeated by Marathas again — forced to pay Chauth + Sardeshmukhi again

Nizam24-48 serves as Mir Bakshi during Nadir Shah's invasion; negotiates Rs 50 lakh settlement; Sadat22-39 defects → Delhi sacked Nizam24-48 leaves Delhi permanently — gives up on reforming the centre; moves to Hyderabad; departure = signal of terminal imperial collapse
Nizam-ul-Mulk24-48 (Asaf Jah I) dies — by this point emperor's sovereignty over Hyderabad purely symbolic (name on coins + Friday Khutba only; zero influence over war, peace, treaties, appointments)
Nazir Jung — Hyderabad Muzaffar Jung — Hyderabad (3 months only) Salabat Jung51-62 — Hyderabad; French dominated under Bussy Nizam-Ali-Khan — Hyderabad
Saadatullah Khan appointed Nawab of Carnatic by Mughal Emperor — last direct imperial appointment to Carnatic

Saadatullah Khan — Nawab of Carnatic; moves capital from Gingee to Arcot; makes post hereditary in family (adopts nephew Dost Ali as heir — without imperial approval); Carnatic still nominally under Nizam Dost Ali Khan — Nawab of Carnatic (adopted nephew of Saadatullah Khan) Dost Ali Khan killed by Marathas under Raghuji Bhonsle @ Chittoor district (near Tamil Nadu border)
Nizam appoints Anwar-ud-din Khan as new Nawab of Carnatic — ends dynastic rule of Saadatullah Khan's family

anchors: Key Pattern — Common 5-Step Formation across all Successor States: (1) Extract Mansab of Subahdar → (2) End Akbar's
checks & balances (fill Diwan, Naib Nazim, war commander with loyalists) → (3) Build strong revenue administration → (4) Convert
Tankha Jagirs → Vatan/Watan Jagirs → (5) Co-opt merchants, bankers, Ijaradars into Mansabdari system. None declared
independence — Mughal symbolic umbrella served their interests. Result = diffused autonomous polity: Nawab at top, multiple
influential actors beneath.
n Prelims Alert (2021): Carnatic was NOT a separate independent state. It was part of Hyderabad Subah — 12 districts south of
the Krishna River. Carnatic had its own Nawab but he reported to the Nizam — making it a state within a state. Nawab of Carnatic
≠ independent ruler; Hyderabad Nizam ≠ ruler of only north Deccan.
n Prelims Alert — Nawab ≠ Subahdar always: A Nawab could administer a sub-region within a Suba (e.g. Alivardi Khan40-56
was Nawab of Patna, a region inside Bengal Subah, before becoming Subahdar of the whole Bengal Subah in 1740). Naib Nazim
= Deputy Subahdar. Subahdar = Nazim = Nawab of the Suba (same Mansab, different titles).

events.label: Bahmani Sultanate — parent of Bijapur & Golconda (Deccan)
Bijapur — Adil Shahi Dynasty; Shahji Bhonsle (Shivaji's father) serves as General & Mansabdar here
Golconda — Qutb Shahi Dynasty
Shivaji Bhonsle born — son of Shahji Bhonsle & Jijabai; early training under guardian Dadaji Kondadev
Shivaji74-80 captures 1st fort @ age 16 — working from Maval region (Pune District, Sahyadri range); gathers army of local warriors & peasants
Shivaji74-80 launches systematic attacks on Bijapur Kingdom; establishes naval force of 20 ships
Aurangzeb58-07 becomes Mughal emperor
Bijapur sends General Afzal Khan (7 feet tall) to kill Shivaji under pretext of negotiations — Shivaji kills him with Bagh Nakh (Tiger Claws) + Bichhwa (dagger)
Shivaji74-80 defeats Mughal General Shaista Khan
Shivaji74-80 sacks wealthy port of Surat; full navy reaches 200 ships

Mughal General Jai Singh lays siege to Fort Purandhar; Treaty of Purandhar 1665 (ToPurandhar1665): (i) surrenders 23 of 35 forts; (ii) accepts Aurangzeb as Emperor but declines personal mansab; (iii) son Sambhaji made Mughal mansabdar rank 5,000; (iv) agrees to support Mughals against Bijapur
Shivaji & Sambhaji visit Mughal court @ Agra — insulted & imprisoned; escape disguised as Sadhus; Shivaji leaves Sambhaji with Brahmin family @ Mathura
Shivaji allows French trading factory @ Rajapur — receives European cannons, lead & saltpetre in return
Shivaji74-80 coronated @ Raigarh Fort as Chhatrapati — legally declares independence from Mughals; Svarajya founded; capital @ Satara; Peshwa HQ @ Poona

Shivaji74-80 reigns — pays officials in cash (no Jagirs -> centralised polity); captures 240 forts over career; peak navy 700 ships; Jaladurg doctrine sea forts: Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg, Suvarnadurg Shivaji74-80 dies of natural causes — 1st Chhatrapati
Chhatrapati Sambhaji80-89 reigns — elder son of Shivaji74-80 Aurangzeb58-07 marches to Deccan — own son Prince Akbar defects to Sambhaji
Aurangzeb58-07 annexes Bijapur; EIC makes Bombay main trade base (fear of Marathas) -> Bombay Presidency established 1687
Aurangzeb58-07 annexes Golconda
Aurangzeb58-07 captures & assassinates Sambhaji80-89 after weeks of torture — convert-or-die; refused; martyr created
Chhatrapati Rajaram89-00 — younger son of Shivaji74-80
Rajaram89-00 dies of tuberculosis @ age 30; widow Tarabai rules as regent in name of infant son Shivaji II
Tarabai rules as regent — holds Maratha state together Aurangzeb58-07 dies; Mughals release Shahu19-49 (son of Sambhaji) from captivity — nominal pacifism, real politics; triggers Maratha Civil War

Bahadur Shah07-12 grants Guru Gobind Singh76-08 high Mansab + promises Anandpur; Mughal Faujdar Wazir Khan of Sirhind assassinates Guru in Nanded — no action against Wazir Khan; Anandpur never given: proof of nominal pacifism with deniability Maratha Civil War — Shahu19-49 vs Tarabai; Sardars & Deshmukhs switch sides; Mughals deliberately encourage divided loyalties Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath13-20 (6th Peshwa) — backs Shahu19-49; makes Peshwa office hereditary in practice by passing it to son Baji Rao20-40 Balaji Vishwanath13-20 convinces Admiral Kanhoji Angre to switch sides from Tarabai to Shahu19-49

Admiral Kanhoji Angre frequently attacks EIC in Bombay — guerrilla warfare at sea; British heavy ships cannot pursue light Maratha vessels in shallow waters; stalemate 1719 turning point: Balaji Vishwanath13-20 + Sayyid Brothers remove Farukhsiyar13-19; install Md. Shah19-48 as puppet; 3 Maratha concessions: (i) Mughal recognition of Maratha autonomy in Maharashtra; (ii) Chauth of Malwa & Gujarat; (iii) Chauth & Sardeshmukhi from 6 Mughal Deccan provinces

Chhatrapati Shahu19-49 reigns — gives Tankha Jagirs (Saranjams) to military commanders; never Vatan Jagirs -> maintains ruler control; Maratha Confederacy takes shape Admiral Kanhoji Angre dies — dominated Arabian Sea for ~30 years
Treaty of Warna 1731 — Shahu19-49 gives Kolhapur to Sambhaji II (son of Rajaram from 2nd wife Rajasbai); two separate Chhatrapati dynasties: Satara line (Shahu) & Kolhapur line (Sambhaji II)

Peshwa Baji Rao20-40 — leads decade of relentless expansion; son of Balaji Vishwanath Nizam24-48 defeats Sayyid Brothers; establishes Hyderabad as independent Successor State (1724) — refuses Chauth & Sardeshmukhi to Marathas
Marathas defeat Mughals in Gujarat — extract 60% of revenue as annual tribute Marathas defeat Hyderabad — regain Chauth & Sardeshmukhi of Deccan
Marathas capture Malwa; push reach into Rajasthan
Marathas defeat joint attack by Nizam24-48 & Gujarat chiefs
Marathas defeat Portuguese & Ethiopian Muslims on Konkan coast; remove them from Konkan
Peshwa Baji Rao20-40 plunders Delhi — holds Md. Shah19-48 prisoner temporarily
Marathas defeat large Mughal army commanded by Nizam24-48
Treaty of Bhopal (ToBhopal1738) — Marathas receive Suba of Malwa (formalising de facto control since 1729) + sovereignty over all lands between Chambal & Narmada
Treaty of Bassein (ToBassein1739) with Portuguese — Marathas annex Bassein (Vasai); by 1739 effectively control Salsette & Bassein

Peshwa Balaji Bajirao / Nana Saheb40-61 — Peshwa office now 3 generations hereditary in practice Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur raids Bengal Suba repeatedly — forces Alivardi Khan40-56 to cede Odisha + pay Chauth of Bengal & Bihar (paid until BoPlassey1757) Ahmad Shah Abdali47-72 launches 1st invasion — checked at Battle of Manupur (Mughal army pitched battle; Sikh misls harassed Abdali's supply lines)

Abdali47-72 launches at least 7 invasions into India Treaty of Sangola 1750 — Peshwa Nana Saheb40-61 forces Chhatrapati Ramraja to sign; all real power transferred from Chhatrapati to Peshwa; Sardars feel less constrained -> factionalism ↑
Chhatrapati Shahu19-49 dies — adopted son Ramraja (Rajaram II) takes over (1749–1777); Chhatrapatis become largely ceremonial
Peshwa Nana Saheb40-61 attacks Hyderabad — Salabat Jung51-62 cedes Khandesh via Treaty of Bhalke
Marathas complete annexation of Gujarat — take Ahmedabad; Peshwa appoints Damaji Gaikwad as Maratha Chief & Governor of Gujarat @ Baroda
Weakened Mughal Empire comes under Maratha military protection — fear of Afghan invasions
Marathas regularly attack Rajputs — extract annual tributes; interfere in succession; never fully conquer Rajputana; also fail to dominate Sikhs
Marathas install Alamgir II54-59 as puppet Mughal emperor @ Delhi
British defeat Maratha Navy — 1 year before BoPlassey1757
Raghunath Rao removes Abdali's son Timur Shah from Lahore — peak Maratha territory; Nana Saheb contemplates making son Vishwas Rao Emperor of Hindustan

phases.label: 3RD BATTLE OF PANIPAT 1761 — BACKGROUND, BATTLE & IMPACT

events.label: Ahmad Shah Abdali47-72 (Durrani) declares himself independent King of Afghanistan after death of Nadir Shah

3rd Battle of Panipat (BoPanipat1761) — Marathas (~50,000) vs Abdali47-72 alliance (~60,000): Abdali + Rohillas under Najib-ud-Daula57-70 (Rohilkhand) + Bangash Pathans under Ahmad Khan50-82 (Farrukhabad) + Awadh under Shuja-ud-Daula54-75

WHY ABDALI WON — 6 factors: (1) Alliance strength: Awadh joins (strategically encircled by Marathas E+W+S); Rohilkhand + Farrukhabad back Abdali hoping Afghan emperor; Sikhs, Rajputs, Jats stay neutral (years of Maratha plundering); (2) Logistics: Abdali cuts supply routes between Maratha camp & Delhi — famine conditions; (3) Terrain: Panipat open plains — no use for Maratha guerrilla tactics; (4) Firepower: Abdali's horse-mounted swivel guns pierce Maratha armour; (5) Military leadership: Abdali + Najib-ud-Daula provide strong coordinated command; (6) Maratha factionalism: Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur REFUSES to fight (opposed to Nana Saheb as Peshwa)

IMPACT: Sadasiv Rao Bhau & Vishwas Rao die fighting; Nana Saheb40-61 dies within weeks; 50,000 Maratha losses (combatants + non-combatants); factionalism deepens; succession of weak/young Peshwas follows; power vacuum filled eventually by EIC
Abdali also suffers heavy losses + anti-Abdali revolt by own generals in Afghanistan; returns home with loot but cannot consolidate any lasting India presence
Deeper consequence: BoPanipat1761 decided neither Marathas nor Abdali would rule India — power vacuum at centre filled by EIC one by one
Peshwa Madhav Rao61-72 — young but brilliant; temporary Maratha revival; younger son of Nana Saheb (elder son Vishwas Rao died @ Panipat) Marathas defeat Mysore — extract tribute
Peshwa plunders Nagpur — retaliation for Raghuji Bhonsle's refusal to fight @ Panipat

Treaty of Hyderabad 1766 — Hyderabad gives Northern Sarkars (Chicacole, Rajmandri, Ellore, MustafaNagar; Guntur added later as 5th) to EIC in return for annual payment of 7 lakh rupees + protection against Marathas & Mysore
Mahadji Scindia recaptures Delhi from Rohilla Afghans (who had taken it in 1761)
Madhav Rao61-72 dies of natural causes

Peshwa Narayan Rao72-73 — brother of Madhav Rao; murdered 1773 in palace conspiracy by uncle Raghunath Rao73-74 Peshwa Raghunath Rao73-74 — usurper uncle; briefly Peshwa Barbhai Mandal formed — 12 ministers under Nana Fadnavis remove Raghunath Rao73-74 (Baarbhai Conspiracy); Nana Fadnavis = 1st to recognise EIC had territorial ambitions, not just commercial; called modern Chanakya; had fought @ BoPanipat1761

Peshwa Madhav Rao II74-95 — infant son of murdered Narayan Rao; Nana Fadnavis rules as regent; overbearing control -> Madhav Rao II commits suicide 1795 1st Anglo-Maratha War — Marathas defeat EIC; only war EIC lost in this period Treaty of Salbai (ToSalbai1782) — Maratha-EIC military alliance; holds until 1795

Mahadji Shinde (Scindia) hires Benoît de Boigne (French) — raises Fauj-i-Hind / Campoo system (each Campoo = integrated infantry + cavalry + artillery = self-sufficient unit); transforms Maratha army into European-style force; Holkar follows (hires Frenchman Dudrenec)
Battle of Kharda — Maratha victory over Hyderabad; last battle between them; EIC stays neutral (ToSalbai1782 still holds)
Madhav Rao II74-95 commits suicide
Peshwa Baji Rao II96-18 — last Peshwa; son of Raghunath Rao73-74
Hyderabad signs Subsidiary Alliance with EIC — 1st Indian state to do so; ends Maratha threat to Hyderabad
EIC captures Delhi in 2nd Anglo-Maratha War

3rd Anglo-Maratha War — Svarajya annexed by EIC; Baji Rao II96-18's rule ends; Maratha Empire finished Last Chhatrapati of Satara line: Shahaji (1839–1848); EIC annexes Satara 1848 Kolhapur Princely State survives — merges into India 1947

anchors: Key Pattern — 3 Phases of Maratha Polity: (1) 1680–1719: Turmoil — continuous Mughal warfare + civil war 1707–19. (2)
1719–1761: Growth & expansion — alliance with Sayyid Brothers 1719 -> Panipat 1761. (3) 1761 onwards: Decline — moments of
strength (1st Anglo-Maratha War 1775-82 won; Battle of Kharda 1795 won) but structural weakness: weak centre + strong Sardars
+ factionalism + tribute not annexation = could not establish all-India rule.
n Prelims Alert (1995) — Sardar-Capital pairings (pin these): Gaikwad → Baroda | Holkar → Indore | Scindia (Shinde) →
Gwalior | Bhonsle → Nagpur. Maratha Empire = Peshwa (Poona/Satara) + 4 Sardars = effectively a Confederation by 1750: weak
centre, strong provinces.
n Mains 2014 Alert — Why so many empire-shaking battles near Panipat? Panipat region = gateway to Delhi from Central
Asia/Afghanistan via Khyber Pass. Sitting ruler in Delhi stops invader at the gate rather than let them reach capital. Practical
factors: vast open plains suit large set-piece battles; good weather; warrior communities nearby for recruitment; agricultural
productivity + Delhi proximity = army supply manageable.

chapters.title: The Jat Kingdom & the Afghan Kingdoms

sections.title: Framework — two more Rebel States alongside the Marathas
Synthesis — Three Rebel States, Same pattern

phases.label: AFGHAN BACKGROUND & SHER SHAH SURI40-45 (15th c – 1556)

events.label: Sur clan (Pashtun tribe) migrates from Sur region of Afghanistan to India during Lodi Sultanate period; Sher Shah's grandfather receives small Jagir in Sasaram (present-day Bihar)
Afghans migrating into North India — poor economic conditions + political instability at home; function as wandering warlords in North India's military labour markets
Farid Khan (later Sher Shah Suri40-45) born in Sasaram, Bihar — 2nd-generation Indian Afghan
Battle of Panipat — Babur defeats Lodis; Sher Shah serves briefly under Mughals after 1526; closely studies Mughal administrative methods — knowledge later turned against them
Battle of Kanauj — Sher Shah Suri40-45 defeats Humayun30-40; drives him into exile to Persia; seizes Delhi throne; Suri dynasty established

Suri Interregnum — brief Afghan interruption of Mughal rule Sher Shah Suri40-45's 5-year reforms (punches far above weight): (i) Admin hierarchy: Centre -> Suba -> Sarkar -> Pargana (Akbar56-05 adopts wholesale); (ii) Grand Trunk Road upgraded (Bengal to NW Frontier); (iii) Dak Chowki postal relay system; (iv) standardised silver Rupiya coin (basis of Indian currency for centuries); (v) careful land surveys; (vi) fair revenue fixed directly with peasant — cuts out Zamindar middleman Sher Shah Suri40-45 dies — Afghans fragment again into competing warlord groups in North India's military labour markets
Humayun30-40 defeats Suris @ Battle of Sirhind — briefly restores Mughal authority
Humayun30-40 dies; Akbar56-05 inherits throne & adopts Sher Shah's admin hierarchy wholesale

Jahangir05-27 — harsh LR policies push Jat Zamindars toward organised resistance; Mughal drive to subordinate local autonomy deepens hostility 1st organised Jat revolt — led by Zamindar Gokla; guerrilla warfare: fast, decentralised, difficult for large Mughal army to counter

Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur formally established by Churaman Jat (1695–1721) @ East Rajasthan (south of Delhi, bordering Mathura & Agra districts) — Zamindar turns peasant discontent over high LR into political & military power; same pattern as Marathas & Sikhs
Churaman95-21 reigns — Jat resistance line: Gokla 1669 -> Rajaram -> Churaman -> Badan Singh -> Surajmal

Maharaja Surajmal56-63 — Jat State reaches peak; centralised State; Mughal emperor formally recognises him as autonomous ruler; reforms: (i) recruits European soldiers to modernise military; (ii) introduces Mughal-style revenue system; (iii) removes relatives from court positions to reduce factionalism; territory: Delhi to Agra + Chambal River to Ganga (present-day Delhi, Haryana, UP, Rajasthan) Surajmal56-63 offers help to Marathas before 3rd Battle of Panipat — alliance fails: Surajmal wanted guerrilla warfare; Maratha commander Sadasiv Rao Bhau wanted traditional set-piece battle; Jats send essential supplies during war
Surajmal56-63 dies — Jat Kingdom collapses; Lohagarh Fort ('Iron Fort') @ Bharatpur — never conquered, even by the British

Jahandar Shah12-13 seizes power by killing father of Farukhsiyar13-19; Farukhsiyar13-19 avenges — removes Jahandar Shah Md Khan Bangash14-43 founds Farrukhabad — rewarded with Nawab title + revenue assignments in Farrukhabad region (present-day Farrukhabad district, central UP, banks of Ganga) for supporting Farukhsiyar13-19 with 12,000 troops; names city after emperor as diplomatic gesture (had first founded Mohammadabad after himself — annoyed Farukhsiyar; Farrukhabad = 'city of Farrukh' = the correction)
Md Khan Bangash14-43 reigns — builds Farrukhabad; nominal Mughal loyalty, real autonomy on ground Md Khan Bangash14-43 dies — succeeded by son Qaim Khan

Safdar Jung39-54 (simultaneously Nawab of Awadh + Wazir of Mughal Emperor) engineers Qaim Khan's death in battle — Farrukhabad formally annexed to Awadh & plundered; textbook proof: Wazir's loyalty to own State, not Emperor
Ahmad Khan Bangash50-82 fights back — retakes Farrukhabad

Marathas (Malhar Rao Holkar + Jayappaji Rao Scindia, sent by Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao40-61) + Jats under Surajmal56-63 drive Ahmad Khan50-82 out of Farrukhabad (Awadh had requested Maratha+Jat intervention in 1751) Marathas sign treaty allowing Ahmad Khan50-82 to return & resume rule — price: hand over half of Farrukhabad to Holkar & Scindia
Ahmad Khan Bangash50-82 fights alongside Ahmad Shah Abdali47-72 @ 3rd Battle of Panipat; with Marathas defeated, recovers full Farrukhabad dominions including the half ceded in 1752
Once Abdali leaves India in 1761, Farrukhabad weakens — external prop removed
EIC annexes Farrukhabad — merged into 'Ceded Provinces' (territories Awadh forced to hand over under Subsidiary Alliance of 1801)
Bangash Pathans participate in 1857 Revolt — ultimately defeated

Katehr region (present-day western UP, centred around Bareilly & Moradabad): local Zamindars & regional governors hire Afghan mercenaries to settle disputes; these fighters — called Rohillas ('Roh' = Afghan homeland; Rohilkhand = land of the Rohillas) — gradually become dominant armed presence

Daud Khan (Afghan commander who consolidated mercenary groups in Katehr) dies; adopted son Ali Md Khan21-48 takes over leadership of Afghan troops — starting point; NOT yet an independent State, but one man now controls significant armed force in region

Ali Md Khan21-48 consolidates methodically over ~2 decades — absorbs lands from Zamindars his men were hired to protect; unites scattered Afghan mercenary groups under sole command; does NOT declare independence yet Nadir Shah's devastating invasion of Delhi — Mughal State completely paralysed; Ali Md Khan21-48 stops paying taxes to Delhi; begins ruling Katehr as independent power; captures & consolidates Bareilly & Moradabad; Rohilkhand effectively born

Emperor Md Shah19-48 formally grants Ali Md Khan21-48 title of Subadar — Mughal co-option strategy (co-opt what you cannot defeat); Katehr officially renamed Rohilkhand; functions as autonomous State under nominal Mughal sovereignty
Ali Md Khan21-48 dies
Najib-ud-Daula57-70 — dominant figure of Rohilkhand; actively supports Abdali at 3rd Battle of Panipat 1761 3rd Battle of Panipat — Rohilkhand under Najib-ud-Daula57-70 fights alongside Abdali47-72
Delhi effectively under Rohilla influence — Mughal emperor Shah Alam II60-06 flees to Awadh Najib-ud-Daula57-70 dies — Rohilkhand weakens (no Abdali support since 1761; external prop removed)
Mahadji Scindia68-94 recaptures Delhi; allows Shah Alam II60-06 to return home (Red Fort)
Most of Rohilkhand annexed by Awadh with EIC help — EIC assists per Treaty of Allahabad (1765) military alliance; remainder becomes autonomous State of Rampur (capital Bareilly) — legally under Awadh
Awadh gives half of itself to EIC under Subsidiary Alliance — Rampur (remnant Rohilkhand) now legally under EIC

anchors: Key Pattern — All 3 Rebel States, Same Arc: Each used opportunity of weakening Mughal Empire to convert local military power
into territorial rule. Each needed external support to peak — Abdali for Afghan kingdoms; Maratha tactical support for
Surajmal56-63. Each collapsed when that external support was removed. None could establish a large, sustainable empire.
n Prelims Alert (2010) — Abdali's IMMEDIATE trigger for 3rd Battle of Panipat 1761: NOT a general desire to plunder India.
Immediate cause: avenge expulsion of his son Timur Shah from Lahore. In March 1758, Raghunath Rao crossed into Punjab &
drove out Timur Shah; Marathas appointed Adina Beg Khan as Governor of Punjab (annual tribute Rs 75 lakh); on Adina Beg's
death, Sabaji Scindia took charge & commanded Maratha garrisons at Attock & Peshawar (on Afghan border). Maratha conquest
of Punjab = direct challenge Abdali could not ignore = immediate trigger.
Note — Sher Shah Suri40-45 vs Bangash Pathans: Same Afghan migrant background, same military labour market entry point.
Sher Shah had a wide-open political window (Humayun30-40 weak, no rival claimants at that scale) -> could seize Delhi throne.
Bangash Pathans had a much narrower window (Awadh pressing, Marathas expanding, EIC rising) -> ceiling was a regional
kingdom, not Delhi.

events.label: Guru Nanak Dev Ji — founder of Sikhism; contemporary of Babur26-30; Sikhism rises from 1500 onwards; 4 core principles: (i) One supreme & formless God; (ii) direct access to God without rituals/priests; (iii) rejection of caste system; (iv) honest living & selfless service
Guru Nanak Dev Ji undertakes 4 major Udasis (spiritual journeys) over 30 years — approx. 30,000 km across India, South Asia, Tibet & Arabia
Guru Nanak Dev Ji settles in Kartarpur (present-day Pakistan) — establishes institution of Langar (free communal kitchen) to promote equality
No major conflict between Sikh community & Mughal State — peaceful coexistence
1st major flashpoint: 5th Guru Arjan Dev executed by Jahangir05-27 — turning point; peaceful spiritual movement begins transformation into martial community
2nd major flashpoint: 9th Guru Teg Bahadur executed in Delhi by Aurangzeb58-07 — hardening of anti-Mughal Sikh sentiment

10th Guru Gobind Singh Ji76-08 establishes the Khalsa @ Anandpur — Sikh military organisation to defend Sikh Panth & struggle for a Sikh State; formal militarisation of Sikh community's political ambitions

Battle of Chamkaur — Guru Gobind Singh's two elder sons (Sahibzada Ajit Singh, 18 & Sahibzada Jujhar Singh, 14) die fighting; same month, two younger sons (Sahibzada Zorawar Singh, 9 & Sahibzada Fateh Singh, 6) buried alive in a wall on orders of Wazir Khan (Mughal Faujdar of Sirhind)
Bahadur Shah07-12 (new emperor) grants Guru Gobind Singh76-08 high Mansab + promises Sikh State @ Anandpur — nominal pacifism; promise never fulfilled

Wazir Khan arranges assassins to attack Guru Gobind Singh Ji76-08 @ Abchal Nagar Sahib Gurdwara, Nanded, Maharashtra; Guru kills assassins himself but succumbs to injuries; dies @ age 42; no action taken against Wazir Khan; Anandpur never given

Guru Gobind Singh Ji76-08 declares Guru Granth Sahib Ji as the final & eternal Guru @ Abchal Nagar Sahib — deliberate: prevents community tension between Jat (dominated Khalsa) & Khatri (all 10 Gurus' community) over succession; Guru Granth Sahib Ji installed @ Akal Takht, Golden Temple, Amritsar
Banda Bahadur08-15 carries forward rebellion from 1708

Battle of Chappar Chiri — Banda Bahadur08-15 defeats & kills Wazir Khan; conquest of Sirhind follows; 1st Sikh State established over territories between River Ravi & River Jamuna — with own coins, own officials & own seal for issuing admin orders

1st Sikh State operational; Farukhsiyar13-19 appoints Abdus Samad Khan as Governor of Lahore specifically to suppress it Jahandar Shah12-13 introduces Ijaradari in Punjab specifically to co-opt Khatri traders; both Jahandar Shah12-13 & Farukhsiyar13-19 offer Mansabs to Khatri traders — traders switch sides (note: adds Mansabdars, worsening Jagirdari Crisis) Banda Bahadur08-15 defeated — 3 reasons: (i) Khatri traders turn against him (constant warfare hurts trade; commercial class needs decisive victors & political stability); (ii) Mughals use Divide & Rule + Ijaradari co-option of Khatri traders; (iii) Hindu Jat Zamindars switch sides — Churaman Jat95-21 goes over to Mughals after they recognise his Jat Kingdom
Banda Bahadur08-15 captured & executed in Delhi by Farukhsiyar13-19
Defeat of Banda Bahadur08-15 does NOT end Sikh State — Mughals too weak to fully reassert control over Punjab; power decentralises among Misl Chiefs

Misls = kinship-based clans; unite during wars (esp. against Afghan invasions) but operate independently otherwise; Misl conquers territory -> lands distributed among members in proportion to military & monetary contribution; even lowest-ranking soldier receives land share

12 major Misls operational in Punjab; Dal Khalsa at centre under leader chosen by Misl chiefs — confederacy structure: weak centre + strong constituent units (mirrors Maratha Confederacy under Peshwas)

Ranjit Singh01-39 of Sukerchakia Misl plays crucial role in defeating Zaman Shah's 3rd Afghan invasion — military success gives platform to establish dominance over other Misls; coronated as King of Sikh State 1801
Ranjit Singh01-39 defeats Zaman Shah's 3rd Afghan invasion — platform for Misl unification
Ranjit Singh01-39 coronated as King of Sikh State; other Misl chiefs reduced to tribute-paying vassals (retain conditional land control in return for loyalty + tribute); 1801 — conquers Lahore
EIC removes Scindias from Delhi; establishes indirect rule through British Resident — context for future Treaty of Amritsar
Ranjit Singh01-39 conquers Jammu from the Dogras
Ranjit Singh01-39 conquers whole of Punjab

Treaty of Amritsar (ToAmritsar1809) with EIC — represented by Charles Metcalfe (British Resident @ Delhi court); 4 outcomes: (i) EIC recognises Ranjit Singh as sovereign ruler of Punjab; (ii) military alliance (links to EIC's Policy of Ring Fence); (iii) Sutlej River fixed as border between Sikh State & Company State; (iv) Ranjit Singh01-39 free to expand on his side of Sutlej without British interference
Ranjit Singh01-39 returns Jammu to Dogras — but within Sikh Empire; Dogras become vassals
Ranjit Singh01-39 removes Afghans from Multan
Ranjit Singh01-39 conquers Kashmir — completing what Marathas left unfinished (Marathas took back Punjab from Afghans in 1758 but not Kashmir; Abdali had captured both during invasions)

Ranjit Singh01-39 conquers Peshawar (present-day Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, bordering Afghanistan along Durand Line) — conquered by Hari Singh Nalwa; reputation so fearsome Afghan mothers used his name to frighten children

Tripartite Treaty — Sikh State + EIC + Shah Shuja of Afghanistan; designed to establish British indirect rule in Afghanistan through puppet Shah Shuja; aim: buffer of Afghanistan + Punjab against feared Russian invasion of British India from NW
Ranjit Singh01-39 dies — Sikh State after his death covered in a later chapter (Anglo-Sikh Wars & EIC annexation)

anchors: Key Pattern — Misl Confederacy mirrors Maratha Confederacy: Both had weak centre + strong constituent units. Both showed
resilience (survived major shocks: Banda's defeat 1716 / Panipat 1761) but also vulnerability (internal factionalism, inability to
centralise). Ranjit Singh01-39 broke the Misl pattern by converting confederacy into a unified kingdom — exactly what the
Peshwas could NEVER do with the Maratha Sardars.
Key Note — Ranjit Singh01-39's State Character: Administration secular: Fakir Azizuddin (Muslim) = Foreign Minister; Dewan
Dina Nath (Hindu) = Finance Minister. Revenue: only 40% land under Jagirdari; rest -> King's treasury directly. Kardar (chief admin
officer @ Taluqa level) = revenue collector + local magistrate + police chief + customs officer; often acted as Ijaradar but ryot
oppression prevented. Inclusive: Sahajdhari Sikhs (non-Khalsa Sikhs) included. State authority stopped @ village level — local
chiefs & clan autonomy respected (links to later Mahalwari Settlement in Punjab where even British respected this tradition).
n Alert — Veer Bal Divas (since 2022): 26th December observed in memory of younger Sahibzadas (Zorawar Singh, 9 & Fateh
Singh, 6) buried alive in a wall on orders of Wazir Khan (Faujdar of Sirhind) in December 1704. Faujdar = district military
commander (comparable to SP today); NOT a Governor — though Wazir Khan wielded greater influence than a typical Faujdar.

sections.title: How did a small southern kingdom stay independent from both the Mughals and the Marathas?
How did Mysore go from being a minor kingdom to one of the most powerful states in 18th-century India?
How did Mysore fund this military machine?
What made Tipu82-99 a different kind of ruler — and why did he still lose?

events.label: ~20 major Rajput clans control Rajputana — multi-polar; no single dominant power

Akbar56-05 co-opts powerful Rajput chiefs rather than fighting all — brought into Mansabdari system as Mansabdars; home territories recognised as Vatan Jagirs (land stays theirs, within Mughal framework); accept Emperor as sovereign, pay tributes, contribute troops; form Hindu bloc in Mansabdari system (~15% of all Mansabdars); Akbar56-05 helps them subdue smaller Rajput chiefs

Child comes to throne of Marwar — Aurangzeb58-07 interferes in succession; trigger for joint Marwar + Mewar revolt; revolt FAILS — other Rajput chiefs refuse to join (fear Mewar would dominate if revolt succeeded); each stands aside; rebellion collapses

Sawai Jai Singh99-43 of Amber — most prominent post-Aurangzeb Rajput figure; simultaneously Mughal Mansabdar + regional state-builder + astronomer + town planner; title 'Sawai' (1.25x more able than any contemporary) conferred by Aurangzeb58-07
Sawai Jai Singh99-43 builds Jantar Mantar @ Delhi (1724) — 1st of 5 observatories
Sawai Jai Singh99-43 founds Jaipur — designed by Vidyadhar Bhattacharya on Vastu Shastra principles; grid-pattern layout; 1st planned city of modern India
Sawai Jai Singh99-43 holds Subedari of Malwa (1729–37) & Agra Sawai Jai Singh99-43 sends scientific delegation to Portugal

Zij-i-Muhammad Shahi published — Sawai Jai Singh's corrected astronomical tables (dedicated to Md Shah19-48); corrects accumulated errors in both Zij-i-Ulugh Begi (Islamic) & Siddhantic (Hindu) tables

Sawai Jai Singh99-43 builds Jantar Mantar @ Jaipur (1734) — largest of 5 observatories; Samrat Yantra (largest sundial in world) measures local time to 2-second accuracy; UNESCO World Heritage Site (2010)
Conference of Rajput rulers @ Hurda — Sawai Jai Singh convenes to forge united front against Marathas; collapses due to internal Rajput rivalries
Treaty of Bhopal (1738) — Malwa (held by Sawai Jai Singh as Subedar) formally annexed by Marathas
Marathas begin regular raids into Rajputana — extract tributes; interfere in succession disputes; never fully conquer the region

Second Anglo-Maratha War — EIC replaces Marathas as regional power; EIC signs Subordinate Alliances (= Subsidiary Alliances) with Rajput states Sawai Ram Singh paints Jaipur pink to welcome Prince of Wales — 'Pink City' name
Dutch East India Company captures Cochin (central Kerala) from Portuguese — establishes Malabar headquarters there

Marthanda Varma29-58 builds strong centralised Travancore State — subjugates local chiefs across region; builds European-style military (modern weapons, trained soldiers); establishes State monopoly over Malabar coast trade; revenues reinvested into military + irrigation + transport infrastructure (Military Fiscalism, small-State model)
Battle of Colachel — Marthanda Varma29-58's army crushes Dutch East India Company; permanently ends Dutch political & military ambitions in Kerala; relegates Dutch to mere merchant status in Cochin

Rama Varma58-98 reigns — Travancore becomes centre of art & scholarship; military strength declines Battle of Bedara / Battle of Chinsura — EIC defeats Dutch in Bengal; crushes remaining Dutch ambitions in India
Haider Ali61-82 of Mysore invades Travancore — annexes Malabar & Calicut (heart of spice trade: pepper, cardamom, ginger; whoever controls Malabar ports controls significant Indian Ocean commerce)
British finally expel Dutch from South Asia (Ceylon / Sri Lanka)
Travancore comes steadily under British influence after 1798
Mutiny of Nair troops in Travancore — over non-payment of salaries; Travancore seeks British help -> forced to sign Subsidiary Alliance (1805); effectively ends Travancore's independence

Velu Thampi Dalawa (PM of Travancore) organises revolt against British Resident — angered by humiliating Subsidiary Alliance terms (heavy financial burden + interference in internal affairs); rallies Nair troops; issues Kundara Proclamation (1809) calling people to rise against British control; revolt suppressed; Velu Thampi takes his own life
Vijayanagar Empire — Mysore part of it; Poligars (local chiefs controlling land, temple wealth, armed men) = real rulers of countryside

Battle of Talikota (also called Rakkasa-Tangadi) — coalition of Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar) decisively defeats Vijayanagar forces; operational end of Vijayanagar as major power (dynasty lingers until 1646)
Vijayanagar Empire formally ends; Mysore gradually becomes autonomous under Wodeyar dynasty
Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar72-04 — Mysore becomes militarily powerful & centrally governed
Wodeyars reduced to figureheads by powerful corrupt Prime Minister NanjRaj
Haider Ali61-82 overthrows NanjRaj — seizes effective power; keeps Wodeyar as nominal head of State; pattern: personality weakens -> king becomes puppet (same as Peshwa-Chhatrapati relationship)

Haider Ali61-82 reigns: (i) takes French assistance for military training + technology transfer + organisational reform; (ii) army structured on European model into Risalas (regiments) — each with commander directly appointed by King (personal loyalty upward), clear chain of command, self-sufficient units; (iii) spends ~20 years subjugating Poligars & Deshmukhs — systematically dismantles non-State power; (iv) Military Fiscalism: Khalisa land expanded, Jagirdari minimised; Deshmukhs removed as intermediaries; State officials collect directly on salaries; detailed field surveys prevent over-assessment; irrigation canals repaired + new ones built; cash crops promoted; sericulture (silk via silkworms) introduced Haider Ali61-82 invades Travancore — annexes Malabar & Calicut -> triggers 1st Anglo-Mysore War (EIC fears losing coastal trade access through Malabar)
1st Anglo-Mysore War 2nd Anglo-Mysore War
events.full: 1767–69 1780–84 — 1st Anglo-Mysore War 2nd Anglo-Mysore War

events.label: Tipu82-99 reigns — pushes Mysore's ambitions further; dream = Vijayanagar 2.0 (dominate all South India + control its international trade) Haider Ali61-82 & Tipu82-99 together develop iron-cased rocket artillery — 100% indigenous; range 2 km; iron cylinder casings do not burst + can take high pressure (unlike cardboard-cased rockets existing since centuries in India & China); later closely studied by British; William Congreve's rockets (early 19th c British military) drawn directly from Tipu82-99's designs Tipu82-99 builds modern navy + establishes government-owned trading company modelled on EIC — conducts oceanic trade in sandalwood, sulphur, rice, pepper, silk & cardamom; sets up 30 trading centres inside & outside India including Muscat, Oman Tipu82-99 formally declares independence — from Wodeyars AND from Mughal Emperor; sends request to Khalifa (religious head of Muslim world) for a sanad recognising him as independent ruler
French Revolution begins — sets France on collision course with European monarchies including Britain; context for Tipu's French alliance strategy

3rd Anglo-Mysore War Tipu82-99 sends ambassador to France seeking military technology + formal alliance against British; exchanges communications with Napoleon; plants Tree of Liberty in Mysore (symbol of French Revolution); becomes member of Jacobin Club (radical org at heart of French Revolution); British take this very seriously — Tipu now seen as not just military but ideological adversary
events.full: 1790–92 1790s — 3rd Anglo-Mysore War Tipu82-99 sends ambassador to France seeking military technology + formal alliance against British; exchanges communications with Napoleon; plants Tree of Liberty in Mysore (symbol of French Revolution); becomes member of Jacobin Club (radical org at heart of French Revolution); British take this very seriously — Tipu now seen as not just military but ideological adversary

events.label: Napoleon attacks Egypt & Middle East — partly to disrupt British trade in Arabian Sea; Tipu82-99 in communication with Napoleon at this point
4th Anglo-Mysore War 4th Anglo-Mysore War ends with death of Tipu82-99 @ Seringapatam — Mysore's power broken; constant warfare drained State faster than Military Fiscalism could replenish

anchors: Key Pattern — Military Fiscalism (Mysore model): Khalisa land expanded + Jagirdari minimised -> State keeps maximum
revenue. Deshmukhs removed as intermediaries -> State collects directly via salaried officers. Detailed field surveys -> fair
assessment -> no over-extraction -> larger tax base. Irrigation + cash crops + sericulture -> peasant prosperity -> larger tax base.
Trade revenue (Tipu's trading company) + modern navy -> strategic depth. Result: even Tipu82-99's enemies acknowledged
Mysore's population was among the most prosperous in India. Collapse cause: ambition-vs-capacity mismatch; constant warfare
drained State faster than Military Fiscalism could replenish.
n Prelims Alert (2001) — Who established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines? Answer: Tipu Sultan
(Tipu82-99). Set up modern embassies in France, Turkey & Egypt. Other Tipu innovations: new coinage; Mauludi Lunisoler
Calendar; government-owned trading company (30 centres incl. Muscat, Oman); iron-cased rocket artillery (Congreve rockets
derived from this); Jacobin Club membership; Tree of Liberty planted in Mysore.
Note — Kundara Proclamation (1809) — exam-tested: Issued by Velu Thampi Dalawa (PM of Travancore) against British
Resident after Subsidiary Alliance of 1805. One of earliest organised resistance movements by an Indian ruler against the
Subsidiary Alliance system. Revolt suppressed; Velu Thampi commits suicide. Dalawa = PM + Chief of Armed Forces; when used
as Dewan under British = Head of ALL administration (revenue, civil, police, criminal justice) since military was with British.

phases.label: BACKGROUND: OTTOMAN BLOCKADE, AGE OF DISCOVERY & TORDESILLAS (1453–1494)

events.label: Trade between Europe & Asia = most profitable business in known world; Arab traders dominate Arabian Sea leg; Italian merchants (Genoa & Venice) carry goods across Mediterranean into Europe; both earn enormous profits at each handoff
Ottoman Empire captures Constantinople (today's Istanbul) — blockades traditional land trade routes connecting Europe to Asia; European traders need a new way east -> Age of Discovery

Age of Discovery: better use of astrolabe + magnetic compass; system of latitudes & longitudes + modern world map; geography as formal discipline; invention of Caravel (ship able to sail at angle against wind)

Treaty of Tordesillas — Pope Alexander VI mediates to resolve Portugal-Spain rivalry; imaginary line drawn ~1,185 miles west of Cape Verde Islands; lands east -> Portugal; lands west -> Spain; Brazil's eastern tip on Portuguese side -> only Portuguese colony in Americas

Vasco Da Gama arrives @ Calicut (Kozhikode, Kerala) — 1st direct sea route Europe-India via Cape of Good Hope; trade permission from Zamorin of Calicut; no factory established on this voyage; goods sell in Europe at 800% profit

Pedro Cabral establishes 1st Portuguese factory @ Calicut — permission from Samoothiri/Zamorin; factory destroyed by Arab merchants; ~50 Portuguese killed; Cabral retaliates by bombarding Calicut; sails south to Cochin
1st permanent Portuguese factory in India established @ Cochin — protected by Raja of Cochin; Cochin serves as 1st capital of Portuguese India

Vasco Da Gama's 2nd voyage — 3 objectives: (i) avenge massacre of Cabral's men; (ii) force Zamorin to submission; (iii) violently expel Arab traders from Malabar; Zamorin refuses to expel Muslims -> Da Gama bombards Calicut + massacres fishermen; Arab-Venetian trade network disrupted

Fort Manuel built @ Cochin by Albuquerque09-15 (then naval commander, not yet Governor) — 1st European fort in India; Albuquerque successfully defends Raja of Cochin against Zamorin; sails back to Portugal 1504

Francisco de Almeida05-09 — 1st Governor of Portuguese Estado da India; introduces Blue Water Policy (naval supremacy over territorial conquest; primary purpose = trade dominance); introduces Cartaz system (naval licensing — all non-Portuguese ships must buy a Cartaz/pass or face attack; targets Arab traders who controlled Arabian Sea for generations) Albuquerque09-15 arrives in India with royal orders to take over — Almeida05-09 arrests him (does not trust him)

Battle of Diu — Almeida05-09 defeats massive joint Muslim naval coalition (Gujarat Sultanate + Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt + Zamorin of Calicut + Ottoman Empire + Republic of Venice); consolidates Portuguese naval supremacy for next century; Albuquerque09-15 released after new Portuguese fleet confirms King's orders

Albuquerque09-15 — 2nd Governor; transforms Portuguese presence from trading enterprise to territorial colonial State; (i) annexes Goa (1510) from Sultan of Bijapur — notable exception to Blue Water Policy; (ii) Luso-Indian policy: intermarriage between Portuguese settlers & Indian women; (iii) integrates local elites; attempts to regulate Sati; promotes Christianity as political control tool Goa annexed by Albuquerque09-15 from Sultan of Bijapur — rare Portuguese territorial conquest on land
Nuno da Cunha29-38 — Governor; Portuguese at peak Portuguese headquarters officially shifted from Cochin to Goa — Goa replaces Cochin as capital of Portuguese India
Bassein acquired from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat
Diu acquired from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat — western coast dominance complete
St. Francis Xavier arrives in India — spearheads mass Catholic conversions in coastal India; lays ideological groundwork for Goa Inquisition
St. Francis Xavier dies on Shangchuan Island off coast of China — NOT in Goa; remains later brought to Goa
events.full: St. Francis Xavier dies on Shangchuan Island off coast of China — NOT in Goa; remains later brought to Goa (Prelims 2021 trap)

events.label: Daman acquired — further western coast consolidation
Goa Inquisition — brutal colonial church court; investigates & punishes heresy; forces cultural/religious orthodoxy; centuries of forced conversions; deep socio-religious backlash
Treaty with Marathas — Portuguese receive Dadra & Nagar Haveli as compensation for destroyed Portuguese ship
Dadra & Nagar Haveli formally acquired from Marathas
Goa, Daman, Diu annexed by independent India — end of Portuguese presence after 1947 people's movement
British Navy defeats Spanish Armada — severely weakens Spanish-Portuguese naval supremacy; British & Dutch ships can now travel safely to Asia via Cape of Good Hope
1st Dutch expedition sails to East Indies (Indonesia) — NOT India; priority = spice trade

VOC (Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie) established by Dutch Parliament Charter — world's 1st multinational company + 1st joint-stock company with publicly tradable stocks on formal exchange; Charter gives VOC powers of a State: wage war, sign treaties, acquire territory, build forts, mint currency
1st Dutch factory in India @ Masulipatnam (Northern Sarkars, Andhra Pradesh) — on farman from Sultan of Golconda
Pulicat (Carnatic) — Fort Geldria; 1st Dutch fort in India; built on ruins of earlier Portuguese structure with Vijayanagara permission; Pulicat = Main Dutch HQ in India (1610–1690)
Dutch factory @ Surat (Gujarat)
Amboyna Massacre — Dutch kill English traders in spice islands; effectively removes English & Portuguese from Indonesia; Dutch dominate East Indies
Dutch factory @ Bimilipatam (Carnatic)
Dutch factory @ Karikal (near Pondicherry)
Dutch factory @ Chinsura (Bengal) — Fort Gustavus; HQ of Dutch Bengal (1655–1795)
Chinsura = HQ of Dutch Bengal
Dutch remove Portuguese from Ceylon (today's Sri Lanka)
Dutch capture Cochin from Portuguese — Cochin becomes HQ of Dutch Malabar ONLY (not overall HQ); overall HQ remains Pulicat until 1690
Treaty of Breda — Anglo-Dutch rivalry settled: (i) British leave Indonesia to Dutch; (ii) Dutch leave British alone in India; (iii) both maintain minor presences in each other's primary domains
VOC at peak — richest private company in the world: 150 merchant vessels, 40 warships, 10,000-soldier army, 50,000 employees
Dutch Main HQ shifts from Pulicat to Nagapattinam (Negapatam) — remains there until 1795
Nagapattinam = Main Dutch HQ in India
Battle of Colachel — Travancore (Marthanda Varma29-58) defeats Dutch; permanently ends Dutch political & military power in Kerala
Battle of Bedara / Battle of Chinsura — EIC defeats Dutch in Bengal; crushes remaining Dutch ambitions in India

Kew Letters — Prince William V (exiled Dutch leader, fled to London) issues legal orders instructing Dutch colonial governors to hand over territories to British for safekeeping (France had occupied Netherlands via French Revolutionary Wars, set up Batavian Republic); British occupy: Cochin, Chinsura, Pulicat, Tuticorin, & coastal Ceylon (Trincomalee & Colombo)
VOC goes bankrupt & dissolved — territorial possessions taken over by Dutch government; become Dutch East Indies (independent Indonesia from 1945)

EIC founded — Royal Charter of Queen Elizabeth I58-03 (1558–1603); 4th joint-stock company in England; 215 London merchant adventurers; stated goal: trade (NOT empire); Charter gives: (i) 15-year monopoly over trade with East Indies; (ii) right to carry gold out of England; (iii) management by Governor, Deputy Governor & 24 members (later Board/Court of Directors)

1st EIC voyage — James Lancaster; sails NOT to India but to Java & Sumatra (Indonesia; 1st EIC factory); on way loots Portuguese ship São Tomé in Strait of Malacca; 1st major EIC profit came from piracy not trade; substantial dividends to shareholders; fleet returns 1603 Charter of King James I03-25 — replaces original 15-year monopoly with perpetual (indefinite) monopoly over trade with East Indies

King Charles I25-49 — attempts taxes without Parliament's consent -> English Civil War (1642–51); Parliamentarians (Protestant) defeat Royalists; Charles I beheaded 1649 English Civil War — Parliamentarians vs Royalists England becomes Republic under Oliver Cromwell

Cromwell's Charter — declares previous Royal Charter invalid; most important legal change: reorganises EIC into permanent joint-stock company (previously raised money per-voyage; from 1657: continuous unified capital fund, money stays invested permanently)
Cromwell dies; son briefly takes over; Republican experiment autocratic & unpopular
Monarchy restored — King Charles II60-85 (1660–85) on throne

Charter of King Charles II60-85 — most consequential in legal terms; transforms EIC from commercial body to quasi-State power; EIC now has: (i) right to build forts; (ii) command troops; (iii) make war & peace; (iv) exercise civil & criminal jurisdiction over settlements in India
EIC given right to mint its own money
England + Scotland unite -> Kingdom of Great Britain (EIC before 1707 = technically English, not British)
British Parliament begins passing Acts for renewal of EIC Charter — power shifts from Crown to elected Parliament; same Parliament legislates governance of India

phases.label: EIC FACTORIES, SETTLEMENTS & KEY PERMISSIONS IN INDIA (1608–1717)

events.label: EIC sends Captain William Hawkins to Jahangir05-27's court — seeks factory @ Surat (most important west coast port; firmly in Portuguese-dominated territory); Jahangir initially gives Hawkins Mansab (rank 400) + Jagir; Hawkins ultimately expelled due to persistent Portuguese pressure
1st (temporary) EIC factory in India @ Masulipatnam (Northern Sarkars, Andhra Pradesh)

Battle of Swally (Battle of Suvali) — Captain Thomas Best leads EIC fleet to decisive victory over Portuguese; Mughal State pleased (Mughal ships perpetually vulnerable to Portuguese piracy); 1612 = military victory & local Mughal governor's temporary parwana
Jahangir05-27 issues imperial farman — legal right for EIC to set up permanent factory @ Surat; 1613 = legally permanent imperial farman

Thomas Roe at Jahangir05-27's court (arrived Surat 1615) — formal ambassador of King James I03-25; Jahangir refuses formal treaty between equals; Roe extracts Royal Farman (1618) via sustained diplomacy + personal rapport: right to establish factories throughout Mughal Empire + liberal trading rights (lower customs duties); Roe's account = major primary source on Mughal Empire New EIC factories @ Calicut (Malabar/Kerala) & Burhanpur (Deccan)

EIC factories established @ Agra, Ahmedabad, Broach (Bharuch) — all within Mughal Empire; operating under Surat Presidency (1618) Surat Presidency established — 1st EIC administrative Presidency in India; coordinates all English trade on west coast before later shift to Bombay (1687); Royal Farman of 1618 from Jahangir05-27 grants liberal trading rights across Mughal Empire

Emperor Shahjahan27-58 orders Bengal governor Qasim Khan to defeat & eject Portuguese from Hugli — Portuguese misusing trade privileges: piracy + slave trade from Bengal base EIC factories @ Balasore & Hariharpur (Odisha) — 1st factories in east India

EIC (led by Francis Day) purchases land @ Madraspatanam village from Hindu Nayakas (provincial governors of Vijayanagara Empire); Fort St George construction begins 1639, completed 1644 — 1st fort built by EIC in India
Fort St George completed @ Madras
EIC factory @ Hugli (Bengal) — 1st EIC factory in Bengal; permitted by nishan from Shah Shuja (Mughal governor of Bengal; son of Shahjahan27-58)
Madras Presidency (Presidency of Fort St George) formally established — London order 1652; implemented in India 1653 (both dates appear in different sources)
EIC factory @ Kasimbazar (western Bengal)

Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1661 @ Whitehall, London — occasion: marriage of King Charles II60-85 to Princess Catherine of Braganza (Portugal); dowry: (i) Portugal pays 500,000 pounds cash; (ii) England receives Bombay + Tangier (Morocco); (iii) England protects Portugal's remaining possessions; guarantees continued Portuguese presence in Goa, Daman & Diu until 1961
British Crown transfers Bombay to EIC @ annual rent of 10 pounds; EIC factory @ Dacca (eastern Bengal)

Anglo-Mughal War (Child's War) — EIC defeated by Mughal forces Bombay Presidency established — replaces Surat as EIC's western HQ; Maratha power growing in Gujarat made Surat risky; Bombay Castle (Casa Da Orta) originally built by Portuguese

Aurangzeb58-07 pardons EIC — imperial order to resume trade; EIC founds settlement @ Sutanuti village (Calcutta establishment; Job Charnock); EIC purchases Fort Saint David @ Cuddalore from Maratha Chhatrapati Rajaram89-00
Provincial farman from Ibrahim Khan (Subahdar of Bengal; approved by Aurangzeb58-07) — duty-free trade in Bengal; EIC pays Rs 3,000 per annum; provincial-level only
Fort William built @ Calcutta — named after King William III89-02
EIC acquires Zamindari of Kolikata, Sutanuti & Govindapur from Sabarna Roy Chowdhury family for 1,300 rupees
Calcutta Presidency (Presidency of Fort William) established — Calcutta eventually accounts for 60% of all EIC trade from India

Imperial farman of Farukhsiyar13-19 — 'Magna Carta of the Company'; secured via Dr William Hamilton's medical treatment of the Emperor; grants dastaks (passes for duty-free movement of goods); imperial-level farman (contrast with 1691 provincial farman)
Fort William College established @ Calcutta by Wellesley98-05 — for training EIC civil servants
England + Ireland unite -> United Kingdom (before 1801, EIC = British not UK)
Calcutta Port Act 1870 creates Calcutta Port Commissioners & Calcutta Port Trust — 1st formal legal authority to govern the port

Danish EIC established — Charter of King Christian IV88-48 of Denmark-Norway; 12-year monopoly over trade with East Indies; driven by envy of Dutch & English profits; financial base weaker, military capacity limited
1st Danish factory @ Tranquebar (Tharangambadi), Tamil Nadu; 1st fort: Fort Dansborg; Tranquebar = official administrative HQ of Danish India until 1845
Brief factory @ Pondicherry under Roland Crappé — quickly abandoned due to lack of resources; long before French arrived
Factories @ Masulipatnam (Andhra Pradesh); Pipli & Balasore (Odisha)
1st Danish company ends
2nd Danish EIC established
Factory @ Serampore (Srirampur / Frederiksnagore), Hooghly District, Bengal — parwana from Nawab Alivardi Khan40-56; most commercially successful & culturally significant Danish trading post in India

Serampore Mission Press established — with Baptist missionaries including William Carey; translates Bible into Indian vernacular languages; runs schools; major contribution to early printing & education in Bengal
All Danish mainland settlements sold to British EIC
Nicobar Islands sold to British (today India's Andaman & Nicobar Islands UT)

phases.label: FRENCH IN INDIA — COMPAGNIE DES INDES ORIENTALES (1664–1954)

events.label: King Louis XIV43-15 — great-grandfather of Louis XVI (overthrown in French Revolution 1789)
French East India Company (Compagnie des Indes Orientales) founded by Jean-Baptiste Colbert under Louis XIV43-15 — started as private company, later nationalised (= PSU in today's terms)
Aurangzeb58-07 issues farman to French — permission to trade @ Surat
French 1st factory @ Surat — on farman from Aurangzeb58-07 (1667)
French factory @ Masulipatnam — on farman from Sultan of Golconda (1518–1687)
Permission from Shaista Khan64-88 (Mughal Governor of Bengal) to set up township @ Chandernagore — but French financial crunch delays actual settlement
French acquire Pondicherry from Sultan of Bijapur (Sikandar Adil Shah72-86) & his local governor Sher Khan Lodi — occupancy sequence: Portuguese (16th c) -> Danes (briefly 1624) -> French (1674)
French actually establish settlement @ Chandernagore (despite 1673 permission) Dutch briefly capture Pondicherry
François Martin01-06 (Governor-General) centralises French admin — makes Pondicherry capital; builds Fort Louis; real founder of French power in India
François Martin01-06 as Governor-General Mauritius established as French colony (proper control only by 1735 under Mahé de La Bourdonnais35-46 as Governor)
French acquire Mahe from local Nair ruler Vazhunnavar (obtained permission 1721; built trade settlement 1724-25 after overcoming rebellion); named after Mahé de La Bourdonnais
French acquire Yanam — permission from Nizam-ul-Mulk24-48 (Asaf Jah I) of Hyderabad

Trade settlement @ Mahe built Mahé de La Bourdonnais35-46 as Governor of Mauritius — arrives from Mauritius with naval fleet in 1746 to help Dupleix42-54 French acquire Karaikal — granted by Pratap Singh39-63 (Maratha ruler of Tanjore/Thanjavur) as reward for French help in his succession dispute
1st Carnatic War — Dupleix42-54 captures Madras from British (with help of Mahé de La Bourdonnais' fleet from Mauritius) British capture Pondicherry from French
Treaty of Paris — British restore Pondicherry to French
British capture Pondicherry again during later conflict

Treaty of Amiens — Britain + France + Batavian Republic; Dutch permanently cede coastal regions of Ceylon to Britain; Ceylon becomes British Crown Colony (ruled directly by British State; NOT by EIC; completely separate from EIC's Indian empire)
British finally return Pondicherry to French
Referendum in Chandernagore — merged into India
French Pondicherry (incl. Karaikal, Yanam, Mahe) transferred to India
Union Territory of Pondicherry formed — Puducherry (Tamil Nadu coast) + Karaikal (Tamil Nadu coast) + Yanam (Andhra Pradesh coast) + Mahe (Kerala/Arabian Sea coast)

phases.label: CEYLON — FROM PORTUGUESE TO CROWN COLONY (1658–1945)

events.label: Dutch remove Portuguese from Ceylon

British military captures Dutch areas of Ceylon — handed to EIC, managed through Madras Presidency Treaty of Amiens — Dutch (Batavian Republic) formally & permanently cede coastal regions of Ceylon to Britain; British government decides Ceylon too strategically important for a trading company

Ceylon declared British Crown Colony — ruled directly by British State through appointed Governor; completely separate from EIC's Indian empire (India = colony ruled by EIC with State-like powers; Ceylon = Crown Colony where British State itself governed directly)
Dutch East Indies (Indonesia) gains independence after WW2

anchors: Key Pattern — EIC Charter evolution = story of British power shifting from Crown to Parliament: 1600 Charter (Elizabeth I):
trade monopoly. 1609 Charter (James I): perpetual monopoly. 1657 Charter (Cromwell): permanent joint-stock company. 1661
Charter (Charles II): quasi-State powers (forts, troops, war/peace, civil/criminal jurisdiction). 1676: right to mint money. 1793+:
Parliament renews Charter — same Parliament that debates & legislates governance of India. A trading company had, step by step
through successive Charters, accumulated the powers of a sovereign.
n Prelims Alert (2021) — St. Francis Xavier: St. Francis Xavier did NOT die in Goa. He died on Shangchuan Island off coast of
China in 1552 while attempting to enter mainland China for missionary work. His body was later brought to Goa (preserved in
Basilica of Bom Jesus, Old Goa). UPSC 2021 tested location of death, NOT burial. Do not confuse the two.
n Prelims Alert (2022) — Dutch & Gajapati Dynasty: Dutch did NOT receive land grants from the Gajapati dynasty of Odisha.
Gajapatis = 15th-century dynasty; power had declined well before Dutch arrived. Do not confuse later local rulers of Odisha coast
with Gajapati dynasty itself.
n Prelims Alert — Pondicherry occupation sequence (mnemonic: PDa-FDu-BFBF->India): Portuguese (16th c) -> Danes
(briefly 1624) -> French (1674) -> Dutch (captured briefly 1693) -> British (captured 1761) -> French (restored via Treaty of Paris
1763) -> British (captured again 1793) -> French (returned 1814) -> India (transferred 1954).

sections.title: How Did a Trading Company Become a State?
The 1st Carnatic War (1746–48) —the Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746)?
The 2nd Carnatic War (1749–54) — How Did Dupleix Invent the Blueprint for Empire in India?

phases.label: BACKGROUND: EIC BECOMES A STATE & TRADE WAR (1661–1691)

events.label: EIC Charter of Charles II60-85 — transforms EIC from commercial body to quasi-State: right to build forts, command troops, make war & peace, civil & criminal jurisdiction over settlements; 1st institutional foundation of British colonial rule
EIC given right to mint its own money

Anglo-Mughal War (Child's War) — named after Josiah Child (Chairman, Court of Directors, London) + John Child (Governor of Bombay & General of all EIC forces); reasons: (i) Aurangzeb's constant warfare disrupting EIC trade (hinterland sourcing); (ii) disputes with Nawab of Bengal over bribes & heavy customs duties; EIC seizes Hugli + attacks Mughal ships in Arabian Sea; Aurangzeb's military crushes EIC in both Bombay & Bengal EIC surrenders — Aurangzeb58-07 pardons EIC; EIC pays Rs 1.5 lakh compensation; Aurangzeb does NOT expel EIC (EIC economically useful: forex/gold for war + export business valuable + Indian bankers earn interest + Indian merchants/artisans/ryots benefit)

Farman (technically Parwana — issued by Subahdar of Bengal, not imperial farman; Aurangzeb's approval given) — restores EIC old privileges; right to duty-free trade in Bengal; EIC pays Rs 3,000 per annum

phases.label: PRE-WAR: SUCCESSION DISPUTES IN CARNATIC & HYDERABAD (1732–1748)

events.label: Maratha rule @ Tanjore begins — Venkoji (Ekoji; half-brother of Chhatrapati Shivaji74-80) conquers Thanjavur region

François Martin01-06 — Governor-General; Pondicherry = French capital; builds Fort Louis; real founder of French power in India Dost Ali Khan32-40 — Nawab of Carnatic; Chanda Sahib = son-in-law of Dost Ali Khan Dost Ali Khan32-40 killed by Marathas under Raghuji Bhonsle @ Chittoor

Austrian War of Succession (1740–48) — European conflict; Britain & France fight each other across Europe, America & India; will directly trigger 1st Carnatic War Dupleix42-54 — Governor-General of French EIC; personal ambitions of empire building + dominating international trade of South India; by 1740 French EIC trade roughly half value of British EIC trade Anwar-ud-din44-49 — appointed Nawab of Carnatic by Nizam of Hyderabad in 1744 Nizam-ul-Mulk24-48 dies — succession dispute: son Nasir Jung48-50 vs grandson Muzaffar Jung50-51

phases.label: 1ST CARNATIC WAR (1746–1748) — INDIAN CHAPTER OF AUSTRIAN WAR OF SUCCESSION

events.label: Dupleix42-54 captures EIC's Fort St George @ Madras — EIC defeated; Nawab of Carnatic Anwar-ud-din44-49 intervenes expecting French to hand over fort; Dupleix refuses

Battle of Adyar / St Thome (1746) — fought on north bank of River Adyar; French force: ~700 French-trained Indian sepoys + 300 French soldiers vs Nawab's 10,000 traditional cavalry; French win decisively; 3 decisive advantages: (i) superior light mobile artillery repositioned rapidly; (ii) tactical discipline — coordinated formations incl. infantry squares (hold ground vs cavalry from any direction); (iii) regular cash salaries (professional reliable fighting force; no desertion between campaigns); 1st conclusive proof: small disciplined European-trained infantry + modern artillery can crush vastly larger traditional Indian army; psychological impact enormous
1st Carnatic War ongoing — French dominant in South India In North America — more strategically important to France — Britain has won

Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748) — ends Austrian War of Succession; both sides return each other's possessions in America & India; Madras returned to EIC; Dupleix's Indian victories traded away at European negotiating table; deeply frustrating for Dupleix42-54

phases.label: 2ND CARNATIC WAR (1749–1754) — DUPLEIX INVENTS THE EMPIRE BLUEPRINT

events.label: Battle of Ambur — Nawab Anwar-ud-din44-49 killed; Chanda Sahib49-52 declared Nawab of Carnatic @ capital Arcot; French backing Chanda Sahib49-52 in Carnatic (mnemonic: Paris & moon/Chanda = symbol of romance) + Muzaffar Jung50-51 in Hyderabad (mnemonic: MuzaFFrance); EIC backs opposite sides — Nasir Jung48-50 @ Hyderabad + Md Ali52-95 @ Carnatic
Nasir Jung48-50 killed — Muzaffar Jung50-51 declared Nizam; Bussy (junior of Dupleix42-54) accompanies Muzaffar Jung50-51 marching toward Hyderabad

Battle of Lakkireddipalli Pass — Muzaffar Jung50-51 killed by Afghan Nawab of Kurnool (felt cheated; not given promised territory); Nawab of Kurnool also killed; Bussy reaches Hyderabad; installs Salabat Jung51-62 as Nizam (son of Nizam-ul-Mulk24-48 + uncle of killed Muzaffar Jung)

PHASE 1 FRENCH GAINS: (i) Hyderabad: Bussy made French Resident + French army stationed for Nizam's protection; payment = Northern Sarkars (present-day Andhra Pradesh); Bussy administers it + keeps revenues; Bussy's methods = brutal terror & massacre of civilians for LR (Andhra folklore: 'boochi' = ghost/feared = derived from Bussy's name); also extracts personal jagirs @ Masulipatnam & Yanam + Rs 2,00,000 pounds for French EIC from Nizam; (ii) Carnatic: Dupleix42-54 declares himself Nawab of all lands between River Krishna & Cape Comorin with Chanda Sahib49-52 as Deputy Nawab; extracts personal jagir Rs 1 lakh/annum @ Villianallur near Pondicherry
DUPLEIX'S EMPIRE BLUEPRINT (later copied by EIC): put candidate in power -> station army at his expense -> extract territory as payment -> sit as real power behind the throne

PHASE 2 — EIC bounces back: Dupleix42-54 obsessed with eliminating Md Ali52-95 @ Trichinopoly -> critical mistake: leaves capital Arcot unguarded; Robert Clive operates from Madras with ~200 Europeans + 300 sepoys; TAKES OVER ARCOT; defends it against massive counter-siege for 53 days; capital now with British; Clive becomes celebrated figure in Britain

French government in Paris refuses to reinforce Dupleix42-54 — anxious to honour 1748 treaty & preserve more lucrative American possessions; by 1754 French lose 2nd Carnatic War Chanda Sahib49-52 escapes to Tanjore (Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu) — beheaded by Pratap Singh39-63 (Maratha Raja of Thanjavur; old rival)

Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) — middle path: (i) French influence retained @ Hyderabad via Bussy + French army + Northern Sarkars; (ii) French factories @ Pondicherry & Carnatic retained; (iii) Md Ali52-95 becomes Nawab of Carnatic -> EIC influence in Carnatic
Dupleix42-54 recalled to France — replaced by Godeheu; reason: high war expenditure; dies in poverty in France in 1763, abandoned by the State he served

phases.label: 3RD CARNATIC WAR (1756–1763) — 7 YEARS' GLOBAL WAR COMES TO INDIA

events.label: 7 Years' Global War — fought across Europe, Americas, Africa & India; directly triggers 3rd Carnatic War; Count de Lally arrives from France with Royal military (French State, not French EIC) + Bussy of French EIC; Eyre Coote arrives from Britain with Royal military (British State, not EIC) + Robert Clive of EIC Battle of Plassey — EIC defeats Bengal Suba; large British Royal military troops already in India for 3rd Carnatic War gave Clive the military strength + Clive's shrewd diplomacy made Plassey possible; without Carnatic there may not have been a Plassey
Robert Clive arrives from Bengal — takes over Northern Sarkars after Bussy abandons them to reinforce Lally @ Carnatic (tactical mistake #1 for French)
Battle of Wandiwash — most decisive battle; French 'washed away'; French lose everywhere after this including Pondicherry (French HQ officially since 1701 with Fort Louis)

Treaty of Paris (1763) — France loses all gains made in India since 1749; restricted to pre-1749 position; France retains only 5 small trading posts: Pondicherry + Mahe + Karaikal + Yanam + Chandernagore; barred from maintaining strong army or fortifying bases
Dupleix42-54 dies in poverty in France — abandoned by the State he had served; same year as Treaty of Paris
Treaty of Hyderabad (1766) — Hyderabad formally cedes Northern Sarkars to EIC in exchange for Rs 7 lakh annually + protection against Marathas & Mysore
French EIC abolished by France — French government gives up ambitions of dominating international trade of India
Hyderabad signs Subsidiary Alliance with EIC — 1st Indian state to do so
Mysore signs Subsidiary Alliance with EIC
Carnatic formally annexed by EIC
Travancore signs Subsidiary Alliance with EIC

anchors: Key Pattern — Dupleix's Empire Blueprint (1749–51); later copied by EIC for next century: (1) Back your candidate in local
succession dispute. (2) Put him in power with French military support. (3) Station French army at his expense. (4) Extract territory
as payment for that army (Northern Sarkars from Hyderabad). (5) Sit in the court as real power behind the throne (Bussy as
Resident @ Nizam's court). Result: political influence + territorial control + revenue — all without formal annexation. EIC refined
this into the Subsidiary Alliance system used to dominate India for the next century.
Key Link — Carnatic Wars -> Battle of Plassey (1757): 3rd Carnatic War (1756–63) brought large numbers of British Royal
military troops to India. This military strength + Clive's shrewd diplomacy = Plassey possible. Without Carnatic, there may not have
been a Plassey. Without Plassey, there may not have been a Company State. Carnatic Wars (fought for trade) thus laid foundation
of British domination of South India AND enabled the territorial empire that followed.
n Prelims Alert (1995) — Battle-to-combatant match (UPSC jumbled pairs; pin all four): Battle of Buxar (1764) = EIC vs Mir
Qasim (with Awadh + Shah Alam II60-06). Battle of Chilianwala (1849) = EIC under Dalhousie48-56 vs Sikhs (2nd Anglo-Sikh
War). Battle of Kharda (1795) = Nizam of Hyderabad vs the Marathas. Battle of Wandiwash (1760) = French vs EIC.
