events.label: 1613 Farman (Jahangir05-27) — right to establish factory @ Surat after EIC defeats Portuguese @ Battle of Suvali 1612
1618 Farman (Jahangir05-27) — right to establish factories in whole of Mughal Empire + liberal trading rights; secured via Thomas Roe (British Resident 1615-19)
1691 Farman (technically Parwana — issued by Subahdar of Bengal under Aurangzeb58-07's approval) — right to DFT in Bengal in exchange for Rs 3,000 per annum; EIC trade brings forex into India

1717 Imperial/Royal Farman (Farukhsiyar13-19) — 'Magna Carta of the Company'; secured via Dr William Hamilton's medical treatment of Emperor; gives EIC: (i) DFT in Bengal, Gujarat & Deccan; (ii) right to use Royal Mint (save cost of converting gold to Indian sikkas); (iii) right to rent 38 villages around Calcutta

Dastak misuse — Dastaks (EIC duty-free permits) misused by EIC officials for own private trade + sold to other exporters; by 1750: private trade by EIC officials ~1,00,000 pounds per annum (roughly 50x their annual salaries); causes customs duty evasion + revenue loss for Bengal Suba

MQK17-27 (Nawab of Bengal) response to 1717 Farman: (i) allows DFT for EIC; (ii) refuses Dastak misuse for private trade; (iii) refuses use of Royal Mint (hurts sovereign authority + govt earns commission on gold-to-Sikka conversion); (iv) allows renting of villages but NOT purchase Alivardi Khan40-56 (Nawab) — pragmatic; follows diplomacy over military confrontation; tolerates EIC provocations because: (i) EIC trade economically beneficial to Bengal; (ii) aware of Battle of Adyar 1746 (proves European infantry's military superiority) EIC begins adding fortifications to Fort William @ Calcutta — strengthening walls, filling gaps, raising height — WITHOUT permission of Alivardi Khan40-56; military challenge to Bengal's sovereign authority; Alivardi Khan tolerates it

phases.label: ROAD TO PLASSEY — SIRAJ56-57 & THE CONSPIRACY (1756–1757)

events.label: Siraj-ud-daula56-57 succeeds Alivardi Khan40-56 — precious grandson (only grandson, through daughter; no sons); young, impulsive; disliked in Bengal court (had disrespected senior Mansabdars; imprisoned Jagat Seth for extortion); immediately stops Dastak misuse -> hurts private trade fortunes of EIC officials

EIC gives asylum to Krishna Ballabh (fugitive from Siraj's court, charged with fraud) for money; then adds new fortifications to Calcutta; Siraj56-57 seizes EIC factory @ Kasimbazar, then captures Calcutta

Black Hole Tragedy — British prisoners locked overnight in small airless guardroom in Fort William; colonial account (J.Z. Holwell, survivor + briefly Governor of Bengal): 146 locked in, 123 died; modern historians: ~30-40 actual deaths; became powerful propaganda tool to justify EIC's military response + demonise Indian rulers

Robert Clive arrives from Madras with Royal military forces — recaptures Calcutta; Treaty of Alinagar (name Siraj had given Calcutta) restores all EIC privileges; Clive destroys Hugli port (used by French); defeats French @ Chandarnagar (7 Years' Global War 1756-63 live); French threat in Bengal neutralised CONSPIRACY — NOT a battle: Mir Jafar (technically Bakhshi of Bengal Suba = war paymaster + head of military intelligence; in practice real commander since Siraj young & inexperienced) approaches Clive; makes deal to remove Siraj56-57

Battle of Plassey — Mir Jafar57-60 ensures bulk of Bengal army does NOT fight + turns back; Siraj56-57 easily defeated; flees; captured & beheaded on Mir Jafar's son Miran's orders; Plassey = no real battle; 1st real EIC military victory comes 7 years later @ Buxar (1764)
Mir Jafar57-60 — Subahdar of Bengal; EIC's puppet; political supremacy of EIC in India begins Holwell builds monument in memory of Black Hole Tragedy — falls into ruin; demolished 1821
Viceroy Curzon99-05 builds marble replica of Black Hole monument @ same spot

Netaji Bose leads agitation to remove Curzon's monument — calls it colonial propaganda to tarnish Siraj's image; uses campaign to build Hindu-Muslim unity; monument shifted from public square to graveyard of St. John's Church, Calcutta (where it stands today)

Immediate financial settlement: (i) Rs 2.25 crore to EIC; (ii) 2,75,000 pounds to Royal British military; (iii) 2,34,000 pounds to Clive personally + personal jagir of 35,000 pounds per annum; scale: ~x32,000 multiplier; in 1760 terms = ~3.5% of Britain's total GDP of GBP 70 million

Additional 2.5 million pounds extracted by EIC from Bengal as 'political gifts' Post-Plassey structural changes: (i) rampant Dastak misuse; EIC officials make fortunes from private domestic trade via Gomastas (Indian agents procure goods from peasants + artisans; cut out Indian merchants; pay no domestic taxes); (ii) trade structure: before Plassey = gold shipped from Britain to buy Indian goods; after Plassey = Bengal's Diwani revenues fund purchase of Indian + Chinese goods (tea, silk, porcelain); gold from Bengal treasury shipped to Britain -> gold inflow flips to gold OUTFLOW -> Drain of Wealth begins; (iii) EIC uses Plassey Plunder to build large standing army (funded from extracted wealth not company profits)

events.label: Mir Jafar57-60 as Nawab — when he can no longer meet EIC's growing financial demands, EIC replaces him with son-in-law Mir Qasim60-63 (efficient administrator) Mir Qasim60-63 — able man; refuses to be puppet; shifts base from Murshidabad to Bihar; (i) punishes Zamindars who underreport LR; (ii) abolishes all internal duties on domestic trade to create level playing field between Indian merchants and untaxed EIC Gomastas; autonomous behaviour intolerable to EIC EIC defeats Mir Qasim60-63 in battle in Bihar; restores Mir Jafar57-60 as puppet Nawab of Bengal (1763-65); Qasim60-63 escapes westward to Awadh
Mir Jafar57-60 — Nawab of Bengal (2nd stint)

phases.label: BATTLE OF BUXAR (1764) — EIC GETS THE RIGHT TO RULE

events.label: Imad-ul-Mulk (Wazir; also called Gaddar-ul-Mulk) blinds Emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur — 1st Mughal Emperor destroyed by own Wazir
Imad-ul-Mulk murders Emperor Alamgir II — 2nd successive Mughal Emperor destroyed by same Wazir; Shah Alam II60-06 leaves Delhi (fears same fate + frustrated with court factionalism)

Shah Alam II60-06 attacks Bengal to establish own kingdom (Bengal had stopped paying tribute since 1751) — defeated by EIC; thereafter lives in Awadh with Shuja54-75 as Wazir; EIC treats him with respect (symbolic sovereignty of Mughal State resides in him = EIC's legal legitimacy in India)
Mir Qasim60-63 forges alliance with Shuja-ud-Daula54-75 (Nawab of Awadh) + Shah Alam II60-06; Shuja54-75 agrees on promise of 3 crore rupees + Bihar territory + treasury after victory

Battle of Buxar (BoBuxar1764) — fought in Bihar; Indian side had prepared DEFENSIVE strategy (lay siege to EIC-held fort); Shuja54-75 loses patience; IGNORES explicit advice of Qasim60-63; switches to OFFENSIVE strategy; direct attack on fort -> hands advantage to EIC; battle closely fought; Indian side appears to be winning at one point; EIC commander Hector Munroe launches final charge -> tables turned; EIC wins; Clive in London at the time

Aftermath: Qasim60-63 escapes + dies in obscurity; Shuja54-75 treated leniently (not beheaded); Shah Alam II60-06 treated with great respect — his symbolic sovereignty = EIC's legal legitimacy in India

phases.label: TREATY OF ALLAHABAD (ToA1765) — LEGAL FOUNDATION OF COMPANY STATE

events.label: Treaty of Allahabad (ToA1765) — signed by Clive (EIC) + Shah Alam II60-06 + Shuja54-75; most consequential treaty in Indian history; lays legal + structural foundation of Company State in India; Clive does insider trading on EIC shares (asks broker to buy before terms become public)

@ THE EMPEROR: EIC promises Shah Alam II60-06: (i) annual tribute of Rs 26 lakh; (ii) military help to recapture Delhi from Rohilla Afghans (who held it since 1761); (iii) Allahabad + Kora (taken from Awadh) to maintain Emperor's status; EIC absorbs itself into existing Mughal legal-political structure = positions itself as a Mansabdar; Bengal = EIC's Watan Jagir in legal terms; in practice: EIC never paid Rs 26 lakh nor supplied army to recapture Delhi (all legal formality)

@ BENGAL — DIWANI: EIC receives Diwani of Bengal Suba (Bengal + Orissa + Bihar) = 1st time EIC formally receives a SOVEREIGN FUNCTION (power to tax); before Buxar: EIC had only trade income (since 31 Dec 1600); from 1765: trade income + tax revenue from richest province of India; Drain of Wealth now LEGAL not plunder

DUAL GOVERNMENT (1765-72): Diwani (revenue + civil admin + civil justice) legally with EIC; Nizamat (law & order + criminal justice + military) legally with Nawab; EIC appoints Deputy Nawab (Naib Nazim) Md Reza Khan as its Diwan; INDIRECT RULE installed: (i) Nawab = puppet; (ii) British Resident stationed @ court; (iii) Resident controls puppet @ AWADH: (i) Shuja54-75 pays Rs 50 lakh to EIC as compensation; (ii) Benaras separated from Awadh (EIC formally annexes 1775); (iii) Kora + Allahabad to Emperor; (iv) EIC granted DFT in Awadh (Dastak misuse begins there too); (v) Policy of Ring Fence initiated: military alliance = if anyone attacks EIC in Bengal, Awadh treaty-bound to help; (vi) Mini Subsidiary Alliance: Awadh army reduced + EIC army permanently stationed in Awadh + paid for by Awadh via annual subsidy

Great Bengal Famine (GBF 1770) — kills ~1 crore people (estimated one-third of Bengal's population); high LR demand + harsh tax collection continues even as crops fail; grain hoarding unchecked; neither EIC nor Nawab takes responsibility for famine relief; LR collection + law & order collapses -> forces EIC to establish Direct Rule

Dual Government formally ended — EIC takes over Nizamat legally from Nawab; replaces Indian administrators with own officers; Direct Rule established in Bengal; Nawab of Bengal = as powerless a figurehead as Chhatrapati of Marathas after Treaty of Sangola 1750
EIC formally annexes Benaras (separated from Awadh at ToA1765)
Hyderabad signs FULL Subsidiary Alliance with EIC — 1st Indian state to do so (NOT Awadh; Awadh had only mini/proto SA in 1765)
Awadh signs full Subsidiary Alliance — army disbanded + foreign policy taken over; architecture drawn at ToA1765 but formal full SA only now

tables.title: ANCHOR TABLE: 7 VICIOUS-CHAIN CONSEQUENCES OF SA FOR INDIAN STATES
lines: # CONSEQUENCE MECHANISM / EXAMPLE
1 Disbanded armies -> mass Military men (Mansabdars + sepoys) lose positions + livelihoods; EIC recruits sepoys
unemployment from OUTSIDE host State to prevent loyalty to Nawab = Divide & Rule
2 EIC compounds military power at EIC maintains + commands Indian State's army; has taken over Foreign Policy -> can
host State's expense deploy these armies for own wars elsewhere; Indian State pays for army that EIC uses
# CONSEQUENCE MECHANISM / EXAMPLE
3 Subsidy = Drain of Wealth High subsidy payments + EIC gradually increases demands; same money could have
been used for host State's own development
4 Tax hikes -> unrest To pay ever-rising subsidy, rulers raise taxes; high taxes -> unpopularity + peasant
resentment + conditions for unrest
5 Maladministration accusations -> Ruler has no real power (British Resident has established Indirect Rule in breach of
annexation treaty's own promise of non-interference); ruler has no power but all responsibility;
starkest example: Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh annexed 1856
6 Territory in lieu of cash When subsidy cannot be paid in cash, EIC takes territory: half of Awadh annexed 1801
as permanent subsidy payment; Hyderabad forced to give Berar 1853
7 Permanent loss of Losing Foreign Policy + military control = Indian States permanently lose ability to form
alliance-forming capacity alliances AGAINST the EIC; SA = sophisticated Divide & Rule instrument at subcontinent
level

anchors: Key Pattern — What SA Is: PoSA = PoIR (informally) + PoRF + EIC Military replacing Indian State's Military + annual subsidy +
loss of Foreign Policy. SA was NOT a Wellesley98-05 invention — it has French root (Dupleix42-54 @ Hyderabad 1751) + British
root (Clive57-67 @ Awadh ToA1765). Wellesley98-05 FORMALISED it as a policy: added Foreign Policy takeover + disbanding of
Indian State's army + implemented State by State across India. EIC via SA got all military + diplomatic powers with NO
responsibility of ruling + NO burden of finances. Every single SA signatory ended up either annexed or permanently dependent.
Key Distinction — Mini SA vs Full SA: Mini/proto SA (ToA1765 with Awadh) = EIC army stationed + paid by Awadh + Awadh
army size reduced + British Resident; BUT Awadh's army NOT disbanded + Foreign Policy NOT taken over. Full SA = army
disbanded + Foreign Policy taken over + British Resident. The legal loophole: EIC maintained army using Indian State's subsidy ->
legal ownership of army arguably still Indian; EIC closed this by taking Foreign Policy = decision of war & peace = right to deploy
army -> legally with EIC.
n Prelims Alert (2018 + 2021 — same Q both years) — What does NOT apply to SA? False option: 'Secure a fixed income for
the Company.' SA's annual subsidy was earmarked ONLY for maintaining EIC army in host State — NOT surplus income for EIC.
True options: maintain large standing army + defend against Napoleonic danger + establish British paramountcy.
n Prelims Alert (1999) — Who kept British flag flying high during Napoleon's era? Answer: Lord Wellesley = Wellesley98-05
(tenure 1798-1805 overlaps Napoleon's offensive phase 1796-1812). NOT Warren Hastings73-85 (pre-Napoleon era). NOT
Francis Hastings13-23 / Lord Hastings (post-Napoleon era). Two different GGs share the surname Hastings — easy exam trap.
n Prelims Alert (2018) — Fort William College: Founded by Wellesley98-05 in 1800 @ Calcutta. Purpose: train British civil
servants in Indian languages, laws & customs BEFORE posting to districts. UPSC tested: institution-founder pair (2018) + purpose
of establishment (2020 + 2021).

events.label: Battle of Colachel — Travancore (Marthanda Varma29-58) defeats Dutch East India Company; permanently ends Dutch political + military power in Kerala; Travancore builds centralised revenue-based State

Marthanda Varma29-58 — builds modern Travancore State; defeats Dutch at Colachel (1741); centralises revenue Hyder Ali61-82 establishes modern arsenal (arms factory) @ Dindigul Fort — with French help (present in Mahe); 1st step in military modernisation before he even comes to full power

Rama Varma58-98 — Travancore; maintains EIC alliance as hedge against Mysore; EIC alliance with Travancore = trigger for Tipu82-99's 1789 attack on Travancore Hyder Ali61-82 seizes effective power in Mysore — overthrows corrupt PM NanjRaj; keeps Wodeyar as nominal head of State

Hyder Ali61-82 reigns: (i) French assistance for military training + technology transfer; (ii) army structured into Risalas (regiments) — each commander directly appointed by King; (iii) iron-cased rocket artillery developed (100% indigenous; range 2 km; iron casings don't burst); (iv) systematically subjugates Poligars + Deshmukhs; (v) Military Fiscalism: Khalisa land expanded; Jagirdari minimised; Deshmukhs removed as intermediaries; sericulture introduced; (vi) State-owned trade model established End of 3rd Carnatic War — Treaty of Paris 1763; EIC dominant in South India; Carnatic under EIC indirect influence since 2nd Carnatic War (Md Ali52-95 on throne)
Hyder Ali61-82 annexes Malabar (heart of spice trade — pepper, cardamom, ginger) + Calicut — critical source of pepper for EIC now under Mysore's control

EIC promises to help Hyderabad invade Mysore in exchange for Northern Sarkars (important to connect Bengal with Madras); Marathas also see Mysore as rival -> EIC crafts triple alliance: EIC + Hyderabad + Marathas to invade Mysore

Treaty of Hyderabad (1766) — Hyderabad formally cedes Northern Sarkars (4 districts: Chicacole/Srikakulam, Rajmandri/Rajahmundry, Ellore/Eluru, MustafaNagar/Kondapalli; Guntur added later as 5th) to EIC in exchange for Rs 7 lakh annually + protection against Marathas + Mysore

Hyder Ali61-82 BREAKS triple alliance through diplomacy: (i) pays Marathas Rs 35 lakh to exit war; (ii) makes alliance with Hyderabad: pays Nizam Rs 20 lakh + promises to make Nizam's son Nawab of Carnatic + agrees to jointly attack Carnatic (under Md Ali52-95, EIC ally)
Hyderabad fears counter-invasion by EIC -> exits by making peace with EIC; EIC navy from Bombay captures coastal areas of Mysore (e.g. Mangalore)
Hyder Ali61-82 outmanoeuvres EIC forces; marches army to the GATES OF MADRAS; EIC fearing destruction of Madras forced to sign Treaty of Madras

Treaty of Madras (1769) — both sides return conquered territories; agree to defensive military alliance (each promises to help other if attacked by third party); PoRF arrangement on paper only — fake alliance in practice
Marathas attack Mysore — EIC REFUSES to honour its 1769 treaty obligation to come to Mysore's defence; Hyder Ali61-82 notes the betrayal
1st Anglo-Maratha War — EIC vs Marathas American War of Independence (1776-83) — France joins against Britain in 1778; France + Britain now in conflict
France enters American War of Independence against Britain
EIC seizes Mahe port (French port in Malabar; under Mysore's military protection) — Hyder Ali61-82 was importing French arms + ammunition through Mahe; final trigger for war
Hyder Ali61-82 invades Carnatic (EIC ally) + captures Arcot

Battle of Pollilur — Hyder Ali61-82 inflicts one of worst defeats ever on a European army in India; Colonel Baillie's disciplined infantry formations annihilated; Hyder Ali's troops use iron-cased rockets to devastating effect; shock to EIC
events.full: Battle of Pollilur — Hyder Ali61-82 inflicts one of worst defeats ever on a European army in India; Colonel Baillie's disciplined infantry formations annihilated; Hyder Ali's troops use iron-cased rockets to devastating effect; shock to EIC (Prelims tested: rocket-warfare innovation by Mysore)

events.label: Triple Confederacy (Marathas + Mysore + Hyderabad) against EIC — engineered by Nana Fadnis (de-facto ruler + most important minister in Peshwa's council; 1st Indian statesman to understand EIC had territorial ambitions not just commercial); Hyderabad joins because EIC illegally occupied Guntur + stopped paying Rs 7 lakh annual payment for Northern Sarkars Treaty of Salbai (ToSalbai1782) — Hastings73-85 signs with Marathas; ends 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82); Marathas withdraw from Triple Confederacy; Nana Fadnis ensures Marathas don't send army in favour of British (Chanakya Neeti: let both rivals destroy each other)
Hastings73-85 returns Guntur to Hyderabad — removes their grievance; Hyderabad exits Triple Confederacy; Mysore now isolated
Hyder Ali61-82 dies of cancer — Tipu82-99 takes over; continues war

Tipu82-99 reigns: (i) builds modern navy; (ii) establishes State-owned trading company (30 trading centres in India + abroad including Muscat, Oman); (iii) trade embargo on pepper, cardamom + sandalwood exports from Mysore-controlled ports; bars local merchants from dealing with British traders; (iv) Mauludi lunisolar calendar introduced (replaces Islamic Hijri; based on Prophet's birth era); (v) sends delegations to France, Turkey (Ottoman Empire) + Egypt seeking anti-British alliances Treaty of Mangalore (1784) — war ends in stalemate; both sides return each other's territories; status quo maintained
Tipu82-99 puts trade embargo on Travancore's pepper exports; Travancore is formal EIC ally
Tipu82-99 attacks Travancore (formal EIC ally) — gives Cornwallis86-93 the justification to declare war on Mysore

EIC forms Triple Alliance with Marathas + Hyderabad to fight Mysore (2nd triple alliance; 1st was 1766-67); King of Coorg signs alliance with EIC + helps Cornwallis86-93's army navigate the mountains (Coorg is in Western Ghats between Mysore and Malabar; Kodavas had been resisting Mysore occupation since Tipu82-99's 1785 brutalities there)

Combined forces of EIC + Marathas + Hyderabad put Mysore under severe military pressure from multiple directions; Tipu82-99 fights hard but cannot hold against coordinated three-front campaign Treaty of Seringapatam/Srirangapatnam (1792): (i) Mysore loses HALF its Kingdom including Malabar, Dindigul + Baramahal; (ii) Tipu82-99 pays war fine of 3 crore rupees; (iii) Tipu82-99 forced to surrender TWO of his own sons as hostages to guarantee compliance
Napoleon begins offensive phase in Europe (1796-1812)

Napoleon attacks Egypt — goal: control Middle East + hurt British trade; exchanges communications with Tipu82-99; Wellesley98-05 uses Tipu's secret letters to French as proof of threat + gets British approval for war

4th Anglo-Mysore War: EIC + Hyderabad fight Mysore (Hyderabad must due to SA of 1798); Peshwa Bajirao II96-18 does NOT send army on advice of Nana Fadnis; Arthur Wellesley (Royal regiment, NOT EIC officer) among key military commanders @ Siege of Srirangapatnam Tipu82-99 dies defending his capital Srirangapatnam — last major military threat to EIC in south eliminated

Post-war division: best parts of remaining Mysore (Kanara, Coimbatore + others) divided between EIC + Hyderabad; remaining central core given to old Wodeyar dynasty; five-year-old Krishnaraja III placed on throne under Subsidiary Alliance (1799); some territory offered to Peshwa conditional on signing SA but Marathas refuse on advice of Nana Fadnis

Dhondia Wagh — former prisoner of Tipu82-99; escapes after Seringapatam (1799); raises mounted force from demobilised Mysore soldiers (SA disbanded army); raids Mysore-Maratha borderlands; styles himself 'King of Two Worlds'; threatens EIC supply lines
Colonel Arthur Wellesley kills Dhondia Wagh in action — EIC formally supreme in southern India by 1801

phases.label: CARNATIC ANNEXED (1801) + TRAVANCORE SA (1805) + KUNDARA PROCLAMATION (1809)

events.label: 2nd Carnatic War — EIC gets indirect influence over Carnatic; Md Ali Wallajah (Md Ali52-95) placed on throne @ Arcot as EIC ally Md Ali52-95 — Nawab of Carnatic; EIC's loyal ally since 2nd Carnatic War Carnatic Debts mechanism: successive Nawabs borrow massive sums from private EIC officials at high interest rates; use Jagirs of Carnatic as collateral; EIC officials collect LR from fertile Carnatic lands directly as interest payment; Carnatic's wealth quietly extracted BEFORE formal annexation
Md Ali52-95 dies; Travancore signs 'Treaty of Perpetual Friendship' with EIC (agrees to pay for British force to protect against Tipu82-99)
Rama Varma58-98 dies — Travancore enters fiscal + political strain
British Resident stationed in Travancore's court — imprint of ToA1765 model; Indirect Rule begins

Carnatic annexed by Wellesley98-05 — six years after death of Md Ali52-95; justifications: (i) maladministration; (ii) Nawab had secretly communicated with Tipu82-99; Wellesley takes view that financially compromised Nawab not worth preserving even as puppet

Velu Thampi Dalawa — Prime Minister of Travancore 1802-09; leads revolt against EIC Travancore signs proper Subsidiary Alliance with Wellesley98-05 — EIC extracts it in exchange for helping king crush revolt by Nair troops (mutinied over non-payment of salary); State now loses sovereignty on standard SA template

Kundara Proclamation (January 1809) — Velu Thampi Dalawa issues from town of Kundara: public call to all Travancoreans to rise against British paramountcy; revolt supported by soldiers + peasants angered by heavy subsidy demands + constant British interference in internal affairs (direct breach of SA treaty's own promise of non-interference); one of most significant early revolts against British in South India
Kundara revolt crushed within months; Velu Thampi dies later in 1809; Travancore reduced to subservient SA state
SA with Cochin — southern consolidation complete; EIC paramount from Krishna to Kanyakumari
By 1809 with Kundara suppressed: EIC sets stage for 2nd + 3rd Anglo-Maratha Wars (1803-05, 1817-19) in north-west + Deccan

anchors: Key Pattern — EIC vs Mysore = clash of two mercantilist Military Fiscalist powers: Both followed Military Fiscalism (maximise
State revenue -> fund ever-stronger military). Both followed Mercantilism (State-directed trade; compete for same coastal routes +
markets). Two mercantilist powers competing over same trade routes + same coastal markets cannot coexist. EIC's diplomatic
advantage: Mysore's aggressive expansion threatened EVERY neighbouring state -> easier to build coalitions against Mysore.
Mysore lost because it fought largely alone; EIC always found coalition partners.
Tipu82-99's Religious Policy — Syncretic but Contradictory: PATRONAGE in Mysore heartland: patronised Sringeri Sharada
Math; wrote to its Shankaracharya; got yajnas conducted before wars; made generous grants to Hindu temples in Mysore.
COERCION in conquered Malabar + Coorg: forced conversions of Nairs + Christians in Malabar; destroyed churches + temples
during military campaigns; brutalities against Kodavas in Coorg (1785) who were resisting Mysore occupation. Conclusion:
secularism was NOT a value for Tipu82-99 but a tactic for domestic stability — values are hardest to change in personality.
n Prelims Alert — Battle of Pollilur (Sep 1780): Tested in UPSC Prelims for rocket-warfare innovation by Mysore. Hyder
Ali61-82's troops use iron-cased rockets to devastating effect — annihilates Col Baillie's disciplined infantry formations. Iron-cased
rockets: 100% indigenous; range 2 km; iron cylinder casings do NOT burst (unlike cardboard-cased rockets); William Congreve's
rockets (early 19th c British military) drawn directly from these designs.
n Alert — Kundara Proclamation (January 1809): Issued by Velu Thampi Dalawa (PM of Travancore 1802-09) from Kundara
town. One of most significant early revolts against British in South India. Causes: heavy subsidy demands + British interference in
internal affairs (breach of SA's own promise of non-interference). Revolt crushed within months; Velu Thampi dies 1809. Dalawa =
PM + Chief of Armed Forces; when used as Dewan under British = Head of ALL administration (revenue, civil, police, criminal
justice) since military was with British.

phases.label: PRE-WAR BACKGROUND — MARATHA FACTIONALISM & 1st WAR TRIGGER (1772–1782)

events.label: Maratha Civil War (brief): Narayan Rao72-73 — Peshwa; murdered 1773 in palace conspiracy by uncle Raghunath Rao73-74 Raghunath Rao73-74 becomes Peshwa after murder of nephew Narayan Rao72-73
Baarbhai Conspiracy (1774) — Nana Fadnis + 11 other ministers of Peshwa's council remove Raghunath Rao73-74 from power

Treaty of Surat (1775) — Raghunath Rao73-74 approaches EIC's Governor of Bombay William Hornby; signs treaty: EIC agrees to help him regain Peshwaship in return for Salsette + Bassein (Vasai, near Mumbai) + some revenue from Bharuch + Surat; pattern: succession dispute + losing claimant + Europeans offer military help in exchange for territory

Warren Hastings73-85 overturns Treaty of Surat to avoid expensive war expenditure; negotiates Treaty of Purandhar (1776) with Nana Fadnis: (i) EIC recognises Madhav Rao II74-95 as legitimate Peshwa; Raghunath Rao73-74 pensioned off; (ii) EIC receives Salsette + Bharuch; (iii) Marathas will not allow French presence in their domain
EIC in Bombay continues sheltering Raghunath Rao73-74; Nana Fadnis retaliates by offering a port to the French; talks collapse; war resumes
Battle of Wadgaon (near Pune) — Nana Fadnis + Mahadji Scindhia + Tukoji Rao Holkar defeat EIC + Raghunath Rao73-74; but war continues inconclusively

2nd Anglo-Mysore War — Marathas also engaged here; pressure on both fronts Treaty of Salbai (May 1782) — negotiated + signed @ Gwalior by Mahadji Scindhia on behalf of Marathas; ends 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82); terms: (i) military alliance: Marathas break Triple Confederacy + agree to fight alongside EIC if Hyder Ali61-82 doesn't restore territories taken from British + Nawab of Arcot (PoRF established by EIC with Marathas); (ii) EIC gets Salsette + Bharuch; (iii) no French settlements in Maratha domain; (iv) EIC returns all Maratha territory captured + recognises Madhav Rao II74-95 as Peshwa + pensions off Raghunath Rao73-74
Mahadji Scindhia dominates Maratha politics until his death in 1794 Madhav Rao II74-95 commits suicide — Bajirao II96-18 becomes Peshwa (formally tenured 1796-1818)

Nana Fadnis dies — the one man who had consistently held Maratha Confederacy together for two decades; factionalism accelerates sharply; Maratha capital Shaniwar Wada @ Pune engulfed in factionalism; Wellesley98-05 waiting for exactly this opportunity

Vithoji Rao Holkar captured + brutally executed on orders of Peshwa Bajirao II96-18 (conducting plundering campaigns on Peshwa's territories); to avenge death of stepbrother, Yashwantrao Holkar prepares retaliation
Yashwantrao Holkar attacks + defeats both Peshwa Bajirao II96-18 + Daulat Rao Scindhia (who supported Peshwa) — Bajirao II96-18 flees

Treaty of Bassein (ToB1802) — Bajirao II96-18 signs Subsidiary Alliance with EIC in exchange for EIC help to regain Peshwaship; great army of Svarajya to be disbanded once EIC reinstates Bajirao II96-18 as puppet Peshwa; triggers 2nd Anglo-Maratha War
Gaikwad of Baroda signs SA (Treaty of Cambay) to get EIC help in a succession dispute — already outside Maratha Confederacy effectively
Scindhia + Holkar + Bhonsle — rivals till now — UNITE against EIC despite differences, triggered by Treaty of Bassein

Battle of Assaye (1803) — Arthur Wellesley (Royal regiment alongside EIC army) vs Marathas; Arthur Wellesley later describes it as toughest fight of entire military career — harder than anything he faced against Napoleon in Europe

CONSEQUENCES of 2nd Anglo-Maratha War: (i) Bajirao II96-18 regains Peshwaship but now EIC's puppet; (ii) Scindhia loses all territory north of River Yamuna including Delhi + Agra + all Gujarat territory; forced to sign SA; British Resident stationed in Delhi establishes PoIR — Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II60-06 now under EIC's indirect control; (iii) Bhonsle of Nagpur loses Orissa (Bhonsle had raided Bengal Suba 1745-51 + extracted Chauth + control of Orissa from Alivardi Khan40-56); Bhonsle stubbornly refuses full SA — forced to sign mini alliance (similar to ToA1765 with Awadh): cedes territory + accepts EIC army paid by Bhonsle but NOT full SA yet; (iv) Jats, Rajputs, Bundelas — previously paid Chauth + Sardeshmukhi to Marathas — now forced to sign SA with EIC as EIC replaces Marathas as dominant regional power Wellesley98-05 recalled to London due to high war expenditure; Cornwallis86-93 despatched with clear orders to follow Policy of Non-Interference (arrives July 1805; dies October 1805)

Vellore Mutiny — under George Barlow (Acting GG 1805-07): cause: new dress codes forbidding sepoys from wearing religious marks (tilaks/turbans) + mandated leather cockades (ribbons shaped like Christian cross on hat; made of cow/pig skin); result: uprising @ Vellore Fort (north Tamil Nadu); often called 'Prelude to 1857'

phases.label: PINDARIS, POLICY OF PARAMOUNTCY & NAGPUR SA (1805–1817)

events.label: Policy of Non-Interference — EIC follows to prevent war expenditure
gives Bhonsle + Holkar time to rebuild military strength + confidence Pindaris — disbanded soldiers of Scindhia + Holkar — begin raiding EIC territory in Northern Sarkars + parts of Madras Presidency

Francis Hastings13-23 as GG — empire builder; Policy of Paramountcy (PoP 1813-58): EIC to be paramount/supreme power in India; will do anything including annexation to protect its interests; re-initiates imperial expansion Policy of Paramountcy (PoP) — British Resident begins treating Bajirao II96-18 as puppet with no real authority Parsoji Bhonsle (Maharaja of Nagpur) suffers from paralysis; Appa Sahib (regent) signs SA under Treaty of Nagpur (1816) for EIC help in factionalism dispute over who would be regent; SA requires disbanding official state army BUT allows retainers + police for internal security

Appa Sahib exploits SA loophole: secretly recruits Arab + Rohilla mercenaries as 'internal security retainers'; once power secured — has Parsoji secretly murdered to become actual Maharaja — now wants to rule independently, not as British puppet

Bajirao II96-18 + Appa Sahib (regent of Bhonsle of Nagpur) + Yashwantrao Holkar UNITE in revolt — determined to end EIC's political domination; violation of SA treaties; triggers 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19); EIC deploys largest military force ever in India: ~1.2 lakh troops

Battle of Sitabuldi (November 1817) — Appa Sahib uses Arab mercenaries to launch surprise close-quarters attack directly on British Residency + adjacent Sitabuldi hills; despite heavily outnumbering garrison, his forces DEFEATED Appa Sahib signed SA 1816 but fought British 1817 — SA terms caused the war; (ii) disbanded army bypassed via Arab + Rohilla mercenaries hired as 'internal security retainers' — SA template's loophole exposed)

CONSEQUENCES of 3rd Anglo-Maratha War: (i) Peshwaship ABOLISHED; Bajirao II96-18 pensioned off to Bithur near Kanpur (his adopted son = Nana Sahib — leads Kanpur revolt in 1857); (ii) Svarajya annexed into Bombay Presidency; (iii) Appa Sahib deposed; replaced by puppet; Bhonsle loses huge territory; (iv) Holkar's SA via Treaty of Mandsaur (1818) — Holkar of Indore forced to sign after decisive defeat @ Mahidpur; (v) Satara + Kolhapur NOT annexed — EIC maintains Chhatrapati's line as symbolic gesture (cost nothing; Chhatrapati powerless figurehead since 1750s; Satara annexed 1848 under Dalhousie48-56's Doctrine of Lapse)

2nd Anglo-Burmese War — under Dalhousie48-56; Pegu (lower Burma) annexed (discussed in later chapter)

1802; signs Treaty of Bassein Dec 1802. 3rd War: Peshwaship had no real authority left (PoP + British Resident); rulers pushed to
revolt by SA's own vicious-chain consequences. Every single war was triggered or enabled by Maratha internal division. The
Marathas never fought the EIC as a unified force — Scindhia, Holkar, Bhonsle, Gaikwad almost never coordinated effectively.
Key Link — Treaty of Bassein (Dec 1802) + 2nd Anglo-Maratha War: Bajirao II96-18 signing SA = Peshwa sells the
Confederacy to the British. Ironically united the rival Sardars (Scindhia + Holkar + Bhonsle) who had been fighting each other. But
too late and too disorganised — EIC wins. After 2nd war: Delhi + Agra under EIC; Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II60-06 now under
EIC's Indirect Rule — the same Emperor who had been puppet of Zulfikar Khan -> Sayyid Brothers -> Irani/Turani -> Safdar Jung
-> Marathas -> now EIC.
n Prelims Alert — Battle of Sitabuldi (November 1817): Tested in UPSC Prelims. Two things to note: (i) Appa Sahib signed SA
in 1816 but fought British in 1817 — SA terms CAUSED the war, not prevented it. (ii) Disbanded army requirement bypassed via
Arab + Rohilla mercenaries hired as 'internal security retainers' — SA template's loophole exposed. Battle of Koregaon (1 Jan
1818): small EIC Mahar soldier force holds off much larger Peshwa army — commemorated as Bhima-Koregaon Victory Pillar.
n Alert — Napier's 'Peccavi' on annexation of Sindh (1843): Sir Charles Napier sends one-word Latin dispatch: 'Peccavi' (= 'I
have sinned'). Pun: 'I have Sindh.' Captures brazenness of the annexation. Annexation by Ellenborough42-44 from 'Char Yaar'
(four Baloch chiefs of Talpur dynasty) WITHOUT any justification.

sections.title: Doctrine of Lapse: Legal Principle vs Pretext
Doctrine of Lapse Applied to Pensions: Nana Sahib + 1857 Link
Annexation in Lieu of Subsidy: Berar (1853)

events.label: Doctrine of Lapse formulated by Court of Directors of EIC — implemented systematically by Dalhousie48-56; principle: if Indian ruler dies without biological heir, rights lapse -> State annexed into British India; deliberately refuses to recognise adopted sons (valid under Hindu law)
Satara (Maharashtra) — #1 Lapse annexation; mnemonic: BHAGAT SAMBHAL JA JHAdio mein UDta SA NAG
Sambhalpur (Odisha) — #2 Lapse annexation
Jaitpur (UP, Bundelkhand region) — #3 Lapse annexation
Baghat (Himachal Pradesh — small hill State near Solan) — #4 Lapse annexation

Peshwa Bajirao II96-18 dies; Dalhousie48-56 refuses to continue State pension of Rs 8 lakh per annum to adopted son Nana Sahib; argument: adopted sons inherit private wealth, not political titles or State pensions; pension refusal -> Nana Sahib becomes key 1857 leader from Bithur
Udaipur (Chhattisgarh, formerly Central Provinces) — #5 Lapse annexation; NOT the famous Rajput kingdom of Udaipur/Mewar in Rajasthan

Inam Commission established @ Bombay Presidency — investigates tax-free grants (inams) made by earlier Indian rulers to Brahmins, temples + others; demands proof of title; insufficient-proof grants confiscated; ~20,000 estates seized in Bombay Presidency alone; Doctrine of Lapse applied to land titles instead of thrones
First railway line opened: Bombay to Thane (1853) — built primarily for army movement; secondarily for administration, raw-material extraction + market creation
Telegraph Department established — ~4,000 miles laid across major cities

Jhansi (UP) — #6 Lapse annexation; Rani Lakshmibai's adopted son refused recognition; she becomes key 1857 leader Nagpur (Maharashtra) — #7 Lapse annexation; Bhonsle of Nagpur; completes 7 States in 7 years

Wood's Despatch (1854) — 'Magna Carta of Indian Education'; blueprint for mass education: vernacular elementary schools, universities, structured education administration; Dalhousie48-56 supports + implements
Post Office Act (1854) — uniform half-anna (2 paise) rate Peshawar to Calcutta; network established
Public Works Department (PWD) — removed from military control, made civilian; GT Road (Peshawar to Calcutta) restored to functionality; canals + bridges built

Treaty of Kalat (1854) — signed by EIC under Dalhousie48-56; negotiated by Major John Jacob; Khan of Kalat surrenders Foreign Policy + allows EIC military outposts inside Kalat territory; EIC pays Khan annual subsidy of Rs 50,000 (reverse-SA pattern: imperial power pays local ruler)

phases.label: ANNEXATION IN LIEU OF SUBSIDY (BERAR 1853) + AWADH (1856)

events.label: Hyderabad signs 1st Subsidiary Alliance with EIC — pays ever-rising subsidy since then
Berar annexed by Dalhousie48-56 — Hyderabad cannot pay subsidy; Berar taken as permanent payment (same mechanism as half of Awadh annexed in 1801 as subsidy payment)
ToA1765 (Clive) — PoIR + PoRF + mini SA established in Awadh
John Shore93-98 replaces Wazir Ali97-98 as Nawab of Awadh with uncle Sadat Ali Khan II in return for annual subsidy Rs 76 lakh + cession of Allahabad fort

Sadat Ali Khan II defaults; Wellesley98-05 imposes full SA via Henry Wellesley; half of Awadh (Gorakhpur + Rohilkhand + Doab = Ceded Districts) annexed as permanent payment; unfair — revenue from territory twice the subsidy
Ceded Districts given full province status as North-Western Provinces (NWP1836)

EIC keeps demanding more subsidy despite permanent 1801 payment; Nawab raises taxes; threat of peasant revolts by 1855; British Resident establishes Indirect Rule; Nawab Wajid Ali Shah has no real power but all responsibility Dalhousie48-56 annexes rest of Awadh on grounds of maladministration — NOT Doctrine of Lapse (Wajid Ali Shah had heirs); Prelims 2008: which State removed on misgovernance pretext = Awadh
Both territories (NWP1836 + Awadh) reorganised as 'North-Western Provinces and Oudh'
Renamed 'United Provinces of Agra and Oudh'
Renamed 'United Provinces'
Became Uttar Pradesh after Independence
Uttarakhand carved out of UP

Maharaja Ranjit Singh01-39 dies — Sikh State was ideal PoRF buffer; after his death factionalism tears State apart: (i) royal family succession fights; (ii) Sindhanwaliyas (Jat clan/misl); (iii) Dogra Rajputs as Wazirs; (iv) Khalsa Army itself (democratic spirit — wanted Panchayat governance; harder for EIC to manage than feudal-loyal army); succession disputes + political murders follow

Duleep Singh43-49 — child of 5 at accession; last Sikh Maharaja 1st Anglo-Sikh War — under Hardinge44-48 Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846) — terms: (i) Khalsa Army size reduced + EIC army stationed (NOT fully disbanded out of respect for Sikh religious sentiment); (ii) fertile Jalandhar Doab (land between Beas + Sutlej rivers) annexed by EIC; (iii) Kashmir Mechanism: Lahore Darbar cannot pay full Rs 1.5 crore war indemnity -> cedes hills between Beas + Indus (Kashmir + Hazara) to EIC; EIC then sells/transfers these to Gulab Singh for Rs 75 lakh Nanakshahee rupees; Gulab Singh recognised as Maharaja of J&K; under British; (iv) PoIR initiated in Punjab: British Resident Henry Lawrence stationed as effective Regent

Treaty of Amritsar (16 March 1846) — formalises Kashmir sale to Gulab Singh; legal foundation of Princely State of J&K; creates Hindu monarchy over Muslim-majority population — origin of 'Kashmir Question'

2nd Anglo-Sikh War — under Dalhousie48-56; reason: Sikh governors of Multan (Mulraj) + Haripur (Chattar Singh) revolt -> empire-builder Dalhousie gets opportunity Punjab annexed from Maharaja Duleep Singh43-49; Koh-i-Noor diamond taken from Duleep Singh + surrendered to British Crown; Punjab initially governed by Board of Administration (Lawrence Brothers + Charles Mansel); last major independent State outside Company State gone; EIC frontier now touches Afghan foothills

phases.label: 2ND ANGLO-BURMESE WAR (1852–53) + MARITIME RING FENCE + PERSIAN GULF

events.label: 1st Anglo-Burmese War (under Amherst23-28) — Treaty of Yandabo (1826); EIC annexes Arakan + Tenasserim (eastern shore of Bay of Bengal) Sindh annexed — by Ellenborough42-44 (NOT Dalhousie48-56); Charles Napier commands; 'Peccavi' dispatch

2nd Anglo-Burmese War (under Dalhousie48-56) — PoRF logic: secure eastern frontier from expansionist Burma; Lower Burma/Pegu annexed; combined with Arakan + Tenasserim (1824-26) = Bay of Bengal effectively becomes a British lake Khan of Kalat gifts port of Gwadar to prince of Oman — Gwadar becomes Omani enclave inside Balochistan coast for over 170 years; British Empire controls everything around Gwadar but never owns it
Treaty of Kalat (1854) — Khan surrenders Foreign Policy + allows EIC military outposts; EIC pays Rs 50,000 annual subsidy (reverse-SA)

Anglo-Persian War — British capture coastal cities including Bushehr + Kharg Island; Treaty of Paris (1857): British withdraw in exchange for Iran giving up claims to Herat in Afghanistan; PoRF logic: protect western land approach to India Pakistan purchases Gwadar from Oman — 11 years after Independence

Treaty of Jacobabad (1876) — signed by British State (NOT EIC; EIC abolished 1858); negotiated by Robert Sandeman under Viceroy Lytton76-80; goes further than 1854: British State can station troops permanently in Kalat + construct railways + telegraphs + act as supreme arbitrator in disputes between Khan + tribal chiefs

Anglo-Russian Convention (1907) — Britain + Russia divide Iran into spheres of influence; southern coastal region along Persian Gulf officially recognised as British sphere; naval dominance in Indian Ocean secured without a single annexation

Anglo-Persian Oil Company (1909) — later Anglo-Iranian Oil Company; today's BP; gives Britain economic control of Iranian coastline; economic imperialism: control the resource + control the coast without the cost of running a colony

J.E. Drinkwater Bethune (Law Member of Dalhousie's Council) opens girls' school @ Calcutta — Bethune School; India's 1st successful secular school for girls; Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar closely associated; Savitribai + Jyotirao Phule's Pune school (1 Jan 1848) predates it as India's 1st girls' school overall
Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar becomes Principal of Sanskrit College — under Dalhousie's tenure
1st railway: Bombay to Thane (1853) — army movement primary purpose
Telegraph Department established — ~4,000 miles laid across major cities
Post Office Act (1854) — uniform half-anna rate Peshawar to Calcutta
PWD made civilian — GT Road restored; canals + bridges built across India
Wood's Despatch (1854) — 'Magna Carta of Indian Education'
Calcutta-Raniganj (coal-rich) + Madras-Arakkonam railway lines by 1856

Roorkee Engineering College established by Dalhousie48-56 Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar appointed Inspector of Schools — under Dalhousie's tenure; Dalhousie actively supports Vidyasagar's work on girls' education + Hindu Widow Remarriage Act 1856
Hindu Widow Remarriage Act (1856) — supported by Dalhousie48-56; Vidyasagar's advocacy
Three universities @ Bombay, Madras + Calcutta officially established — groundwork was Dalhousie48-56's; officially under Canning56-62 (Dalhousie left India 1856)
Dalhousie48-56 hands over to Canning56-62 — Canning inherits the empire Dalhousie built + the revolt his annexations had sown seeds of

Revolt of 1857 — almost every major leader annexation-aggrieved: Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi Lapse 1854); Nana Sahib (pension refused 1851); Bahadur Shah Zafar37-57 (titular dignity Dalhousie sought to end); court of Awadh (annexed 1856); disbanded Sikh soldiery; dispossessed talukdars + inam-holders (Inam Commission 1852)

Government of India Act 1858 — abolishes Company State; transfers power to British Crown; Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858: formally ends Doctrine of Lapse + pledges to respect treaties + rights of Indian rulers; Paramountcy -> Subordinate Union; no further annexations after this
Treaty of Jacobabad — Kalat; Policy of Subordinate Union, not PoP

tables.title: ANCHOR TABLE: FIVE-POLICY ARC (1600–1947)
lines: # POLICY PERIOD CORE LOGIC
1 Policy of Relative Isolation ~1600–1813 EIC militarily not confident; primary interest = trade; stays out of Indian
politics; selective warfare + diplomacy to protect trade; signs alliances
(ToA1765, ToSalbai1782)
2 Policy of Indirect Rule (PoIR) + ~1765–1858 PoIR: British Resident in court controls admin without formal annexation;
Policy of Ring Fence (PoRF) (overlap) PoRF: military alliance with frontier State as buffer against external
threats
3 Policy of Subsidiary Alliance 1798–1858 EIC subordinates Indian rulers: takes over Foreign Policy + Military; both
(PoSA) funded by Indian State's annual subsidy; promises non-interference
(routinely broken via illegal PoIR)
4 Policy of Paramountcy / 1813–1858 Francis Hastings13-23 declares EIC paramount/supreme power; will
Subordinate Isolation interfere + annex if needed; Indian States sealed in diplomatic bubble —
no communication with other States without EIC as gatekeeper; = PoSA
minus the rights of the Indian State
5 Policy of Subordinate Union 1858–1947 After 1857: EIC abolished; British Crown takes direct control; Indian
rulers legally part of British Empire ('princes' not 'kings'); all external
sovereign functions with British Crown; domestic functions remain with
Indian Prince; = PoParamountcy + Sovereignty formally with British
Crown

anchors: Mnemonic — 7 Lapse States: BHAGAT SAMBHAL JA JHAdio mein UDta SA NAG = Baghat + Sambhalpur + Jaitpur + Jhansi +
Udaipur + Satara + Nagpur. Key: Udaipur here = Chhattisgarh (Central Provinces), NOT the famous Rajput Udaipur/Mewar of
Rajasthan.
Key Pattern — Dalhousie's 3 Annexation Instruments under PoP: (1) Doctrine of Lapse: 7 States 1848-54. (2) Wars: 2nd
Anglo-Sikh War 1848-49 (Punjab); 2nd Anglo-Burmese War 1852-53 (Pegu/Lower Burma). (3) Annexation in lieu of subsidy: Berar
1853 (Hyderabad cannot pay); Awadh 1856 (maladministration grounds). By end of Dalhousie's tenure: Company State controls
63% of India (home to 78% of population). No further annexations after 1857 revolt + Government of India Act 1858.
n Prelims Alert (2008) — Awadh annexed on misgovernance pretext: Awadh 1856 annexation = NOT Doctrine of Lapse
(Wajid Ali Shah had heirs). Grounds = maladministration. Two Treaties of Amritsar to distinguish: (i) 1809: Ranjit Singh01-39 +
EIC; Sutlej = Sikh-EIC boundary. (ii) 1846: Kashmir sale to Gulab Singh; legal foundation of Princely State of J&K.;
n Alert — Gwadar: In 1783, Khan of Kalat gifts Gwadar to prince of Oman — Omani enclave inside Balochistan coast for 170+
years. British Empire controls everything around Gwadar but never owns Gwadar itself. Pakistan purchases Gwadar from Oman
only in 1958 (11 years after Independence). Today: heart of China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).

sections.title: Orientalism (1765–1813): Rule India, the India Way
Three New Ideologies (Post 1813): Liberalism + Utilitarianism + Evangelicalism
Forward Policy in Afghanistan: Ellenborough42-44  → Lytton76-80
Foreign Ideologies Motivating India's Anti-Colonial Struggle

phases.label: ORIENTALISM (1765–1813): RULE INDIA THE INDIA WAY

events.label: English Civil War + Glorious Revolution — world's 1st modern democracy; root of British civilisational confidence
Industrial Revolution in Britain — birthplace; root of British civilisational confidence
Seven Years' Global War — Britain wins; becomes top global power; root of WMB American political movement begins (War of Independence 1776-83) — anti-colonial counter-ideology to WMB

Orientalism dominant British imperial ideology — India's ancient past was glorious even if its present is degenerate; rule India according to its own customs + laws; EIC not yet militarily confident; one cultural insult could trigger mass resistance

American War of Independence — challenges imperial superiority assumptions; inspires colonised peoples worldwide Calcutta Madrasa established by Warren Hastings73-85 (as GG of Bengal) — primarily for study of Islamic law + customs; 1st Orientalist institution
Asiatic Society of Bengal founded by Sir William Jones (Puisne Judge @ Supreme Court Calcutta) — to study Asian history, antiquities + culture; 2nd Orientalist institution
French Revolution — liberty, equality, fraternity; counter-ideology to WMB; inspires anti-colonial nationalists worldwide
Sanskrit College @ Banaras established by Jonathan Duncan (British Resident @ Benares) — study of Hindu law + philosophy; 3rd Orientalist institution

Fort William College @ Calcutta established by Wellesley98-05 (as GG of Bengal) — trains newly recruited EIC civil servants in Indian languages + administration; 4th Orientalist institution; Wellesley98-05 also wants to keep French republican ideas away from his officers (French Revolution 1789 had overthrown monarchy 1792)
Leipzig (1813) — Britain financially backs coalition that defeats Napoleon; leads allied armies to final victory @ Waterloo (1815)
Battle of Waterloo — Britain + Prussia defeat Napoleon; Britain now undisputed global power; Orientalism gives way to more aggressive ideologies
European revolutions of 1830 — democratic uprisings; anti-colonial counter-ideology
European revolutions of 1848 — democratic uprisings; anti-colonial counter-ideology

Cornwallis86-93 — implements rule India the ENGLISH WAY; 4 key actions: (i) all-British senior admin: replaces Indians in senior positions with British officials (corrupt-native-needing-honest-foreigner narrative); (ii) Rule of Law via codification: Charter Act 1793 establishes civil law + protection of individual rights + private property; reintroduces separation of powers at district level (District Collector no longer also District Judge); (iii) Permanent Settlement 1793 in Bengal: Zamindars converted into large landlords on English model; (iv) Aloof Elite: EIC officials discouraged from mixing with Indians; Indian wives discouraged; Eurasians barred from EIC service; EIC officials prevented from purchasing land in India Cornwallis86-93's motivation: had commanded British army's defeat in American War of Independence; watched British settlers develop deep roots -> fought for independence as homeland; determined not to allow same in India: 'Keep rulers separate from ruled; never let India become home' Cornwallis Code / Charter Act 1793 — separation of powers at district level; civil law + individual property rights; foundational document of British India's legal architecture

Wellesley98-05 — shares authoritarian instinct with Cornwallis; Fort William College (1800) also keeps French republican ideas from officers Thomas Munro (later Governor of Madras 1820-27) — Ryotwari Settlement (1801-07, 1820+) in Madras Presidency: Orientalist in form (ancient Indian model of State collecting revenue directly from peasant without intermediaries) but Authoritarian in substance (all collection by EIC officials; no Indians in senior roles); hybrid of Orientalism + Authoritarianism = Conservatism Thomas Munro as Governor of Madras (1820-27) — Ryotwari Settlement expanded; Elphinstone implements same in Bombay; Malcolm + Metcalfe follow same Conservatism school
events.full: 1798-05 1801-07 1820-27 — Wellesley98-05 — shares authoritarian instinct with Cornwallis; Fort William College (1800) also keeps French republican ideas from officers Thomas Munro (later Governor of Madras 1820-27) — Ryotwari Settlement (1801-07, 1820+) in Madras Presidency: Orientalist in form (ancient Indian model of State collecting revenue directly from peasant without intermediaries) but Authoritarian in substance (all collection by EIC officials; no Indians in senior roles); hybrid of Orientalism + Authoritarianism = Conservatism Thomas Munro as Governor of Madras (1820-27) — Ryotwari Settlement expanded; Elphinstone implements same in Bombay; Malcolm + Metcalfe follow same Conservatism school

phases.label: POST-1813 SHARP TURN: LIBERALISM + UTILITARIANISM + EVANGELICALISM (1813–1857)

events.label: Charter Act 1813 — (i) ends EIC monopoly over Indian trade; non-EIC British businesses enter India freely (economic liberalism for British businesses, NOT Indian ones); (ii) legalises entry of Christian missionaries into India (Evangelical influence; Charles Grant, Court of Directors + MP, influences this)

Post-1813 sharp turn: EIC confident it has defeated all major Indian powers; openly rules India the British way; new economic motive: India with western tastes + education = market for British manufactured goods

James Mill publishes History of British India (1818) — declares India's great past a myth; argues India needs an effective schoolmaster imposing good governance from above; joins Court of Directors; pushes for Law Commission 1834; Utilitarianism's most influential text

William Bentinck28-35 as GG — high-water mark of Liberal confidence in India; 4 headline interventions: (i) Sati Abolition Act 1829; (ii) Thuggee Suppression 1830s-40s under Captain William Sleeman; (iii) Macaulay's Education Minute 1835; (iv) Cornwallis Code progressively revised into uniform criminal procedure Sati Abolition Act 1829 — under Bentinck28-35; Liberal ideology in action; criminalises widow-burning

Thuggee + Dacoity Suppression under Captain (later Major-General Sir) William Sleeman — under Bentinck28-35; Thuggee + Dacoity Department set up 1835; 3 tools: (i) informant networks infiltrating Thug bands; (ii) approver testimony; (iii) swift judicial commissions; over 3,000 Thugs convicted 1831-1841; dismantles organised highway murder cults on GT Road; Prelims 1997 anchor
Charter Act 1833 — Liberal-influenced; Macaulay appointed legal member of GG's council; Law Commission established
Law Commission (1834) — under Macaulay; codifies western-style laws for British India by 1837; both Liberalism + Utilitarianism push for it; leads to Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860

Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education (1835) — makes English medium of higher instruction, displacing Persian; proposes creation of 'Brown Sahibs' (brown on outside, British on inside); class of Indians serving as cultural intermediaries between British rulers + Indian masses
Western-style laws codified for British India by 1837 (Law Commission's work under Macaulay)

1st Anglo-Afghan War — under Auckland36-42; Forward Policy origins; disaster: retreat from Kabul; almost entire British-Indian army wiped out; only one European survivor reaches British India; Rs 1.5 crore expenditure; Auckland36-42 recalled Ellenborough42-44 initiates what later called Forward Policy — punitive return to Kabul 1842 to restore British prestige; doctrine of pushing frontier outward
Lex Loci Act / Removal of Religious-Caste Disabilities Act (1850) — allows convert to retain inheritance rights in family property; removes practical obstacle to conversion; Evangelical influence

Revolt of 1857 — shakes British psychologically: scale of Indian violence against British rule (soldiers, civilians, women, children) breaks the paternalistic narrative; many British conclude Indians simply beyond redemption through reform

Post-1857 SIX-FRONT SHARP SHIFT: (i) reformist impulse retreats sharply; (ii) racial sciences shift from language to physical features — Indians classified as inferior + fundamentally different race; (iii) Aryan Invasion Theory twisted: intermarriage over millennia degraded Europeans who came to India (even India's ancient greatness now used as evidence of inferiority); (iv) 'Dogs and Indians not allowed' signs @ clubs + parks; (v) authoritarianism increases; distrust of sharing power; (vi) social reforms slow sharply
Government of India Act 1858 — EIC abolished; power to British Crown

Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 — formally ends Doctrine of Lapse; pledges religious tolerance + non-interference in Indian customs (explicit acknowledgement that missionary + reformer interference was major grievance of 1857); social + political reforms from here mainly in response to Indian pressure, not British initiative
Irish Home Rule movement (1870-1914) + Irish armed struggle for independence (1916-21) — direct anti-British inspiration for Indian nationalists
Treaty of Jacobabad (1876) — under Viceroy Lytton76-80; tightens Paramountcy-era instruments over Kalat/Balochistan; PoIR fully arrives (Resident now IS the court)

Lytton76-80 — post-1857 architect of harder imperialism; Forward Policy in Afghanistan (2nd Anglo-Afghan War 1878-80); Vernacular Press Act 1878 + Arms Act 1878 (reinstates racial privilege) 2nd Anglo-Afghan War (1878-80) under Lytton76-80 — Forward Policy; Treaty of Gandamak 1879 (mini SA: British Resident stationed + army stationed + FP taken + Khyber Pass + some lands to British + Rs 6 lakh annually to Amir); war continues after massacre of British Resident Louis Cavagnari @ Kabul
Vernacular Press Act 1878 + Arms Act 1878 — under Lytton76-80; reinstates racial privilege; substantive home -> Print Culture chapter
Treaty of Gandamak (1879) — mini SA with Afghanistan under Lytton76-80's 2nd Anglo-Afghan War

Ripon80-84 — reverses Forward Policy; withdraws British forces from Afghanistan (Liberal government in London demands pendulum swing) 3rd Anglo-Burmese War 1885-86 — under Dufferin84-88; field commander: General Henry Prendergast Upper Burma annexed — under Dufferin84-88; King Thibaw deposed + exiled to Ratnagiri; last major territorial extension of British India; Upper Burma merged with Lower Burma (British from 1852); governed as province of British India until 1937 separation
events.full: Ripon80-84 — reverses Forward Policy; withdraws British forces from Afghanistan (Liberal government in London demands pendulum swing) 3rd Anglo-Burmese War 1885-86 — under Dufferin84-88; field commander: General Henry Prendergast Upper Burma annexed — under Dufferin84-88; King Thibaw deposed + exiled to Ratnagiri; last major territorial extension of British India (Prelims 2000 anchor); Upper Burma merged with Lower Burma (British from 1852); governed as province of British India until 1937 separation

events.label: Gandhi goes to South Africa (1893-1915) — anti-colonial training from Indian-diaspora struggles

Curzon99-05 — post-1857 architect of harder imperialism; empire as project of prestige + paramountcy + racial hierarchy Partition of Bengal (1905) — under Curzon99-05; post-1857 authoritarian mindset applied administratively; substantive home -> Swadeshi Movement chapter
Anglo-Russian Convention (1907) — Britain + Russia divide Iran into spheres of influence; British sphere = southern coastal region along Persian Gulf; final piece of Maritime Ring Fence
Anglo-Persian Oil Company (1909) — later Anglo-Iranian Oil Company; today's BP; economic imperialism: control the resource + coast without cost of running a colony

Irish armed struggle for independence against Britain — direct inspiration for Indian nationalists Russian Revolution (1917) — gives Indian left peasant-worker mobilisation model + anti-imperial vocabulary
Wilson's Fourteen Points (1918) — principle of self-determination; makes continued British rule increasingly indefensible internationally

Ottawa Conference (1932) — formalises Imperial Preference; locks India's trade into Empire-first structure; British goods enter Indian ports at lower tariff than German, Japanese or American competitors; subordinates Indian industrial interests to British manufacturing needs

n Prelims Alert (1999b) — Spirited Forward Policy towards Afghanistan: Answer = Lytton76-80 (2nd Anglo-Afghan War
1878-80 + Treaty of Gandamak 1879). Ripon80-84 REVERSED the Forward Policy. Dufferin84-88 = Upper Burma 1886 (NOT
Afghanistan). Memory hook: Lytton = Forward; Ripon = Retreat.
n Prelims Alert (2000) — Last major territorial extension of British India: Answer = Dufferin84-88 (Upper Burma, January
1886). NOT Dalhousie (his last = Awadh 1856); NOT Lytton (tightened Paramountcy instruments but no annexations); NOT Curzon
(Partition of Bengal 1905 = administrative reorganisation, not territorial extension). Memory hook: Dufferin = 1886 = Upper Burma =
last major extension.
n Prelims Alert (1999a) — Imperial Preference: Answer = Special privileges on British imports in India (preferential/lower tariff
rates for British goods vs other competitors). Formalised @ Ottawa Conference 1932. NOT racial discrimination (separate
phenomenon); NOT general subordination of Indian interest (too vague); NOT preference to British political agents over Indian
Princes.

sections.title: The Mughal Blueprint for Land Revenue

phases.label: BENGAL: THREE EXPERIMENTS IN LAND REVENUE (1765–1885)

events.label: EIC receives Diwani (right to collect LR) of Bengal + Orissa + Bihar through ToA1765; appoints Deputy Subadar Muhammad Reza Khan as Diwan; Mughal system continues (Orientalism); Patta system ignored almost immediately; rents extracted far beyond patta records

Dual Government (Experiment 1) — EIC holds Diwani; Nawab holds Nizamat; frantic over-extraction; back-to-back droughts hit Great Bengal Famine (GBF 1770) — kills between 50 lakh + 1 crore Indians; EIC DOUBLES land revenue demand in 1770 + uses brutality to collect; British whistleblowers write to London newspapers; famine destroys agrarian economy; LR income collapses

By 1772: EIC on verge of bankruptcy (rampant corruption by 'Nabobs' + GBF 1770 + heavy army expenses + Dual System costs); EIC approaches British Government for emergency bailout; Parliament grants GBP 1.4 million @ 4% interest conditional on parliamentary oversight -> directly leads to Regulating Act of 1773

Farming System of Warren Hastings73-85 (Experiment 2) — revives Mughal Ijaradari; right to collect LR in each district auctioned to highest bidder (Revenue Farmer); supervised by European District Collector; Revenue Farmers extract maximum from ryots to recover bid + earn profits; many demands impossibly high -> peasants pay nothing; rural population ruined; LR income does NOT improve
Reza Khan made scapegoat — imprisoned without trial on corruption charges (1772-74)

Cornwallis86-93 (GG of Bengal) sent with one primary assignment: fix the LR problem Base year for Permanent Settlement — 10/11 of Zamindar's pre-existing revenue calculated from 1789-90 collections Permanent Settlement Act 1793 (PS1793) — applied in Bengal + Orissa + Bihar + North Madras + Benaras (mnemonic: BOB migrated from North Madras to Benaras + Settled Permanently); 4 pillars: (i) Landowner = Zamindar (given full proprietary rights for 1st time; land becomes commodity: sold, purchased, leased, rented, mortgaged); (ii) Settlement with Zamindar; (iii) Assessment permanent: fixed at 10/11 of pre-existing revenue, absolutely fixed forever; (iv) Sunset Clause: Zamindar fails to pay by evening of deadline -> land auctioned to anyone who agrees to pay required LR
Cornwallis Code — Charter Act 1793 brings: separation of powers at district level (District Collector no longer also District Judge); civil law + individual property rights

PS1793 Impact: (i) short-term: frequent land auctions; Jotedars (rich farmers) + Zamindar family members buy; eventually stabilises; Zamindars become loyal to British (show during 1857); (ii) long-term: British get certainty + regularity of LR income (objective achieved); (iii) Cornwallis's core economic vision FAILS: Zamindars do NOT invest; absentee landlordism emerges (lease to intermediaries; move to cities); (iv) Ryot becomes 'tenant at will' — evicted without protection; Patta system ignored; high rents; Abwabs continue despite being illegal; (v) wave of peasant revolts after 1793

Wellesley98-05 reverses Cornwallis's removal of Zamindari police powers through Regulation VII of 1799 — Zamindar gets back: (i) seize tenant's property without court order on rent default; (ii) imprison tenants; (iii) increase rents at will
By 1801: Thomas Munro convinces Court of Directors to replace PS1793 in Madras with Ryotwari — PS survives only in North Madras
GBF consequences + PS1793 abuses + Zamindari coercive powers contribute to agrarian grievances feeding into 1857 revolt

Rent Act of 1859 — after decades of peasant revolts; protections for tenant ryots in Bengal: (i) tenant cultivating same plot continuously >12 years gains occupancy rights (cannot be evicted without court order; rent not increased without just cause); (ii) Patta system revived; (iii) Zamindars lose power to imprison tenants; (iv) IN PRACTICE: poorly implemented; Zamindars find loophole: evict tenant JUST BEFORE 12 years -> permanently deny occupancy rights

Indigo Revolt (1859-63) — ryots fight specifically for occupancy rights; driven partly by Rent Act 1859 loophole exploitation by Zamindars Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873) — ryots fight for occupancy rights
Ripon80-84 sets up Rent Commission (1880) — reviews Zamindar-ryot relations in Bengal

Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 (Act III of 1885) — passed under Dufferin84-88 (Bengal Legislative Council); (i) rights of all stakeholders clearly defined in law; (ii) Zamindari powers significantly reduced; (iii) occupancy rights strengthened: even tenants who cultivated different plots in same village for total >12 years get occupancy rights over last plot cultivated (closes 12-year loophole); (iv) implemented sincerely this time
Alexander Read + Thomas Munro first experiment with Ryotwari in parts of Madras (1792 onwards) — settlement done directly with ryot; ryot held legal title to land

Munro convinces Court of Directors in London to replace PS1793 in Madras with Ryotwari — reason: no big Zamindars in Madras; State fiscal stress from Carnatic Wars + Anglo-Mysore Wars; Poligars (Vijayanagar-era landed magnates with private armies) resist Zamindari; Munro's Scottish ideology: yeoman farmer = hero of agrarian society

Phase 1 (Madras): gross produce basis; 33-50% of estimated gross produce demanded; technically complex + arbitrary surveys; severe over-assessment -> widespread poverty + land abandonment; ryot cycle: crop failure -> borrow from moneylenders -> default -> lose mortgaged land Munro leaves for Britain — Ryotwari system diluted in his absence

After 3rd Anglo-Maratha War annexing Svarajya — Bombay EIC initially uses Patils + Deshmukhs to collect revenue (nod to Orientalism); Elphinstone (disciple of Munro) later brings Ryotwari to Bombay Munro returns as Governor of Madras (1820-27) — firmly re-establishes Ryotwari; applies across Madras Presidency R.K. Pringle applies Economic Rent theory (Ricardian) to Bombay Ryotwari — net produce basis (gross crop value minus cost of cultivation: seeds, manure, bullocks, labour, implements); BUT faulty calculations -> excessive 55% demand
Wingate Settlement (1835) — Bombay Survey System by Wingate + Goldsmid; assesses land fairly + fixes reasonable annual amount for 30 years; implemented across Bombay Deccan by 1847
Wingate-Goldsmid Bombay Survey System implemented across Bombay Deccan
Madras Torture Commission Report (1855) — exposes severe oppression in Madras Ryotwari; leads to Madras Rules 1855/1864

Madras Rules (1855/1864) — cap LR demand at maximum 50% of net produce / rental value for 30 years; addressing these grievances keeps Madras relatively quiet during 1857 revolt US Civil War (1861-65) — Union naval blockade cuts Confederate cotton exports; Indian cotton exports BOOM (premium prices); Bombay Deccan cotton boom End of US Civil War — US raw cotton floods global markets again; Indian cotton premium collapses; Bombay Deccan peasants who had taken moneylender loans during boom now face crisis

Bombay Deccan Peasant Riots (1875) — caused by: massive indebtedness to Marwari + Gujarati moneylenders; collapse of cotton prices post-US Civil War; Ryotwari over-assessment; Mirasidar abuse of concentrated powers

phases.label: MAHALWARI SETTLEMENT — NW PROVINCES, PUNJAB, CENTRAL PROVINCES (1801–1856)

events.label: Half of Awadh annexed (Ceded Districts) — forms nucleus of North-Western Provinces; Taluqdars + Primary Zamindars dominated the agrarian economy

Severe over-extraction of LR in Awadh/NW Provinces by EIC; Taluqdars who resist lose milkiyats (landed estates); entire class of landed magnates crushed; Revenue officers (Amils/Amalguzars at district level + Tehsildars at sub-district level) grow powerful buying up best lands in auctions; moneylenders + bankers + merchants also acquire milkiyat lands Holt Mackenzie's recommendations implemented through Regulation VII of 1822 — creates Mahalwari Settlement; Mahal = community of people at village/estate/district level

Mahalwari hybrid structure: (i) in most areas: ryot = landowner; settlement with Mahal via Lambardar (representative); Mahal decides internal distribution of LR demand; (ii) in some areas: Taluqdar = landowner; settlement with Taluqdar; law recognises occupancy rights of ryots + mandates recording of rents (Patta system has legal backing); collection by State officers

R.M. Bird introduces Revised Mahalwari System in NW Provinces: (i) assessment at Mahal level (not individual plot level); (ii) individual contribution decided by community internally; (iii) if Mahal's collective LR falls short -> State can auction individual ryot lands; (iv) LR fixed at 66% of Rental Value (Net Assets) for 30 years, subject to State revision
Ceded Districts given full province status as NWP1836 (North-Western Provinces)

Dalhousie48-56 extends Mahalwari to Punjab + Central India Awadh annexed — summary settlement done (LR decided WITHOUT field surveys because surveys take time); result: unjust demands for many ryots + consequent landlessness

All Mahalwari failures feed into 1857 revolt: crushing of Taluqdars 1801-22; unjust revenue demands; summary settlement 1856; landlessness of ryots; NW Provinces + Awadh = among most intense theatres of 1857 rebellion

anchors: Key Pattern — Commercialisation of Agriculture: British demand LR in CASH (not kind as under Mughals). To generate cash,
ryots compelled to shift from food crops (rice, wheat, millets) to cash crops (indigo, cotton, opium, jute, sugarcane). Higher the
revenue demand -> greater pressure to grow cash crops -> food security declines. When droughts/floods hit: less food grain in
reserve (land planted with indigo/cotton instead). Direct link: high cash-revenue demands + forced shift from food to cash crops ->
late-19th-century famines. Prelims 2021 answer: commercialisation of Indian agriculture.
n Prelims Cluster — PS1793: 2001: Why did Zamindars not issue pattas under PS? = no official check upon Zamindar (State
only supervised 10/11 payment; everything below = beyond State supervision). 2011: Why did litigation surge after Cornwallis's
1793 settlement? = Making EIC overlord of Zamindars (Sunset Clause auctions titles on default -> legal petitions multiply). 2024:
Which correct? Statement 1 (Ryotwari peasants exempted bad harvest) = WRONG; Statement 2 (PS Zamindar removed if failed to
pay) = CORRECT (Sunset Clause). Answer = 2 only.
n Prelims Cluster — Ryotwari (2012 + 2017): 2012: Ryotwari correct statements: rent paid directly by peasants to govt
(CORRECT) + govt gave pattas to ryots (CORRECT) + lands surveyed + assessed before taxed (CORRECT) -> answer = all 3.
2017: Architects of Ryotwari: Cornwallis (WRONG = PS architect) + Alexander Read (CORRECT) + Thomas Munro (CORRECT)
-> answer = 2 + 3 only. Memory hook: Read + Munro = Ryotwari (Scottish yeoman); Cornwallis = Permanent (English landlordism).
n Prelims 2000 — Match the LR system: Big feudal landlords = Zamindari System (PS1793 gave Zamindars full proprietary
rights). Revenue farmers / rent collectors = Jagirdari System (Mughal Jagirdar = apex revenue collector). Peasant with right to
sublet/mortgage/transfer/sell = Ryotwari System (ryot holds legal title). Revenue settlements at village level = Mahalwari System
(Mahal-level assessment, R.M. Bird 1833).
