Conquest in India: Policy vs Drift

phases.label: CHRONOLOGY: ALL ACTS, PROVISIONS & KEY EVENTS (1757–1947)

events.label: Battle of Plassey — EIC becomes a political power; begins receiving Bengal LR (Diwani) informally
Treaty of Allahabad (ToA1765) — EIC formally receives Diwani of Bengal + Orissa + Bihar; American political revolution begins (Stamp Act crisis)
British State demands GBP 400,000 per annum from EIC arguing State helped in conquest
Great Bengal Famine (GBF 1770) — kills 50 lakh to 1 crore; EIC doubles LR demand; 'Nabobs' (corrupt EIC officers) embarrass British State; first whistleblowers write to London newspapers

EIC goes bankrupt; Parliament grants GBP 1.4 million @ 4% interest conditional on parliamentary oversight; Select Committee of Parliament set up to study EIC's affairs + advise on EIC-State relationship

Regulating Act 1773 — @GG: (i) Governor of Bengal Presidency elevated to GG(Bengal); (ii) Governors of Bombay + Madras subordinated to GG(Bengal) in matters of war + peace; (iii) commercial affairs untouched; (iv) Supreme Council of Bengal: GG + 4 councillors; all decisions by majority vote; GG only has casting vote; (v) legislative function given to GG's council; @Br State: (i) Parliament's right to regulate EIC's political affairs legally recognised for 1st time; (ii) GG to collect info + send to CoD; CoD submits political info to British State; (iii) Supreme Court to be set up @ Calcutta: 1 Chief Justice + 3 puisne judges (all chosen by Crown); (iv) EIC officials barred from accepting gifts from Indians
Warren Hastings73-85 — 1st GG(Bengal); formally assumes office 1774 Supreme Court set up @ Calcutta; 1st Chief Justice = Sir Elijah Impey (1774); conflict between SC + GG's Council over jurisdiction

Treaty of Surat (1775) — signed by Governor of Bombay WITHOUT GG's approval; vague 'emergency circumstances' clause exploited; leads directly to 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82); proves weakness of Regulating Act 1773
Adam Smith publishes Wealth of Nations (1776) — argues for Free Market Economy (Laissez Faire); monopoly under intellectual attack since 1776

Amending Act of 1781 (Bengal Judicature Act / Declaratory Act) — resolves SC jurisdictional conflict; SC jurisdiction now: (i) all cases within Calcutta's territory; (ii) British subjects in Bengal Presidency EXCLUDING cases from official acts of EIC officials; (iii) EIC property cases @ Fort William
American War of Independence ends — USA created; Britain loses 13 North American colonies; 1783 anxious British State cannot afford to lose India; shifts from supervision to direct control

Pitt's India Act 1784 (East India Company Act) — @Br State: (i) Double Government (1784-1833): political affairs under Board of Control (BoC) in London — 6 members (1 Secretary of State as President + Chancellor of Exchequer + 4 Privy Council members); commercial affairs remain with CoD; (ii) BoC to superintend, direct + control all civil, military + revenue govt of British territorial possessions in East Indies; (iii) Secret Committee of 3 directors within CoD through which BoC can send confidential orders directly to India; (iv) CoD must send all incoming/outgoing India letters to BoC; (v) Dual Control over GG (1784-1858): BoC can pass binding orders to CoD AND directly to GG; (vi) EIC retains commerce + patronage; @GG: (i) Council reduced from 4 to 3 councillors; CIC mandatory as ex-officio ordinary member; (ii) GG given regular vote + casting vote; (iii) Governors of Bombay + Madras subordinated to GG in matters of war, peace + revenue; (iv) 'emergency circumstances' vagueness resolved; (v) Council of 3 created under each Governor of Bombay + Madras; (vi) 'Conquest in India is repugnant to the wish, policy and honour of this nation' — bans imperial expansion

Warren Hastings73-85 impeachment trial by Edmund Burke (Philip Francis letters to London); Hastings73-85 spends life savings defending himself; ultimately acquitted; Clive similarly tried 1773 + acquitted

Amending Act of 1786 — (i) GG given veto over his council in extraordinary circumstances; (ii) EIC empowered to appoint same person to both posts of GG + CIC; Cornwallis86-93 insists on this + becomes 1st person to hold both posts

Cornwallis86-93 — GG + CIC (1st person to hold both); GG Council (1786) = GG + CIC (ordinary member) + 2 Councillors Charter Act 1793 — @Br State: (i) 'Subjects of Crown cannot acquire sovereign powers over territory on own but only on behalf of Crown' — EIC now only manager/agent of British State; (ii) BoC size decreased to President + 2 junior members; (iii) salary of BoC members now paid by EIC (link to 'Home Charges' in Drain of Wealth); (iv) EIC charter renewed for 20 years — 1st time by Parliament (not Monarch); (v) Principal Servants (GG, Governors, CIC of EIC army, Councillors) to be appointed by EIC only after approval of Crown; @GG: (i) GG's power over council + Governors of Bombay + Madras increased further; when present in Madras/Bombay GG can supersede their Governors; (ii) CIC changed from ordinary member to extraordinary member; CIC seat given to civilian; GG Council (1793) = GG + CIC (extraordinary member) + 3 Councillors; (iii) Code of all regulations governing Bengal mandated; courts bound to follow; all laws to be printed in vernacular languages
Permanent Settlement Act 1793 (PS1793) — Cornwallis Code; Zamindars converted into large landowners; separate subject
Supreme Court set up @ Madras (similar to Calcutta 1774)

Charter Act 1813 — Hallmark: Westernisation of India begins; @Br State: (i) 'undoubted sovereignty of Crown over Indian territorial possessions' re-clarified; (ii) EIC's monopoly over trade with India ENDED; EIC retains monopoly over Tea + Opium trade + trade with China; (iii) Cultural Colonialism begins: Christian Missionaries can enter India with licence from CoD or BoC; push to education + social reforms mandated; EIC to spend Rs 1 lakh per annum on education; (iv) Charter renewed for 20 years
Napoleon dies on St. Helena — EIC had been using island as maritime asset
Supreme Court set up @ Bombay

Charter Act 1833 / St. Helena Act — @Br State: (i) EIC loses monopoly over Tea trade + Opium trade + trade with China; commercial function FULLY ENDED; EIC now only political function as agent of British State; Double Government of EIC affairs (1784-1833) ends; (ii) BoC supervisory power extended to all administrative affairs in India including implementation of laws + officers' transfers + postings; (iii) President of BoC renamed Minister for Indian Affairs; @GG: (i) GG(Bengal)-in-Council elevated to GG(India)-in-Council (LANDMARK); GG(India) made Executive + Legislative head of British India; (ii) Legislative powers of Governors of Bombay + Madras taken away (restored via Indian Councils Act 1861); (iii) centralisation in GG peaks in 1833; decentralisation back to provinces begins in 1861; (iv) Law Member (Thomas Macaulay) added to GG's council for legislative sittings only — grain of separation of power between executive + legislative; Executive Meetings (1833) = GG + CIC + 3 ordinary members; Legislative Meetings (1833) = above + 1 Law Member; (v) Racial equality promised: 'no person to be deprived of chance to enter EIC service on grounds of religion, race, birth or colour'; UCS + subordinate judicial positions (below district judge, e.g. Munsifs) opened to Indians; (vi) Charter renewed for 20 years; (vii) St. Helena taken over from EIC by British State; (viii) Island of St. Helena = remotest place; Napoleon imprisoned + died here 1821
Law Commission set up under Macaulay — codification of laws; work completed by 1837 but deliberation + updates continue

Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education (1835) — makes English medium of higher instruction, displacing Persian; debate on western vs Indian education settled in favour of western education in English; begun under Charter Act 1813
Law Commission's codification work completed by 1837
Doctrine of Lapse formulated by Court of Directors of EIC

Charter Act 1853 — @Br State: (i) Charter now valid 'till Parliament specifies otherwise' (no fixed renewal; permanent sword over EIC); (ii) EIC loses patronage — Civil Services Exam introduced; 1st exam held 1855 in London; EIC hardly controls policies in India from this point; (iii) Covenanted Civil Services (CCS) opened to Indians (UCS had been opened in 1833); (iv) Revenues of British India placed under control of British Parliament; @GG: (i) deeper separation of powers: 6 more Legal Members added for Legislative Meetings (4 representing Bengal + Bombay + Madras + Northwest Provinces + Chief Justice of Calcutta SC + 1 regular judge of Calcutta SC); Law Member of 1833 promoted to full executive ordinary member; Executive Meetings (1853) = GG + CIC + 4 ordinary members; Legislative Meetings (1853) = above + 6 Legal Members = 12 persons total; (ii) GG empowered to appoint Lieutenant Governor (LG) for Bengal
Dalhousie48-56 appoints Frederick James Halliday as 1st LG of Bengal (1854) — under authority of Charter Act 1853
1st Civil Services Exam held in London (1855)
Revolt of 1857 — EIC blamed for mismanagement; many British killed; EIC's monopoly on violence broken; British public demands ending EIC rule; Royal Military arrives October 1857 to turn tide

Government of India Act 1858 (Act for Better Government of India) — @Br State: (i) EIC rule replaced by direct rule of British State; (EIC formally dissolved 1874); (ii) Mughal sovereignty over Indian territory legally ended (Mughal State 1526-40, 1556-1858 legally comes to an end); (iii) Policy of Subordinate Union towards Indian Rulers: British Crown now sovereign over whole India; British India (63% territory, 78% population) ruled directly by GG; Princely States ruled by Indian Princes under Paramountcy with Crown (Sovereignty + Defence + Communications + FA with Crown; domestic affairs with Prince); (iv) Zafar37-57 pensioned off to Rangoon in Burma; (v) Secretary of State for India (SoS) replaces President of BoC; (vi) Council of India (India Council) replaces BoC in London; SoS heads it with 15 members; 7 members of EIC's CoD absorbed for continuity; (vii) Dual Control over GG (1784-1858) ENDS: as 'Viceroy + GG' now reports only to SoS; (viii) no change in actual powers of GG(India) as Viceroy + GG
Canning56-62 (Charles Canning) becomes 1st Viceroy + GG of India (1858)

Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858) — (a) disclaim intention to annex Indian States (direct walkback from Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse + Awadh annexation 1856); (b) places Indian administration under British Crown; (c) promises religious non-interference + fair treatment of all subjects + opportunity in public service without discrimination of race/creed; (d) grants amnesty to 1857 revolt participants with limited exceptions
Civil Procedure Code (CPC 1859) — fruit of Law Commission 1834
Indian Penal Code (IPC 1860) — Macaulay's draft from Law Commission 1834; enacted as IPC 1860
Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC 1861) — further fruit of Law Commission 1834; legislative powers of Governors of Bombay + Madras restored via Indian Councils Act 1861
EIC formally dissolved (1874)
Royal Titles Act (1876) by British Parliament — empowers Queen Victoria to take title of Kaesar-i-Hind / Empress of India
Imperial / Delhi Darbar organised by Lytton76-80 — Victoria coronated as Kaesar-i-Hind; she had been unofficially using this title since 1858
Archibald Percival Wavell — GG + Crown Representative under Government of India Act 1935 Louis Mountbatten — 1st GG of partitioned India (symbolic head)
C. Rajagopalachari — 1st Indian GG (June 1948 – 26 Jan 1950)
Rajendra Prasad — 1st President of the Republic of India
India replaces IPC 1860 + CPC 1859 + CrPC 1861 with Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) + Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) + Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam

GG/Bengal -> GG/India + Bentinck28-35 first GG/India + Macaulay Law Member (Englishman, NOT Indian) + St. Helena Act + EIC
commercial function fully ended.
n Prelims Alert (2005) — Regulating Act 1773: Statement 1: Hastings73-85 established regular police force on British pattern =
WRONG (Cornwallis Code 1793). Statement 2: Supreme Court established @ Calcutta by Regulating Act 1773 = CORRECT
(1774 operational; 1 CJ + 3 puisne judges; Sir Elijah Impey 1st CJ). Statement 3: IPC came into effect in 1860 = CORRECT.
Answer = 2 and 3 only.
n Prelims Alert (2019) — Charter Act 1813: S1: Ended trade monopoly of EIC in India except for trade in tea and trade with
China = CORRECT (+ Opium also retained). S2: Asserted sovereignty of British Crown over Indian territories held by Company =
CORRECT. S3: Revenues of India now controlled by British Parliament = WRONG (this was Pitt's India Act 1784 via BoC). Answer
= 1 and 2.
n Prelims Alert (2014) — Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858: Correct objects: (1) Disclaim intention to annex Indian States
(walkback from Doctrine of Lapse + Awadh 1856). (2) Place Indian administration under British Crown. WRONG: 'Regulate EIC's
trade with India' (EIC commercial function fully ended in 1833; Proclamation had nothing to do with EIC trade). Answer = 1 and 2.

chapters.title: EIC Administration: Judiciary, Civil Services, Police

sections.title: Administration as the Machinery of the State

events.label: Mughal judicial system in Bengal: CIVIL courts (Sadar Diwani Adalat at top; Pandits judge Hindu cases; Maulvis judge Muslim cases; Zamindar holds Kachari/revenue court at local level; appeals: Zamindar -> Amil -> Sadar Diwani Adalat); CRIMINAL courts (Nizamat/Faujdari Adalats; Islamic law applies to all regardless of religion; Kazis = judges; Muftis = Islamic law experts; Faujdar = executive police chief executes sentence; Naib Nazim heads Sadar Nizamat Adalat)

Dual Government — EIC gains Diwani rights (revenue + civil courts); Nawab retains Nizamat (criminal); Muhammad Reza Khan heads both Diwani + Nizamat on EIC's behalf; EIC does not impose own system (Orientalism); hands-off approach -> poor revenue collection + deteriorating law + order + GBF 1770 Hastings73-85 ends Dual Government; assumes direct administration of both Diwani + Nizamat; British DC made judge in Diwani courts (assisted by Pandits + Maulvis for personal law); Kazis + Muftis continue in Nizamat courts but supervised by European DC; Sadar Diwani Adalat + Sadar Nizamat Adalat now headed by Governor (later GG) + Council members

Naib Nazim Muhammad Reza Khan imprisoned without trial (accused of corruption + poor law-and-order); conditions still fail to improve; released 1774 + reinstated as head of Sadar Nizamat Adalat Hastings73-85 adjustments: (i) attempts separation of revenue + judicial powers in principle (DC not to also be judge — overlaps remain in practice); (ii) 18 Mofussil courts set up at district level, each headed by European judge (replaces Diwani Adalats; brings justice physically closer to people)

Supreme Court (SC) set up @ Calcutta under Regulating Act 1773 — 1st Chief Justice = Sir Elijah Impey (1774); hears cases involving British subjects in Bengal under British law; completely separate from Indian court hierarchy; similar courts follow: Madras (1800), Bombay (1823)

Committee of 11 Pandits compiles Hindu law into single legal code — English translation published as 'Gentoo Code' (1776); 'Gentoo' from Portuguese 'Gentios' (derogatory term for Hindus by monotheistic Christians)
Gentoo Code published — English translation of compiled Hindu law
EIC commissions codification of Islamic law — translates Al-Hidayah (authoritative Arabic manual) first into Persian by Indian scholars, then into English as The Hedaya (1791)
Code of 1781 — makes written orders compulsory + prescribes rules for court functioning

Amending Act of 1781 (Bengal Judicature Act) resolves SC jurisdictional conflict — SC jurisdiction: (i) all cases within Calcutta's territory; (ii) British subjects in Bengal Presidency EXCLUDING cases from official acts of EIC officials; (iii) EIC property @ Fort William
The Hedaya published — English translation of Al-Hidayah; codification of Islamic law for courts

Cornwallis Code 1793 (Judiciary): (i) DC stripped of ALL judicial powers — confined to revenue collection + administration; proper separation of powers; post-PS1793 zamindars needed courts they could trust; (ii) 18 Mofussil courts replaced by Diwani Adalats at district level + City Courts for urban areas; Bengal divided into 4 divisions (Patna, Murshidabad, Calcutta, Dacca) with Provincial Court of Appeal in each; Sadar Diwani Adalat shifted from Murshidabad to Calcutta; (iii) Faujdari/Nizamat Adalats abolished; 4 Provincial Courts of Circuit set up (courts that physically move around division); Sadar Nizamat Adalat @ top; Anglo-Muhammadan law applied (hybrid of Islamic law + British modifications — used for ~70 years until IPC 1860); 3 British modifications: (a) intent not weapon determines murder (abolishes Hanafi 'weapon' rule); (b) relatives cannot pardon murderer — crime = offence against State not private dispute (ends Diyat/blood money); (c) mutilation abolished; replaced by 7-14 years hard labour; (iv) Lawyers now permitted to appear in courts (creates new Indian professional class); (v) All courts headed by European officials; Kazis + Muftis retained as assistants only; office of Naib Nazim abolished
Cornwallis Code also mandates: code of all regulations governing Bengal to be framed; courts bound to follow; laws printed in vernacular languages
Supreme Court @ Madras established

Munro's advice: Madras replaces Bengal judicial system — separation of revenue + judicial powers ENDED in Ryotwari areas; European DC + subordinates given judicial powers so disputes resolved at ground level; more Indianisation at lower judiciary since DC's subordinates include Indian officials; downside: enormous concentration of power in one official
Bombay: Ryotwari system applied by Elphinstone; same judicial model as Madras
Supreme Court @ Bombay established

Bentinck28-35 abolishes divisional courts — both Provincial Courts of Appeal (civil) + Courts of Circuit (criminal) that Cornwallis86-93 created; reason: become parking grounds for inefficient officers; high pendency; high expenditure; judicial powers + pending cases transferred to District Judges Charter Act 1833 judicial impact: GG of India = single central legislative authority for all of British India; laws apply equally to Indians + Britishers alike; One Law Member (Macaulay) added to GG's Council; Law Commission (1834) set up under Macaulay for systematic codification; subordinate judicial positions below rank of District Judge opened to Indians
Law Commission set up under Macaulay — codification of laws; work substantially complete by 1837

Bentinck28-35 replaces Persian in courts — vernaculars in lower courts + English in higher courts; legal backing via Act XXIX of 1837; causes anxiety among Muslim elites (Persian education was pathway to admin careers); creates Sadar Diwani + Sadar Nizamat Adalats in NW Provinces
Civil Procedure Code (CPC 1859) — fruit of Law Commission 1834
Indian Penal Code (IPC 1860) — Macaulay's draft from 1834 Law Commission; enacted 1860
Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC 1861)

Indian High Courts Act 1861 — establishes High Courts in Madras, Bombay + Calcutta in 1862; Calcutta HC created by merging Sadar Diwani Adalat + Sadar Nizamat Adalat + Supreme Court @ Calcutta; finally ends dual-track system of separate courts for Indians + British

GOI Act 1935 (implemented 1937) — establishes Federal Court; hears inter-governmental disputes (Centre vs Province, Province vs Province) + appeals from High Courts; direct ancestor of today's Supreme Court
Supreme Court of India set up under Constitution of India 1950 — continues Federal Court's role with expanded jurisdiction
India replaces CPC 1859 + IPC 1860 + CrPC 1861 with BNS (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) + BNSS (Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita) + BSA (Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam)

EIC officials recruited by nomination (patronage) — posts purchased or handed through patronage; EIC Directors lobby British Parliamentarians with job offers for their sons; breeds corruption + incompetence; training: essentially on the job

Cornwallis86-93 — Founder of Civil Services: organises EIC officers into 2 tiers: (i) Covenanted Civil Service (CCS) = like today's Group A; senior officers sign formal legal contract ('covenant') with EIC's CoD in London before sailing; high defined pay; clear career path; under Cornwallis86-93 reserved STRICTLY for Europeans; (ii) Uncovenanted Civil Service (UCS) = like today's Group B; junior officers hired locally in India; lower pay; less formal; space where Indians allowed to serve (initially very low-level clerical; gradually expanding to Deputy Collectors + Deputy Magistrates 1830s-40s); Key: Cornwallis86-93 did NOT introduce merit-based selection; entry still patronage-based until Charter Act 1853; introduced strict SENIORITY for promotions; massively increased salaries to reduce corruption; curbed private trade by EIC officials; introduced Separation of Powers (DC stripped of judicial powers 1793)

Fort William College, Calcutta (1800-1806) — set up by Wellesley98-05; trains EIC officials in Indian laws, customs + languages Haileybury College, London (East India College) — trains EIC civil servants 1806-1858 Charter Act 1833 opens UCS to Indians — primarily to reduce admin cost; Bentinck28-35 goes slightly further; encourages recruitment of Indians to some senior positions
Charter Act 1853 — LANDMARK: mandates Civil Service Examination for CCS; Indians eligible to appear; CCS opened to Indians on paper

Select Committee of Parliament under Macaulay recommends exam-based recruitment; Civil Services Commission established in London (1854); 1st examination held 1855 in London; BUT: maximum age 18-23 (deliberately low); syllabus dominated by English Literature (produces 'Brown Sahibs'); exam only in London (travel cost + inferior preparation for Indians)
British universities — train EIC/British India civil servants from 1858 onwards
Crown reduces maximum permissible CS exam entry age to 23 years (1859); subsequently reduced further: 22 (1860), 21 (1866), 19 (1876, implemented 1878)
Satyendranath Tagore (brother of Rabindranath Tagore) — 1st Indian to clear CCS exam (1864)
Four more Indians clear CCS exam (1867)
Parliament gives directions for Indianisation of civil services

Statutory Civil Services Act 1878 (under Lytton76-80) — lateral entry via nomination; loyal elite Indians nominated to posts previously reserved for CCS officers; instead of holding exam in India or raising age limit

Aitchison Commission — appointed by Dufferin84-88 in 1886; report 1887; recommends dropping 'Covenanted' + 'Uncovenanted' terms; divides services into 3 tiers: Imperial Civil Service (ICS) + Provincial Civil Service (PCS) + Subordinate Civil Service

CCS renamed ICS (Indian Civil Service) by executive order under Lansdowne88-94 per Aitchison Commission 1887 recommendations — NOT by ICA 1892 (exam trap); Statutory Civil Services abolished; Provincial Civil Services recruited through exams + selection held in India

Islington Commission set up 1912 — report published 1917; recommends 25% Indians in senior positions via exam + promotion from PCS; REJECTS simultaneous exam in India (real reason: British fear more Indian candidates)

GOI Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) — mandates: (i) simultaneous examination in India (1st held 1922); (ii) Public Service Commission for India set up (established 1926); (iii) gradual increase to 33% Indians in senior positions; ICS restructured: All India Services (AIS) + Central Civil Services (due to Dyarchy dividing subjects between Centre + Provinces)
1st simultaneous CS examination in India (1922) — under GOI Act 1919 mandate

Lee Commission / Royal Commission on Superior Civil Services (1923) — context: Khilafat Movement (1920-24) + Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22); equal numbers British + Indian members; report (1924) recommends: (i) 20% senior positions filled by promotion from PCS; (ii) 40% Indians via exam; (iii) 40% Europeans via exam; (iv) achieve 50:50 ratio within 15 years via exam
Public Service Commission established (Oct 1926) with Ross Barker as 1st Chairman; services continue as AIS (ICS, IPS, Indian Forest Service) + Central Services + Provincial Services
GOI Act 1935 — mandates Federal Public Service Commission (set up 1937) + Provincial PSCs; by 1947 more than 50% civil service positions Indianised
Federal Public Service Commission established (1937) — direct predecessor of today's UPSC
Federal PSC becomes Union Public Service Commission under Article 378 of Constitution of India (Transition Provision); AIS governed by Article 312
events.full: Federal PSC becomes Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) under Article 378 of Constitution of India (Transition Provision); AIS governed by Article 312

events.label: Mughal police system in Bengal: Naib Nazim (overall head) -> Faujdars (rural districts) / Kotwals (towns + urban areas) / Zamindars (villages; held police duties + paid village watchmen from own resources)

GBF 1770 leads to sharp increase in crime; Hastings73-85 replaces Faujdars with English Magistrates (DC/DM) in rural districts; Zamindars retain police duties under DM's supervision; PROBLEM: very few DMs; poor supervision; Zamindars oppress masses freely

Irish Constabulary model established in Ireland (1787) — centralised, hierarchical, quasi-military police force; designed as much for suppressing political agitation as preventing ordinary crime; British colonial tool; British later use as blueprint for India

Daroga System of Cornwallis86-93: (i) ENDS police powers of zamindars (under PS1793 they are agrarian capitalists, not local police); (ii) each district divided into thanas of 30 sq miles each; (iii) each thana under Daroga (Indian) appointed + supervised by DM; (iv) DM = supreme head of law + order in district; chain: Darogas -> DM -> central government; RESULT: Daroga-Zamindar nexus develops (zamindars bribe darogas; zamindars maintain private armed men / lathiyals; nexus = instrument of oppression of rural poor)
Wellesley98-05 restores police powers to zamindars through Regulation VII of 1799 — acknowledges Daroga system has failed
Supreme Court @ Madras 1800 (judiciary, not police — for context)
Daroga system extended to Madras — later abolished due to failures; resulting atrocities exposed by Madras Torture Commission Report 1855
Sindh annexed — Charles Napier sets up Sindh Police on Irish Constabulary model immediately after conquest; first road-test of Irish model in India
Punjab post-annexation — Irish Constabulary model applied (road-test)
Bombay — Irish Constabulary model applied (road-test)
Madras Torture Commission Report 1855 — exposes severe oppression by revenue officials; leads to corrective measures
Madras — Irish Constabulary model applied (road-test)

1st Police Commission (1860) — set up by Canning56-62 under M.H. Court; formalises what had proved effective (NOT Charles Napier — exam trap; Napier gave blueprint; Court's commission drew national map); borrows heavily from successful Sindh model for Police Act 1861

Police Act 1861 (March 1861) — creates provincial police structure across all provinces: (i) each Province of British India to have own police organisation; (ii) clear hierarchy: Inspector General (IG, head of provincial police, reports to Governor/LG) -> Superintendent of Police (SP, in charge of district police, reports to DC/DM) -> Sub-Inspector (SI, in charge of thana, reports to SP NOT DC); (iii) operational accountability: SI -> SP -> IG; political accountability: SP to DC/DM, IG to LG/Governor; (iv) 1861 BUILT THE STRUCTURE only; 1861 simply posted military officers or nominated European men into senior posts; no formal cadre, no competitive exam; 'Police Raj' created — Indians excluded from all senior positions; emphasis on intelligence collection + political surveillance
1st open competitive exam for senior police posts held in London (1893); top candidates appointed as probationary Assistant Superintendents of Police under SoS for India

2nd Police Commission (Curzon99-05 sets up; Sir Andrew Fraser heads; report 1903) — organises superior police officers into single unified all-India cadre: Imperial Police (IP) (informally Indian Police); Provincial Police Service (PPS) created with rank of DySP (Deputy Superintendent of Police) for Indians at officer level; CID (Criminal Investigation Department) set up in every province; Department of Criminal Intelligence (1903) set up = forerunner of today's IB (Intelligence Bureau); IP itself kept CLOSED to Indians — Fraser Commission does NOT recommend Indian entry into IP Fraser Commission scheme implemented from ~1905
Direct entry into elite IP officially opened to Indians; simultaneous exams in England + India from 1921 (result of Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms / GOI Act 1919)
Simultaneous IP exams in England + India from 1921
Only 20% of SPs were Indians (1931) — British reluctant to hand over district-level police command
More Indians posted as SP — non-availability of British candidates (most recruited for WW II 1939-45)
IP administratively replaced by Indian Police Service (IPS) via Home Ministry resolution (1948)
IPS given formal statutory backing via All India Services Act 1951; governed by Article 312 of Constitution

anchors: n Prelims Alert (2010) — DC stripped of judicial powers 1793: Why? Answer = absolute power in one person was undesirable
(separation of powers principle); post-PS1793 zamindar class needed courts they could trust. NOT: efficiency of revenue collection
(partial); NOT: judicial power must be European-only (wrong — Cornwallis removed Indians from revenue positions too). Memory
hook: DC = revenue only from 1793; judge function separate.
n Prelims Alert (2010) — Who created the Covenanted Civil Service? Answer = Cornwallis86-93. NOT Hastings73-85 (1st GG;
did judicial plan but not CCS structure). NOT Wellesley98-05 (set up Fort William College 1800 for training but did not create CCS
structure). NOT Bentinck28-35 (opened UCS to Indians via Charter 1833; didn't create CCS). Memory hook: Cornwallis86-93 =
founder of CCS + UCS two-tier structure 1793; ICS renamed by executive order 1892 per Aitchison Commission 1887 = NOT by
n Alert — Police Act 1861 trap: 1st Police Commission 1860 = M.H. Court (NOT Charles Napier — Napier gave the Irish
Constabulary blueprint via Sindh 1843; Court's commission drew national map). Police Act 1861 (March 1861) = built the structure
only; NOT a service cadre. IP cadre formalised by 2nd Police Commission (Fraser Commission) 1902-03 under Curzon99-05. IPS:
1948 Home Ministry resolution -> 1951 AIS Act -> Article 312 of Constitution.

chapters.title: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture

sections.title: Why Social Reform Began in the 19th Century
Who Led the Reforms — Over Time
Raja Ram Mohan Roy & the Brahmo Samaj (1828)

phases.label: SOCIAL REFORM — ORGANISATIONS, ACTS & KEY FIGURES (1803–1929)

events.label: Eran Pillar Inscription of Bhanugupta — earliest firm epigraphic evidence of Sati (MP, Sagar district); Rig Veda itself contains passage where wife goes to pyre but is called back to world of living
Child sacrifice @ Sagar Island (Sagar Dwip, where Ganga meets Bay of Bengal) banned by Wellesley98-05 — early sign colonial government willing to use executive power against specific social practices

Hindu College, Calcutta (later Presidency College) co-founded by Sir Edward Hyde East (Chief Justice, Calcutta SC) + David Hare (watchmaker-reformer) + Raja Ram Mohan Roy; Hare School founded 1818 by David Hare
Calcutta School Book Society co-founded by David Hare + Radhakanta Deb — elementary schools + textbooks in English + Bengali
Ishwar Chandra Bandyopadhyay (Vidyasagar) born 26 September 1820 in Bengal; earns title 'Vidyasagar' (ocean of knowledge) in 1839
Calcutta Unitarian Committee founded by Roy with William Adam (Scottish missionary) — reflects Roy's universalist engagement with Christian theological ideas alongside Hindu reform

Sanskrit College Calcutta set up under Amherst23-28 on recommendation of Orientalist faction — Roy OPPOSES it (wants Western sciences, not classical learning); later transformed by Vidyasagar from within
Jyotirao Phule born (1827-1890)

Brahmo Samaj founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1828) — works against idolatry, priestcraft, polytheism + Sati; monotheism; Roy = Father of Modern India; uses Upanishads to argue authentic Hinduism is monotheistic; Brahmo Samaj initially avoids women's issues broadly + caste (considered too sensitive)

Bengal Sati Regulation (Regulation XVII) 1829 — under Bentinck28-35; makes Sati punishable as culpable homicide; Roy wins the scripture debate (Sati is murder per the Shastras); Bentinck pre-condition: must be proven from Indian scriptures first

Dharma Sabha founded by Radhakanta Deb specifically to oppose Sati abolition; sends petition to Privy Council in London -> petition rejected; among earliest instances of Indian groups using metropolitan legal system as battleground for Indian policy
Roy dies (1833) — two years before Macaulay's Minute finalised; his advocacy directly influences the 1835 English Education Act

Young Bengal's Society for Acquisition of General Knowledge under Tarachand Chakravarty (President) + Ramgopal Ghosh (VP) — founded 1838; Derozio died December 1831 (Eurasian teacher @ Hindu College; original name = Derozians/Ultra-Reformers/Radicals; 'Young Bengal' = retrospective label)
Vidyasagar earns title 'Vidyasagar' from Hindu Law Committee exam (1839)
David Hare dies of cholera in Calcutta (1842); Christian missionaries refuse burial; laid to rest within grounds of Presidency College; thousands join funeral procession; M.G. Ranade born 1842
Durgamohan Das (Bengal); also: Bombay Millhands Association context later
Jyotirao Phule opens India's 1st girls' school @ Pune (1 January 1848) with wife Savitribai Phule as 1st female teacher; stones + dung thrown at Savitribai on way to school daily
1848: Paramhansa Mandali founded in Maharashtra — relies purely on rationality; fails for same reason as Young Bengal (religious society cannot be moved by reason alone)
Bethune School for Women set up by J.E. Drinkwater Bethune (Law Member of Dalhousie's Council + President of Council of Education); Vidyasagar closely associated + serves as Secretary

Lex Loci Act 1850 (Caste Disabilities Removal Act 1850) — protects property + inheritance rights of converts; before this Act, Hindus who converted forfeited right to ancestral property; Act removes this deterrent to conversion; removes strongest social-economic hold of orthodox community on individual choice

Vidyasagar becomes Principal of Sanskrit College Calcutta (1851) — under Dalhousie's tenure; threatens resignation if lower-caste students not admitted; introduces Western sciences alongside Sanskrit; 20 Model Schools set up; ends physical punishment in schools
Vidyasagar writes book on miseries of widowhood + submits petition with 1,000 signatures for widow remarriage law (1855)
Vidyasagar submits petition with 25,000 signatures to LG of Bengal demanding ban on polygamy (1855); follows with two books against polygamy in 1871 + 1873
Hindu Widow Remarriage Act (26 July 1856) — under Dalhousie48-56; first remarriage under Act takes place 7 December 1856; Vidyasagar marries his own son to a widow

Vidyasagar becomes Inspector of Schools (Bengal 1856) — under Dalhousie's tenure; Nov 1857-May 1858: opens 25 schools for female education with 1,300 girls enrolled at any given time (even during 1857 Revolt); attendance, books + transport all free
IPC Section 375 (1860) — sets minimum age of consummation at 10 years (statutory rape definition); earliest legislative attempt on child marriage age
Phule sets up infanticide prevention centre (1863) — safe home for anonymous deliveries for pregnant widows + survivors of sexual assault + orphanage; practical institutional solution

Brahmo Samaj splits — 1st split 1866: (i) Keshab Chandra Sen forms Brahmo Samaj of India (1866) — radical: wants break from Hinduism, inter-caste marriages, mass outreach; (ii) Debendranath Tagore forms Adi Brahmo Samaj (1866) — gradualist: remains within Hindu fold; Vishnu Shastri Pandit forms widow remarriage society in Maharashtra 1866 — orthodox rivals immediately set up counter-organisation

Prarthana Samaj founded 1867 by Atmaram Pandurang with help of Keshab Chandra Sen — Brahmoism transplanted to Maharashtra; gradual reform from within Hinduism (Debendranath Tagore's method, not Keshab's); membership: Western-educated Marathi Brahmins + Gujarati merchants + Parsi community; M.G. Ranade = most important figure; R.G. Bhandarkar + K.T. Telang assist; opens branches in Gujarat, Karachi + Madras
Female Infanticide Act 1870 by Mayo69-72 — passed but legislation alone cannot reach problem at its roots; girl-child mortality continues through nutritional neglect
Vidyasagar's 1st book against polygamy (1871); 2nd book 1873

Brahmo Marriages Act 1872 — under Mayo69-72 (Mayo assassinated Feb 1872 before Act passed; credit for groundwork belongs to his administration); gives legal validity to inter-caste marriages + widow remarriages; CATCH: bride + groom must first formally leave Hinduism -> severely limits real-world impact

Jyotirao Phule writes Gulamgiri (Slavery 1873) — equates condition of Shudras + Ati-Shudras with African American slaves; dedicates to American abolitionists; founds Satyashodhak Samaj 1873 (Truth-Seekers' Society) — challenges orthodoxy + caste system; starts newspaper Din Bandhu (1877) for oppressed classes

Arya Samaj founded 10 April 1875 @ Bombay by Swami Dayanand Saraswati (original name: Mool Shankar; from Gujarat; 20 years wandering -> Mathura -> Swami Virajananda directs to Vedas); Satyarth Prakash (Light of Meaning of Truth 1875) — written in Hindi for mass reach; attacks idolatry, polytheism, animal sacrifice, untouchability, child marriage, birth-based caste; critically examines Christianity, Islam, Jainism, Buddhism; motto: 'Krinvanto Vishvam Aryam' (Make this world noble)

Sir Syed Ahmed Khan founds Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College @ Aligarh (1875) — later Aligarh Muslim University (AMU); institutional heart of Aligarh Movement; social positions: supports widow remarriage, opposes triple talaq, polygamy, purdah, child marriage; advocates Western + female education; political position: India = summation of Quams (nations/communities); Hindu + Muslim Quam separate; Muslim Quam deserves special status
Din Bandhu newspaper launched by Phule (1877) for oppressed classes
Arya Samaj fails in east + west India; succeeds in Punjab + NW Provinces especially post-Dayananda's death 1883

Phule's Cultivator's Whipcord (1881) — shows how religion + bureaucracy + economic exploitation combine to grind down Shudra cultivators; advocates economic self-reliance + land reforms; night schools for peasants

Poona Sarvajanik Sabha founded by Ranade in 1870 (one of earliest regional political organisations, precursor to INC; focused on rights of peasants in Bombay Presidency; prominent members include Tilak + Gopal Hari Deshmukh); Indian National Social Conference — 1st session held alongside INC's Madras session 1887; argues social reform on Doctrine of Logic (reason, evidence, human welfare) not religious authority

Swami Dayanand Saraswati dies 1883 — Arya Samaj becomes more popular + more aggressive after his death; disciples establish Dayanand Anglo-Vedic (DAV) College Trust; 1st DAV High School opens @ Lahore 1 June 1886 (Lala Hans Raj headmaster; Shaheed Bhagat Singh educated at DAV School Lahore)

Rakhmabai Case 1884-1888 — married as infant; husband takes to court for denial of conjugal rights; Rakhmabai fights back (marriage invalid); Malabari's Rakhmabai Defence Committee supports her; orthodox Hindus support husband; she loses in court (post-1857 orthodox Hindu opinion strong enough); Queen Victoria herself overrules decision + dissolves marriage
events.full: Rakhmabai Case 1884-1888 — married as infant; husband takes to court for denial of conjugal rights; Rakhmabai fights back (marriage invalid); Malabari's Rakhmabai Defence Committee supports her; orthodox Hindus support husband; she loses in court (post-1857 orthodox Hindu opinion strong enough); Queen Victoria herself overrules decision + dissolves marriage (Prelims 2020: Age of Consent + Restitution of Conjugal Rights context, NOT women's education)

events.label: Ranade's Poona Sarvajanik Sabha 1870; Essays on Indian Economics (1898) — 1st systematic analysis of Indian economy from Indian perspective; Father of Indian Economics; Rise of Maratha Power — asserts Maratha cultural identity; Maharashtra Girls Education Society co-founded with R.G. Bhandarkar
Mohammadan Educational Congress set up by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (1886) — deliberate rival to INC (which he views as Hindu organisation)

1st DAV High School @ Lahore opens 1 June 1886 (Lala Hans Raj headmaster); Negative Revivalism post-1883: Pandit Lekh Ram + Pandit Guru Dutt run aggressive Shuddhi movement; Singh Sabha movement among Sikhs intensifies in response; Muslims launch Tanzim + Tabligh movements; Cow Protection Movement -> Cow Killing Riots 1893

Narayana Guru (1856-1928 born into Ezhava community, Travancore; denied temple entry + public roads + education) consecrates 1st temple @ Aruvippuram (1888) — Shiva idol; open to all castes; reply to upper-caste critics: 'This is not a Brahmin's Shiva. This is an Ezhava's Shiva.' — all without leaving Hinduism, without converting, without legislation

Phule dies 1890; Bombay Millhands Association co-founded by Phule + Narayan Lokhande (main founder 1890) — one of earliest organised efforts for rights of industrial workers in India (not formal trade union: no membership fees, formal rules, or funds)
Death of 11-year-old Phulmoni due to sexual abuse by husband (1890) brings child marriage issue to a head; Lansdowne88-94 introduces Age of Consent Bill 1891

Age of Consent Act 1891 (Act X of 1891, March 1891) — raises minimum age of consummation to 12 years; Tilak argues British have no right to interfere in Indian custom; R.G. Bhandarkar's research shows Dharmashastras permit marriage after puberty; Bill passed despite fierce controversy

Ramakrishna Mission founded by Swami Vivekananda 1897 (Ramakrishna Paramhansa = temple priest, not Western-educated; offered undiluted Hindu spiritual tradition to educated Bengalis disillusioned by Chakri/office work); Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions @ Chicago 1893 — argues Western materialism + Indian spiritualism must come together; makes him internationally famous; also: Cow Killing Riots 1893 (result of Cow Protection Movement)

Ramakrishna Mission founded by Swami Vivekananda (1897) — named after his Guru; dual purpose: spread Vedanta + social service; 'service of Jiva is worship of Shiva'; concept of Daridra Narayan (God residing in the poor); Sister Nivedita (Margaret Noble, Irish disciple) supports Anushilan Samiti revolutionary groups in Bengal; Nivedita School @ Calcutta opened 1898
Nivedita School @ Calcutta opened by Sister Nivedita (1898)
By 1900: only 38 widow remarriages had taken place in Maharashtra; reform succeeded only in Haryana (where widow remarriage was already accepted practice)
Vidyasagar dies 1891; M.G. Ranade dies 1901
Shri Narayana Dharma Paripalana Yogam (SNDP) founded 1903 by Narayana Guru — for social, educational + economic upliftment of Ezhava community + lower castes broadly

Jamia Millia Islamia founded 1920 @ Aligarh in United Provinces — breakaway from AMU when Gandhi calls students to leave British-supported institutions during Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22); AMU stays pro-British; breakaway group founds Jamia Millia — anti-colonial Islamic activism, pro-independence; founding leaders: Abdul Majid Khwaja, Maulana Mehmud Hasan, Maulana Md Ali, Hakim Ajmal Khan, Dr Mukhtar Ahmed Ansari
Gandhi visits Narayana Guru @ Sivagiri ashram (1925) — describes him as one of greatest men he ever met; Narayana Guru dies 1928
Sharda Act (Child Marriage Restraint Act) 1929 — raises minimum marriage age to 14 for girls + 18 for boys
Calcutta Madrasa set up by Warren Hastings73-85 (1781) — study of Arabic, Persian + Islamic law; trains Indians to assist EIC in ruling India the Indian way
Asiatic Society of Bengal founded by William Jones (1784) — Puisne Judge @ Calcutta SC; for Oriental research; Dwarkanath Tagore (grandfather of Rabindranath) was member

Sanskrit College @ Benaras (Banaras Sanskrit College) set up by Jonathan Duncan 1791 — trains Pandits for administering Hindu law; administrative need of colonial state; NOT the Calcutta Sanskrit College (1824)
Fort William College, Calcutta set up by Wellesley98-05 (1800) — trains newly-arrived British civil servants in Indian languages, laws + customs; William Carey taught Bengali + Sanskrit here
Charter Act 1813 — legalises entry of Christian missionaries + mandates Rs 1 lakh p.a. on education; push to westernisation begins

Hindu College Calcutta (1817) — co-founded by Sir Edward Hyde East + David Hare + Raja Ram Mohan Roy; later Presidency College (where Derozio taught); Calcutta School Book Society 1817 (David Hare + Radhakanta Deb)
Sanskrit College Calcutta (1824) — set up under Amherst23-28; Roy opposes it; Vidyasagar later transforms from within (Principal 1851); Hare School founded 1818 by David Hare
General Assembly's Institution Calcutta founded by Alexander Duff 1830 (NOT Hindu College 1817 — UPSC trap); later Scottish Church College
Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education (1835) — settled in favour of Western education in English; Orientalists vs Anglicists debate resolved; Roy's advocacy influences it (Roy died 1833)

English Education Act 1835 — goal: promote European literature + science; medium: English only; no more govt money for Oriental works; no new stipends for Oriental institutions (existing institutions not abolished); Downward Filtration Theory: educate urban elite only; they transmit downward at no additional State cost; high fees block urban poor; rural areas get nothing

William Adam's 3 Reports on Vernacular Education (1835-38) — appointed by Bentinck28-35; surveys indigenous education in Bengal + Bihar; core findings: (i) over 1,00,000 Pathshalas in Bengal + Bihar alone — almost every village had one; (ii) children of all castes (except absolute lowest/untouchables) often sat together; (iii) extreme flexibility: no fixed fee (paid in kind — rice/grain), no printed books, no separate buildings, no annual exams, no timetables (suspended during harvest — synchronised with agrarian calendar); (iv) curriculum: strictly functional — basic literacy, arithmetic, accounts; flatly contradicts 'India was illiterate before British' colonial narrative Knowledge of English made compulsory for government jobs (1844) — serious blow to vernacular languages
Roorkee Engineering College set up 1847 (became university 1949; IIT Roorkee 2001)
Bethune School for Women 1849 — J.E. Drinkwater Bethune; Vidyasagar as Secretary; brings female education under grants-in-aid
Vidyasagar becomes Principal of Sanskrit College Calcutta 1851 — opens to non-Brahmin students; introduces Western sciences

Wood's Despatch (WD1854) — 'Magna Carta of English Education in India'; from Charles Wood (President of BoC1784) to Dalhousie48-56; most comprehensive education policy statement; KEY SHIFT from Macaulay's Downward Filtration Theory: (i) Western education for masses in VERNACULARS at elementary level; vernaculars + English at high school; English at college level; (ii) sets up Education Departments in Provincial govts; (iii) Teacher Training programmes; (iv) continues female education support; (v) sets up universities in Madras, Bombay + Calcutta; real goals: cheap clerks + spread Western culture + glorify British rule + moral development; IMPACT: Dalhousie lays groundwork; 3 universities officially opened in 1857 under Canning56-62; 2 more follow: Panjab University Lahore (1882) + Allahabad University (1887); overall result: FAILURE (female education neglected, high fees block mass education, mass infrastructure never built)
Vidyasagar becomes Inspector of Schools (Bengal) 1856 — under Dalhousie's tenure

Bombay, Madras + Calcutta universities officially established 1857 — under Canning56-62 (groundwork = Dalhousie); Bankim Chandra Chatterjee + Joddu Nath Bose among 1st graduates of Calcutta University 1858
Bankim Chandra Chatterjee + Joddu Nath Bose among 1st graduates of Calcutta University 1858

Subject of Education transferred to Provinces 1870; British decrease funding for higher education in Bengal (real reason: educated Indians producing increasingly nationalist writing; Anglo-Indian press calls college-educated Indians 'seditious')

Under Ripon80-84, education made free enterprise — private institutions can open schools + colleges with State financial assistance; Hunter / Indian Education Commission (1882-83): (i) transfer education to Municipalities (urban) + District Boards (rural); (ii) focus on mass vernacular education; (iii) strengthen female education; (iv) divide secondary into literary + vocational; (v) special fund for backward communities (rejected); Panjab University Lahore 1882
Allahabad University 1887
Ranade's Essays on Indian Economics (1898) — 1st systematic analysis of Indian economy from Indian perspective

Indian Universities Act 1904 — Curzon99-05; universities under direct govt control; govt can veto/amend Senate regulations; decreased fellows per university; most fellows to be govt nominees; stricter affiliation for private colleges (attacks nationalist + Swadeshi institutions); Rs 5 lakh p.a. for education; also: Indian Agricultural Research Institute @ Pusa Bihar 1905 (funded by Henry Phipps)
Indian Agricultural Research Institute @ Pusa Bihar (1905)

Bill to make primary education compulsory moved by Gopal Krishna Gokhale in Imperial Legislative Council 1911 — rejected; UPSC A/R 1998: Assertion correct (1st such Bill rejected 1911); Reason CORRECT (Govt alarmed: mass literacy would breed political consciousness + discontent)

Sadler Commission (1917-19) — Dr Michael Sadler; key recommendations: (i) college entry after class 12 (not class 10); (ii) strengthen secondary education; (iii) universities must be residential, autonomous + unitary; 7 new universities established under Chelmsford16-21 including Osmania University (Princely State of Hyderabad); GOI Act 1919 formally gives Education to Provinces GOI Act 1919 — formally gives subject of Education to Provinces

Hartog Committee (1929) — rapid growth in schools + colleges at cost of quality; at end of class 8 students should choose vocational or academic; only deserving students proceed to class 9; strengthen primary education

Wardha Scheme of National Education (1937) — proposed by INC when it forms govts in several provinces; shaped by Gandhian philosophy; developed by Zakir Hussain Committee: (i) Learning by Doing — activity-based; (ii) English only after class 8; (iii) handicraft skilling as regular curriculum; (iv) free + compulsory education in vernaculars until 7 years of age; sharp contrast with Macaulay's vision

Sargent Plan 1944 (Sargent Report) — John Sargent (Educational Advisor to GoI); last major education blueprint of British era; 40-year timeline to achieve 100% literacy (furiously rejected by Indian leaders); structure: Pre-Primary (3-6); Basic Elementary free/universal (6-14): Junior Basic 6-11 + Senior Basic 11-14; High School (11-17, selected): Academic stream + Technical/Vocational stream; University: 3-year undergraduate; also: adult literacy within 20 years; 1st British report explicitly mandating education of physically + mentally differently-abled; nationalist criticism: 40-year timeline = insult; British drafted utopian plan without allocating funds
By 1921: 92% illiteracy; only 2% of women literate — outcome of 86 years of British education policy

phases.label: PRINT CULTURE — NEWSPAPERS, ACTS & KEY OFFICIALS (1556–1942)

events.label: Printing press arrives in India (1556) — brought by Portuguese to Goa; operated by Joao de Bustamante; initially for religious texts; over two centuries before it becomes tool for political + social debate

Bengal Gazette (English) launched in Calcutta by James Augustus Hicky (1780) — India's 1st newspaper; shut down 1782 by Warren Hastings73-85 for criticising the British; press + power in conflict from the very beginning
Calcutta Gazette founded 1784 by Francis Gladwin — EIC patronage; semi-official organ
Bombay Herald founded 1789 by William Ashburner — 1st newspaper in Bombay; renamed Bombay Gazette 1791
Bombay Courier founded 1790 by Luke Ashburner (William's brother); later merged with Times of India

Censorship Press Act by Wellesley98-05 (1799) — wartime pre-censorship during Anglo-Mysore Wars; UPSC A/R 1998: Act CORRECT; Reason (alarmed about Indian Renaissance/nationalism) FALSE: 1799 regulation was wartime censorship during French Revolutionary Wars era (anxiety about French sympathisers + revolutionary ideas in Calcutta's Anglo-Indian press); Indian nationalism was NOT yet a political phenomenon in 1799; correct answer: A true, R false
Sambad Kaumudi (Bengali) founded 1821 by Roy — advocates social reforms
Mirat-ul-Akhbar (Persian) founded 1822 by Roy — promotes liberal ideas
Licensing Regulations by Acting GG John Adams (1823) — requires licences for press operation; forces closure of Roy's Mirat-ul-Akhbar
Udant Martand 1826 — India's 1st Hindi newspaper (weekly); founded by Pandit Jugal Kishore Shukla
General Assembly's Institution Calcutta founded by Alexander Duff 1830 — NOT Hindu College 1817
events.full: General Assembly's Institution Calcutta founded by Alexander Duff 1830 — NOT Hindu College 1817 (UPSC trap)

events.label: Metcalfe Act (Press Liberation Act) 1835 — by Charles Metcalfe (GG 1835-36); revokes licensing laws; earns him title 'Liberator of the Indian Press'
Samachar Sudha Varshan 1854 — 1st daily Hindi newspaper; founded by Shyam Sundar Sen
Neel Darpan (1860) — Bengali novel by Dinabandhu Mitra (context: indigo plantation conditions)

ASI (Archaeological Survey of India) founded 1861 by Alexander Cunningham as Director-General; reorganised as permanent department 1871; documents, excavates + preserves India's built heritage; 5 field antiquarians tested as block by UPSC: Alexander Rea + A.H. Longhurst + Robert Sewell + James Burgess + Walter Elliot
events.full: ASI (Archaeological Survey of India) founded 1861 by Alexander Cunningham as Director-General; reorganised as permanent department 1871; documents, excavates + preserves India's built heritage; 5 field antiquarians tested as block by UPSC: Alexander Rea + A.H. Longhurst + Robert Sewell + James Burgess + Walter Elliot (Prelims 2023: associated with archaeological excavations NOT English Press / churches / railways)

events.label: Indian Mirror (English) 1861-62 — founded by Manomohan Ghosh; major backing from Debendranath Tagore; Keshab Chandra Sen plays major role in early years Bengalee (English) 1862 — founded by Girish Chandra Ghosh; bought by Surendranath Banerjee 1879 -> transformed into powerful nationalist voice
Durgesh Nandini 1865 — 1st Bengali novel by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee

Amrita Bazar Patrika (Bengali + English from 1878) 1868 — founded by Sisir Kumar Ghosh; major nationalist publication; converts overnight from Bengali to English in 1878 specifically to escape Vernacular Press Act
Vernacular Press Act (Gagging Act) by Lytton76-80 (1878) — targets regional-language newspapers specifically; Som Prakash, Dacca Prakash + Samachar directly affected
The Hindu (English) founded 1878 in Madras by G. Subramania Iyer + M. Veeraraghavachariar — started as weekly; became daily 1889
Kesari (Marathi) + Mahratta (English) 1881 — founded by Bal Gangadhar Tilak; promotes nationalism
VPA repealed by Ripon80-84 (1882); Swadesamitran (Tamil) 1882 — founded by G. Subramania Iyer

Anandamath 1882 — novel by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee; gives India concept of Bharat Mata (Mother India as goddess) + contains Bande Mataram (anthem of Indian National Movement); Bankim = 1st graduate of Calcutta University (established 1857)
Sudharak (Marathi) 1887 — edited by Gopal Krishna Gokhale
Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions @ Chicago 1893

Cinema arrives in India: 7 July 1896 — Times of India carries advertisement of Lumiere Brothers ('marvel of the century, wonder of the world living photographic pictures'); 1st cinematograph screening @ Watson's Hotel, Bombay; Prelims 1996: date = 7 July 1896, location = Bombay (NOT Calcutta), brothers = Lumiere
Newspaper (Incitement of Offences) Act 1908 — under Minto05-10; allows seizure of presses inciting violence

Indian Press Act 1910 — under Minto05-10; mandates security deposits from newspapers; fines + confiscation of printing presses for publications criticising colonial policies; repealed 1921 after Tej Bahadur Sapru Committee recommendations
Al-Hilal (Urdu) 1912 — founded by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad (NOT Comrade = Md Ali Jauhar; NOT Indian Sociologist = Shyamji Krishna Varma; NOT Zamindar = Zafar Ali Khan); Prelims 2008
Raja Harishchandra (1913) — 1st Indian feature film; Dadasaheb Phalke; Gitanjali 1913 by Rabindranath Tagore

Jana Gana Mana — composed by Tagore in Bengali; translated into English by Tagore himself @ Madanapalle (present-day Andhra Pradesh) in 1919; also set to music @ Madanapalle; Prelims 2021 trap: Madanapalle = Tagore + Jana Gana Mana English translation (NOT Theosophical Society HQ which = Adyar Madras)
Indian Press Act 1910 repealed 1921
Indian Press (Emergency Powers) Act 1931 — under Irwin26-31; suppresses coverage of Civil Disobedience Movement (1930-34)
Foreign Relations Act 1932 — bars criticism of foreign govts allied with Britain
Press Regulating Act 1942 — wartime censorship during WW II

chapters.title: Pre-1857 Peasant & Tribal Revolts and Post-1857 Tribal Uprisings

sections.title: Understanding the Character of Pre-1857 Revolts

phases.label: CIVIL UPRISINGS — LED BY DISPOSSESSED ELITE (1778–1817)

events.label: Treaty of Faizabad 1775 — Benaras annexed by EIC; Raja Chait Singh of Benaras made big zamindar under EIC; owns military + fort; later PS1793 formally brings Benaras into Bengal-BOB-North Madras-Benaras revenue settlement

Raja Chait Singh Revolt, Benaras — estates seized due to non-payment of LR; revolts; Hastings73-85 confronts him; crushed Bishnupur + Birbhum Revolts, Bengal — local zamindars + ryots squeezed by revenue demands (PS1793 precursors) rise against EIC revenue machinery; minor in scale but UPSC distractors — worth recognising by name + date

Nawab Wazir Ali — deposed Nawab of Awadh (ruled only 1797-98 before being replaced by Sadat Ali Khan II on Shore93-98's orders); revolts 1799 with peasant support Poligar Revolts, South India — Poligars = traditionally autonomous local chiefs in South India; British Rule of Law + equality before law hurt their elevated social status (same grievance as taluqdars in 1857); Ryotwari settlement takes away their lands; high LR demands on peasants bring popular participation; revolts + crushed

Post-2nd Anglo-Maratha War — SA imposed British Resident on Maratha states; Bundela chiefs suffering under Resident interference revolt with peasant support Dewan Veluthampi Dalawa Revolt — after SA of 1805 with Travancore; British Resident begins interfering in Travancore's internal affairs (breach of SA's promise of non-interference); Veluthampi (Dewan of Travancore) revolts alongside Nair troops + peasants; Kundara Proclamation (Jan 1809); crushed 1809

Paika Rebellion, Khurda, Odisha — Paikas = traditional landed militia/warrior class of Odisha; led by Bakshi Jagabandhu (military commander of Raja of Khurda) + marginalised zamindars; goal: restore lost hereditary privileges, authority + rent-free estates (Jagirs); massive grassroots support from peasants + salt makers + tribal Kondhs of Ghumsar -> true multi-class uprising; EIC grievances: stripped Paikas of rent-free tenures after conquering Odisha 1803; extortionate revenue in silver (Sicca) not traditional cowrie shells; banned local sea-salt production (monopoly -> sky-high prices); dethroned revered Raja of Khurda; rebels: destroyed police stations, courts + salt monopoly offices; briefly captured Puri; forced EIC forces to retreat; proclaimed Raja of Khurda as sovereign; British declared martial law; crushed by 1818; Bakshi Jagabandhu leads jungle guerrilla war until surrendering 1825; heavily debated as candidate for India's true 'First War of Independence'

phases.label: PEASANT REVOLTS — LED BY PEASANTS THEMSELVES (1760–1831)

events.label: Sanyasi + Fakir Rebellion, North Bengal + Bihar — peaks around 1800 with ~50,000 participants; two groups: Dasnami Sanyasis (Hindus; peasants + small traders) + Madari Fakirs (Muslims; held revenue-free/rent-free tenures now ended by EIC); cooperate despite different religions because economic grievances identical + philosophical common ground; grievances: high LR, high rents post-PS1793, EIC monopoly over domestic trade in Bengal; Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's Anandamath (1882) inspired by this rebellion; Vande Mataram from Anandamath -> anthem of INM; Prelims 2006: Anandamath = Sanyasi Rebellion (NOT Bhil uprising / NOT Rangpur-Dinapur / NOT Bishnupur-Birbhum)

Rangpur Rebellion, North Bengal — Farming System of 1772 unleashed revenue farmers Debi Singh + Gobinda Singh on peasantry; British officials collude with them; came after GBF 1770 which already broke economic spine of peasantry; ACTION: Rangpur peasants target grain stores of Debi Singh + Gobinda Singh (loot them); attack prisons + free imprisoned ryots; attack local courts (targeted: knew exactly what oppressed them); run own government funded by self-imposed taxes; RESULT: crushed by EIC

Mysore Revolt — Wodeyar Dynasty restored 1799 after Tipu82-99 defeat; SA 1799 requires heavy annual subsidy to British; Wodeyar government imposes high LR to meet this; peasants revolt against both Wodeyar administration + British agents; RESULT: EIC crushes revolt (obligation under SA 1799 to protect ruler)

Pagal Panthi Revolt, East Bengal — leaders: Karim Shah -> Tipu Shah; grievance: against zamindars for high rents, illegal abwabs + denial of occupancy rights; Tipu Shah promises lower rents once zamindars + British defeated (political programme delivered through religious leadership); RESULT: crushed by EIC Titu Mir, 24 Parganas — belongs to Wahabi sect; teaches reformist philosophy of Shah Waliullah of Delhi; followers = poor peasants with distinct physical identity (unique beard + dress = marker of resistance); grievances: tax on beards by local zamindar + oppression by indigo planters, zamindars + British officials; action: set up own government with self-imposed taxes; built famous bamboo fort @ Narkelberia village; RESULT: crushed by EIC army
Faraizi Movement, Bengal — father-son-grandson: Haji Shariatullah (1830s) -> Dudu Mian (mid-century)

-> Naya Mian (1870s); belief: Quran = only true source of Islamic law; purge Islam of un-Islamic practices = return to original faith; grievances: oppression by indigo planters, zamindars + British officials; Dudu Mian's slogan: 'land belongs to God -> any rent or tax on land is ungodly' (economic injustice framed as sin = far more powerful mobilising argument); set up own government, courts + collected own taxes; RESULT: crushed; W.W. Hunter's The Indian Musalmans argued British neglect of Muslims contributed to Faraizi movement + British should favour Muslims for political stability -> long-term policy consequences for Hindu-Muslim relations

Moplah / Mopilla Revolts, Malabar coast — Moplahs = Muslim ryots of Malabar; Janmies = Brahmin princely families = big landlords; traditionally land earnings shared among Janmies + Moplahs + supervisors (all had customary rights); British rule: Malabar annexed after 3rd Anglo-Mysore War (1789-92); British recognised only Janmies as legal landowners; Moplahs lost ALL customary rights overnight; became exploited tenants; British Orientalists give ideological cover (Lord Parshuram gifted all land to Janmies); character: economically-driven revolt takes communal colour because oppressor + oppressed have different religious identities; 1921 Moplah Rebellion recurs during Non-Cooperation Movement (see NCM chapter); RESULT: crushed by EIC army

Pahariya Revolt, Rajmahal Hills — Pahariyas = earliest tribals to resist British encroachment; hill-dwelling hunter-gatherers + shifting cultivators; EIC extends revenue collection + admin control into Rajmahal Hills; revolt against destruction of autonomy + livelihood; British respond with military force + containment policy (push Pahariyas further into hills)

Bhil Revolts, Khandesh + Rajputana Hills, Western India — British annexation of Maratha territories after 3rd Anglo-Maratha War 1818 brings Bhil homelands under direct EIC control; new LR demands + entry of plains-based moneylenders + curtailment of traditional forest rights -> series of uprisings 1818-1831; British suppress militarily + deploy Bhil Corps (locally recruited force) as pacification strategy Ramosi Uprising, Western Ghats near Pune — Ramosis = hill tribe; traditionally employed as watchmen + guards under Maratha state; lost customary occupations + status after British takeover of Maratha territories; dispossessed + marginalised; revolt against British authority 1822; localised but violent; put down by force

Khasi Uprising — leader: U Tirot Sing; grievance: British construction of Brahmaputra Valley-Sylhet Road brings influx of outsiders (British businesses, Indian agents, British officials) into Khasi territory; loss of Khasi land + disruption of way of life; RESULT: crushed Kol Uprising, Chhota Nagpur + Singhbhum — tribal autonomy of Kols destroyed by British rule; Raja of Chhotanagpur farms out tribal lands to merchants + moneylenders (outsiders called Suds); Kols lose customary land rights; ACTION: Kols target property of Suds (NOT their lives — tribals knew their oppressors); RESULT: crushed by army Kandh / Kondh Uprising, Odisha (Ghumsar/Kalahandi) — leader: Chakra Bisoi; grievance: British ban human sacrifice (practice tied to Kandhs' religious ritual of Meriah = sacrifice to Earth Goddess for good harvest); British view = humanitarian intervention; Kandhs' view = attack on religion + autonomy; prolonged resistance; RESULT: eventually crushed Santhal Hool / Rebellion, Rajmahal Hills (Jharkhand) — Santhals call homeland Damini-i-koh (skirts of the hills); British open it up for settlement bringing non-Santhal zamindars + moneylenders = Dikus (outsiders); railway + road construction devours Santhal land; leaders: brothers Sido Murmu + Kanhu Murmu; ACTION 1: 1855 Santhals give British FORMAL PRIOR WARNING (public declaration of revolt to come = political action not mere violence); ACTION 2: rise with bows + arrows against 'unholy trinity' (British + zamindars + moneylenders) to win back fatherland from Dikus; British authority collapses in region; British retaliate: burn villages + kill ~50,000 Santhals; RESULT: revolt crushed with extreme ferocity; POLITICAL IMPACT: separate administrative unit 'Santhal Parganas' created with formal protections for tribal culture + identity; restrictions imposed on transfer of Santhal land to non-tribals within Santhal Parganas (early form of protective land legislation acknowledging Diku problem); Prelims 2018: both measures correct = answer C

loss of Khasi land + disruption of way of life; RESULT: crushed Kol Uprising, Chhota Nagpur + Singhbhum — tribal autonomy of Kols destroyed by British rule; Raja of Chhotanagpur farms out tribal lands to merchants + moneylenders (outsiders called Suds); phases.label: KEY COLONIAL ACTS DRIVING TRIBAL DISPOSSESSION

events.label: PS1793 + Farming System 1772 — Bengal peasants: zamindar made legal landowner; ryot has no occupancy rights; high rents, abwabs, eviction at will; Rent Act 1859 supposed to correct (12-year occupancy right) but poorly implemented
Charter Act 1813 — Christian missionaries enter India; adds religious dimension to tribal economic grievances

Indigo System — in Bengal until 1860; Bihar until 1918; European planters force ryots to cultivate indigo; loan at outset -> ryot always obligated (bonded labour logic); indigo exhausts soil; sold back to planter below market rate; perpetual indebtedness
Rent Act 1859 — occupancy right for ryots who cultivated same plot continuously >12 years; POORLY IMPLEMENTED in Bengal; zamindars find loophole: evict just before 12 years

Indian Forests Act 1878 (under Lytton76-80) — divides forests into 3 categories: (1) Reserved Forests: most commercially valuable; ALL traditional rights extinguished; no grazing, no firewood, no Jhum; sole purpose = unhindered commercial timber extraction for railway boom (each mile of railway track = ~2,000 wooden sleepers); (2) Protected Forests: commercial potential but too much existing local usage to close immediately; permitted unless specifically prohibited; transitional category (many quietly upgraded to Reserved over time); (3) Village Forests: forests assigned to specific village communities; very few actually created; colonial state dictates strict rules on usage; ownership never surrendered; LEGAL MASTERSTROKE: transformed customary rights (exercised for generations) into 'privileges granted by mercy of colonial state' -> collecting firewood / grazing a cow / clearing small patch for subsistence crop = trespass on ancestral land; Forest Rights Act 2006 attempts to begin correcting what this Act did customary right; British claim monopoly over manufacture + sale of all intoxicating liquors + drugs; auction right to tap palm trees + sell liquor to highest-bidding contractors; contractors raise prices steeply to recover investment; traditional brewing without govt licence = criminalised; tribal communities' drinks (toddy/mahua) tied to religious rituals, festivals + daily nutrition; excise duties on liquor = 2nd largest source of provincial revenue (after LR); grievance feeds temperance/anti-liquor strand of INM (Gandhi's call to picket liquor shops in NCM + CDM)

phases.note: Abkari System — before British rule: brewing local liquor from palm sap (toddy) or mahua flowers =

events.label: Rampa Rebellion Phase 1, Rampa Hills, Andhra — Muttadars (local estate holders, roughly = Poligars/Taluqdars) lead with popular participation; grievances: (i) commercial exploitation of forests; (ii) land acquisition for road construction; (iii) loss of lands to moneylenders + merchants; (iv) prohibition of Podu cultivation (shifting cultivation = Jhum equivalent); (v) restriction on use of forest resources; (vi) tax on toddy (Abkari system); RESULT: crushed by 1880

Munda Ulugulan (Great Tumult), Chhota Nagpur — leader: Birsa Munda; grievances: loss of lands to outsiders + oppression by British officials + missionary activities of Christian missionaries in tribal areas; RELIGION: people believe Birsa has supernatural healing powers + British bullets will turn to water when fired at him (psychologically necessary: makes resistance feel possible against vastly more powerful enemy); POLITICAL SYMBOLISM: Birsa chose Christmas 1899 to launch Ulugulan (deliberate: rising against British power on most sacred day of religion missionaries were using to erode Munda identity); RESULT: crushed by British; Prelims 2020: 'Ulgulan' or 'Great Tumult' = Birsa Munda's Revolt 1899-1900 (NOT 1857 revolt / NOT Mappila 1921 / NOT Indigo Revolt 1859-60)

Rampa Rebellion Phase 2 — 1920: Rampa tribals' movement merges into Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement (NCM); form of Civil Disobedience = violation of forest laws; leadership: Alluri Sitarama Raju (Andhra)
After NCM withdrawn 1922 — Alluri Sitarama Raju concludes India can be liberated only by force; re-initiates Fituri (violent rebellion)
Alluri Sitarama Raju captured + executed (1924) — revolutionary martyr in Andhra tradition; celebrated in popular memory to this day

tables.title: ANCHOR TABLE: ALL PRE-1857 REVOLTS — QUICK REFERENCE

anchors: Key Pattern — Religion as Organiser (pre-1857 vacuum): Pre-1857 India had no political parties, newspapers with mass reach,
or formal organisations. Religion filled the organisational vacuum — it provided leadership, coordination, ideology, community +
habit of collective action. When a whole sect revolted, it already had all five. This is why so many revolts had religious framing even
when the core grievances were economic. After 1857: WEMC creates newspapers + political organisations (INC 1885) —
gradually replacing religion as the organiser.
Key Pattern — Indian Forests Act 1878 (structural dispossession): Railway boom = 2,000 wooden sleepers per mile = need
for absolute state control over best forests. 3 categories: Reserved (all rights extinguished) + Protected (transitional; many
upgraded to Reserved) + Village Forests (very few created; strict rules). Legal masterstroke: customary rights -> 'privileges granted
by mercy of colonial state' -> collecting firewood = trespass on ancestral land. Forest Rights Act 2006 attempts to begin correcting
this.
n Prelims Alert (2006) — Anandamath + Sanyasi Rebellion: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's Anandamath (1882) was
inspired by the SANYASI REBELLION. NOT Bhil uprising / NOT Rangpur-Dinapur uprising / NOT Bishnupur-Birbhum rebellion.
Vande Mataram from Anandamath -> anthem of Indian National Movement.
n Prelims Alert (2018) — Santhal Parganas: After Santhal Hool 1855-56 was crushed, colonial government: (1) Created
separate administrative unit 'Santhal Parganas' with formal protections for tribal culture + identity. (2) Made it illegal for a Santhal to
transfer land to non-tribals within Santhal Parganas (early protective land legislation). Answer = Both 1 and 2 correct.
n Prelims Alert (2020) — 'Ulgulan' / 'Great Tumult': Ulgulan = Birsa Munda's Revolt of 1899-1900 in Chhota Nagpur. NOT the
Revolt of 1857 / NOT Mappila Rebellion of 1921 / NOT Indigo Revolt of 1859-60. Birsa chose Christmas 1899 as political
symbolism against missionary activities eroding Munda identity.

events.label: PS1793 — Sunset Clause: Zamindar loses land on non-payment by deadline; Kunwar Singh of Jagdishpur, Bihar loses lands under this clause; bitter grievance feeding into 1857
Charter Act 1813 — Christian missionaries enter India; presence in cantonments from 1813 creates anxiety about forced conversion among sepoys
Punjab annexed — Punjabi + Gurkha soldiers thereafter actively help British in 1857 (stayed loyal)

Enfield Rifle replaces Brown Bess musket — new cartridge (greased with tallow) must be bitten before loading; rumours: cow + pig fat used in grease; land on already-fertile ground of fear that British engineering loss of Hindu + Muslim identity to ease conversion; Bombay + Madras regiments stay quiet in 1857

Canning56-62 announces Mughals to be called only 'Princes' henceforth + will vacate Red Fort — signals end of Mughal symbolic sovereignty; allowance for serving outside home region abolished (double blow: economic + religious — upper-caste men feared loss of caste serving far from home or crossing water)

Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act 1856 + earlier: Sati Abolition Act 1829 + Lex Loci Act 1850 (gives inheritance rights on conversion to another religion = incentivises Christian conversion) — all seen as direct interference in religion

Annexation of Awadh — single largest source of recruits for Bengal Army was Awadh; nearly every family had a member in British Indian Army; annexation felt like personal betrayal; summary settlement fixed LR without field surveys -> unreasonable demands; peasants unable to pay -> lands auctioned or lost to moneylenders

Mangal Pandey (sepoy, 34th Bengal Native Infantry BNI, Barrackpur near Calcutta) fires at European officers; fellow sepoys REFUSE to arrest him; Mangal Pandey hanged 8 April 1857; Jemadar Ishwari Prasad (refused to restrain Pandey) hanged 22 April 1857; 34th BNI disbanded as collective punishment
Sepoys @ Meerut MUTINY — march to Delhi next day; proclaim Bahadur Shah Zafar37-57 (last Mughal Emperor; 1837-1857) as Emperor of Hindustan
By end of May: revolt spreads across NW Provinces + Awadh; civil population joins; British rule collapses across large swathe of north + central India
Delhi falls — British recapture Delhi 20 September 1857; Delhi = symbolic heart of revolt; when Delhi falls, symbolic heart falls with it
Revolt broadly continues until spring 1858

WEMC (Western Educated Middle Class) OPPOSES the revolt — believes in benevolence of British rule; benefits from new economy + jobs; Prelims 1998: educated middle class OPPOSED the revolt Territories NOT affected by 1857 revolt: CHITTOR
